ipc-title__text: The stupid second coming of Sauron
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I should have been warned not to watch this TV series becaue unfortunately I watched a bit of the Lord of the Rings movies some years ago.What a garbage that was!And sooo stupid!The TV series is even worse than the movies and that says a lot!The third movie is basically the same as the second with some stupid orc armies trying to storm some castle with the same failed strategy again, while they could have just laid siege to it and waited for everyone in there to die of hunger and thirst.I never understood who this "Sauron" thing was anyway and what was so special about these rings.Perhaps because they never really tell you?They were always called "Rings of Power" - but what powers exactly?And why did this Sauron-eye-thing want to exterminate everyone in Middle Earth?And then? Hover above his mountain as some giant eye surrounded by orcs?Wait...couldn't he have just continued to do so without all the killing?And if this "One Ring" (what a creative name for one ring, duh) could only be destroyed in that volcano - why not just fly there with one of these giant birds and drop it in there?Could have saved me from watching three stupid movies.In my defense though, I always thought they would get better instead of worse.At least the production design, the actors and the direction was top notch - and you were being transferred into some wondrous fantasy world that was nice to look at for a short time, but nothing else.The TV series does not answer any questions you might have about the origin of it all.Nothing makes any sense and everything in that version of Middle Earth looks just horrible.The elves all have big and square heads with giant pointy ears.The costume design is cheap and everyone there looks like cosplayers.The overall production design is ridiculous and schmaltzy and has some cheap 1970s theme-park feel to it.The special effects look crappy and appear to have been made by one guy alone in his mother's basement on one very old computer.Or perhaps it was "The One Guy" with the power of "The One Computer" - as they would say in Middle Earth.The actors are all unknowns (for good reason) and perhaps were cast because they were cheap.And all are mis-cast. None of them is the right for the role they are supposed to portray - even if that role itself is stupid.Everything in this series feels out-of-place and just not right.There is no singular great vision - just a lot of untalented people creating a miserable fantasy world while telling a stupid story.That's why I switched off the first season half way through the first episode.Nevertheless I even thought to give the second season a try.To its credit I lasted there for one and a half episode.Only the parts when the Sauron-guy (who apparently is also some shape-shifting mud creature and not only some giant eye floating above some mountain) schemes and tries to reach his goals while pretending to be a human, are modestly interesting.The rest I skipped fast-forward because they were so stupid.There is some beardy old geezer wandering through the desert with some little girls with a lot of dirt in their hairs who seem to come from Ireland.What?Why do they speak with a thick Irish accent in Middle Earth???And what are they doing in the desert?Skip!Then there are these dwarves who for some stupid reason still live in some giant caves although there is some nice and sunny landscape right outside and even in Middle Earth the stone ages must be over.And they are all from Scotland!What?Why do they speak with a thick Scottish accent in Middle-Earth?And why don't they all look like pale vampires when they constantly live in a cave?And why are they all so small when the cave they live in is so huge?Skip!Then there are these ridiculous looking elves in their cosplay outfits and cheap hair styles.They are mostly standing around in their old 70s-theme-parks and they are just staring at each other while talking about some boring stuff at length.Over and over and over again.Skip!Then there are these stupid rings everyone is so keen about.The elves with the giant ears and square heads have made them for some reason....But why? And what are these rings even there for?Who knows?The only "power" these crappy rings right out of an old chewing gum vending machine have, is that everyone who puts them on looks at them bewildered and at length..."Uhhhhhh, look at this ring, uhhhhh, sooo powerful, uhhhhh.... sooo shiny......"Sooo stupid!Skip!Okay, I skipped all of that nonsense (and more) and watched only the Sauron-in-disguise-parts.Though I never understood what he really wanted or why he needed one of these stupid rings, I continued to watch because I thought maybe there is some kind of big reveal coming...Instead, this Sauron guy suddenly turns into some kind of elfish Jesus and he comes down from the heavens to the mere mortals and immortals ("immortals" - ipc-title__text: Would Tolkien hate it? Not so sure.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: In recent years many people seem terribly upset about the 'liberal politics being shoved down their throats'. One wonders what are they talking about? Ah, yes - LGBTQIA+ characters and a cast that is not exclusively white.And with the arrival of "The Rings of Power" here we go again. Apparently there is 'lack of believability'. Yes, hobbits, dwarfs, orcs, wizards, dragons and talking trees are all fine, perfectly normal and very, very realistic. The line is crossed when they sport different skin colour. I also find it very curious when someone assures you that they're not bigots, racists or homophobes but when they come home from work they turn to TV for a little bit of escapism. I get it, I have nothing against a bit of escapism, engage in it from time to time myself. One wonders what they're trying to escape from, because apparently the inclusion of diverse characters ruins everything and makes the escape impossible.But of course it's none of those ugly sentiments one might suspect - it's all to do with their wish to stay true to the original and respect the author who wouldn't like any of those progressive ideas and had he lived today he wouldn't include any of that pc nonsense in his work. They're sure of that. I find it a bit of a stretch because Tolkien was clearly a humanist subscribing to humanistic values who believed in peaceful coexistence and cooperation among many very different peoples.The show looks beautiful and considering the limits posed on the production (not having rights to most of Tolkien's work) I think Amazon has done pretty well. I look forward to seeing how the story will unfurl.As for my rating - I gave the show 10/10. Not because I think the show is perfect, but because I believe it deserves a fair chance and I don't think it should be dragged down by some people's narrow-minded world view.

ipc-title__text: The stupid second coming of Sauron

Hover above his mountain as some giant eye surrounded by orcs?Wait...couldn't he have just continued to do so without all the killing?And if this "One Ring" (what a creative name for one ring, duh) could only be destroyed in that volcano - why not just fly there with one of these giant birds and drop it in there?Could have saved me from watching three stupid movies.In my defense though, I always thought they would get better instead of worse.At least the production design, the actors and the direction was top notch - and you were being transferred into some wondrous fantasy world that was nice to look at for a short time, but nothing else.The TV series does not answer any questions you might have about the origin of it all.Nothing makes any sense and everything in that version of Middle Earth looks just horrible.The elves all have big and square heads with giant pointy ears.The costume design is cheap and everyone there looks like cosplayers.The overall production design is ridiculous and schmaltzy and has some cheap 1970s theme-park feel to it.The special effects look crappy and appear to have been made by one guy alone in his mother's basement on one very old computer.Or perhaps it was "The One Guy" with the power of "The One Computer" - as they would say in Middle Earth.The actors are all unknowns (for good reason) and perhaps were cast because they were cheap.And all are mis-cast. None of them is the right for the role they are supposed to portray - even if that role itself is stupid.Everything in this series feels out-of-place and just not right.There is no singular great vision - just a lot of untalented people creating a miserable fantasy world while telling a stupid story.That's why I switched off the first season half way through the first episode.Nevertheless I even thought to give the second season a try.To its credit I lasted there for one and a half episode.Only the parts when the Sauron-guy (who apparently is also some shape-shifting mud creature and not only some giant eye floating above some mountain) schemes and tries to reach his goals while pretending to be a human, are modestly interesting.The rest I skipped fast-forward because they were so stupid.There is some beardy old geezer wandering through the desert with some little girls with a lot of dirt in their hairs who seem to come from Ireland.What?Why do they speak with a thick Irish accent in Middle Earth???And what are they doing in the desert?Skip!Then there are these dwarves who for some stupid reason still live in some giant caves although there is some nice and sunny landscape right outside and even in Middle Earth the stone ages must be over.And they are all from Scotland!What?Why do they speak with a thick Scottish accent in Middle-Earth?And why don't they all look like pale vampires when they constantly live in a cave?And why are they all so small when the cave they live in is so huge?Skip!Then there are these ridiculous looking elves in their cosplay outfits and cheap hair styles.They are mostly standing around in their old 70s-theme-parks and they are just staring at each other while talking about some boring stuff at length.Over and over and over again.Skip!Then there are these stupid rings everyone is so keen about.The elves with the giant ears and square heads have made them for some reason....But why? And what are these rings even there for?Who knows?The only "power" these crappy rings right out of an old chewing gum vending machine have, is that everyone who puts them on looks at them bewildered and at length..."Uhhhhhh, look at this ring, uhhhhh, sooo powerful, uhhhhh.... sooo shiny......"Sooo stupid!Skip!Okay, I skipped all of that nonsense (and more) and watched only the Sauron-in-disguise-parts.Though I never understood what he really wanted or why he needed one of these stupid rings, I continued to watch because I thought maybe there is some kind of big reveal coming...Instead, this Sauron guy suddenly turns into some kind of elfish Jesus and he comes down from the heavens to the mere mortals and immortals ("immortals" - what???) of Middle Earth.Yes, they literally show you that, with clouds, rays of light, music and all.The reveal I thought was coming was in fact the stupid "second coming of Sauron" in front of some crappy CGI clouds.Now I've had it!Switch off!I even tried to read the books about the cheap "power rings" from an old chewing gum vending machine some years ago.And it is no wonder why the movies and the TV series are so bad considering the stupid source material.The author created a wonderful yet superficial fantasy world with lots of fancy names, characters and places - but he could not even come up with a decent and believable story to take place in that world.The fancy fantasy world can also not gloss over the fact that the people living there are really not very bright - to say the least.These Middle-Earthians are all a little bit, well, let's say, really stupid.For thousands of years they have not made any progress in science or within their primitive societies.While on the other continents around them, people there got rid of their stupid kings and queens and now have giant 8K TV sets to watch crappy fantasy shows on, the Middle-Earth-Dumbos still (literally) live in caves, have never heard of democracy and their greatest achievement after thousands of years is ......... NOTHING.Oh, my...what a stupid story about some veeery stupid people!And while the stupid movies are a letdown from the stupid books, with the stupid series, the ring-saga has reached its stupid rock bottom.Don't waste your time - or buy yourself some cheap ring from an old vending machine, look at it and say for hours:"Uuhhhhhh, my precious, uhhhhhh, ahhhh, so shiny"I promise this makes for better entertainment than the whole stupid lord of the rings garbage.

I also find it very curious when someone assures you that they're not bigots, racists or homophobes but when they come home from work they turn to TV for a little bit of escapism. One wonders what they're trying to escape from, because apparently the inclusion of diverse characters ruins everything and makes the escape impossible.But of course it's none of those ugly sentiments one might suspect - it's all to do with their wish to stay true to the original and respect the author who wouldn't like any of those progressive ideas and had he lived today he wouldn't include any of that pc nonsense in his work. ipc-title__text: Beautiful Remarkable Achievement that Honours Source Material A++
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Having read the Lord of the Rings and Simarillion, I spent my time watching this with a permanent smile on my face to see the storylines come to life, and to hear the beautiful mythologies from long before even this era. I wish Joseph Mawle was still playing Adar, his eyes were so expressive of the sorrow he carried, but Sam Hazeldine has also done a great job.I follow along each character's story with open curiosity and wonder, delighting at the rich world they're painting and the demonstrations of the full world around us. The Stranger's experiences and his warm bond with Nori give us sweet joyful comedic moments, and his development is captivating.But Sauron/Vickers is the real gem here, his acting is award worthy, and the writing of Sauron's inner journey is the most fascinating and compelling aspect of the show. Likewise, Galadriel's inner turmoil is perfectly expressed through Clark's facial expressions. Elrond's conviction is seen clearly through the actor's subtle expressions, just as is the pain such a decision causes him. The themes of fate and our choices is a captivating one, especially when certain beings recognise that perhaps there are signals from The One when unexpected fortune falls in their path.Despite the haters, this show is made with love for those who actually do love the world Tolkien created, those who have read the Simarillion and those who appreciate creative explorations of that world and time while also honouring that world and time. This includes the overarching themes and mythologies Tolkien painstakingly created. The producers obtained feedback and approvals from the Tolkien estate, how much more do those haters want?The directors and writers have done an excellent job at loving this world and bringing it to life for the small screen. My life is better because these scenes are in it, not just in my head from reading the written pages. To hear them speak of Morgoth, the light of the Valar, and the flows of fate, brought chills. I never thought I would see new material on these beloved stories.Great job to the cast and crew for the enormous task at hand, especially knowing how much negativity and hate there is out there. I hope that they see how much it is positively impacting so many of us who love and appreciate the original source material and who can also appreciate the remarkable achievements they've made here.

ipc-title__text: Waiting for the bus to Faerie
ipc-html-content-inner-div: The light of the Elves is fading, Gil-galad tells Elrond in Amazon's The Rings of Power. We need mithril to preserve our immortality.Poor Elves. It's true they desperately lack something that will keep their realm from withering to dust. But it isn't mithril. It's good storytelling.Narrative transportation is a term some theorists use for the state of being completely immersed in a captivating story. Whether we're reading a book, listening to a storyteller, or watching a film, we all know what being transported feels like. We disengage from our own world to the point where we may not see or hear what's going on around us. We get fully swept up in what's happening to the people in the story. We care about them. We wonder about their motives, question their choices, anticipate their fates. As the story plunges them into peril our pulse may quicken, our breathing rate may change, we might sit up straighter or lean forward. We are utterly invested in what's happening on the page or the screen. It matters to us. Like magic we are transported to another realm. The realm of a good story that's well-told.J. R. R. Tolkien had a word for this realm and for the narrative enchantment that takes us there. He called it "Faerie."You may not consciously know when you've arrived in Faerie, because you're so fully immersed you can't step back and critically assess what's happening to you. But once you've left you have no doubt you were there. And you yearn with all your heart to go back.This enchantment doesn't just happen. Not every story sweeps us breathlessly into Faerie. It takes the skill, effort, imagination, and loving attention to detail of great storytelling to weave this spell. When a story fails to transport us anywhere we feel cheated, stuck in our own lives, waiting for a bus that doesn't come.Amazon's The Rings of Power has left me by the side of the road waiting for the bus to Faerie. The unengaging one-note characters, the illogical plotting, the spasmodic pacing, the cringey pseudo-profound dialogue, the hamhanded straining for relevance ... all of these problems and more reveal that the show's creators don't understand what Faerie is, what it meant to Tolkien, and how to bring it to life for viewers.The light of the Elves truly is fading, and Rings of Power is helping to extinguish it.

ipc-title__text: The Snore of the Rings -- and how Amazon got us all to squabble over soulless product
ipc-html-content-inner-div: The Rings of Power, Amazon's serialized take on various Lord of the Rings lore, is one of those shows where those who hate it and those who love it are equally insipid, just in different ways about the same things. As one podcast pointed out when promo material was coming out, both camps have stopped short of setting up a Ouija board to summon J. R. R. Tolkien from beyond the grave to see what he really thinks about changes/expansions being made to his legendarium.Inevitably, the big talking point is "diverse casting", and the past few months of online discourse have been one obtuse take after another (from phony veils of "science" to espouse racist preference, to vows to consume soulless product as anti-racist activism). Eventually, most of these were put to rest, as most of us joined hands and resoundingly agreed on the following: Rings of Power is weirdly empty, and would be a huge bore no matter how "accurate" its elves and Harfoots looked. You could copy-and-paste Tom Bombadil from the first illustration ever created for Tolkien's works and everything else would still fall short.Much like Amazon's previous venture into High Fantasy literature, The Wheel of Time, this show would feel like a nonchalant rush job even if I didn't know how these events are "supposed" to play (its prologue is especially breezy and it proceeds to cut too quickly between storylines that move too slowly). Even if I didn't have Peter Jackson's towering interpretation to compare it to, it would still seem like a generic YA adaptation at best, and a student project by Californian theater kids at worst (complete with dialogue that throws in "subtle" references to modern society, including a rally that reads as if someone ran the Goobacks episode of South Park through an "old-timey dialogue" filter).It isn't simply "wrong", from a puritan fanboy standpoint, that we no longer experience this fantastical world through the prism of humble peasants like we did in the books and movies. The problem is that we are introduced to various factions at once, who go on and on about lore and whatnot, giving us little reason to care about anyone beyond the fact that we recognize them from LOTR. Look no further than Netflix's The Dark Crystal: Age of Resistance if you'd like to see a High Fantasy show that works for new and old fans alike.However, the show's nowhere near as bad as some feared -- and still insist in their pissy YouTube podcasts. Sometimes the money (of which Amazon reportedly spent a record amount, even if there are now straight-up conspiracy theories on where the rest of it went) is on the screen: the various elven and dwarven locations are wondrous to behold and the orc suits are a damn sight better than the Fantasy phone app rejects from 2012's The Hobbit.Few of the actors bring the appropriate gravitas to the characters they've been assigned, they rarely seem convinced of their digital surroundings, and there are plenty of needlessly stoic performances, but even then, I wasn't as irked as I thought I would be. I did like Lenny Henry, as well as the sound design and also the music. In fact, I'll be fair: The Rings of Power doesn't feel like a fan film -- or an algorithmically-concocted streaming-site product -- the way Obi-Wan Kenobi did. It may still feel like a theater production with an occasionally huge budget, but it isn't completely incomprehensible that someone would like this.I guess my main issue with people who defend the series (of which there are indeed still a few; some of them genuine, the rest looking to get a rise out of the YouTube dweebs) is that they can't seem to keep their story straight.One second they'll be telling you that Tolkien was actually super-duper progressive and would've readily approved of changes being made to his world -- not just altering the characters' appearance, mind you, but also writing out Númenor's tradition of male-only heirs. The next second they'll be painting Tolkien as an archaic bigot (who was also utterly opposed to fan-fiction in ANY shape) and relish the idea that his mythology isn't accurately represented; that this is a deconstruction rather than a celebration. Similarly, I'm wondering if this is supposed to really be "a new generation's Lord of the Rings" when so much of it aims to replicate the movies.Either way, it doesn't matter. If the idea really was to make this the new definitive take on Tolkien's world and usurp that of Peter Jackson, I say "good f-cking luck" to Amazon. (Even at their most "boring", the films still kept us endeared, seeing as they got their main material straight from Tolkien -- who, despite being an inspiration to so many, has a way of writing characters and dialogue that is entirely his own.) If that wasn't the intent, this is still pretty bad. Even Bakshi and Rankin/Bass got the essence down more successfully than this. I'm less sure about the Russian bootleg one.I'll follow it through out of curiosity, but I'm betting the sands of time will swallow this one whole. Sometimes things that SHOULD be forgotten are lost.

ipc-title__text: Oh dear, it blew up on the launchpad!
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Affirmative action is not the primary reason this show is bad. Making a conscious effort to bring more actors from underrepresented minorities into modern films and television is a positive thing. Cynically choosing a well-established IP dating from the 1930s based on a time and place where people of color simply do not fit into the picture naturally in order to cash in on its proven financial success and then shoehorning activists into the cast with little or no acting experience for purely political reasons is. But that's not even the real issue here. It's more of a side note. A red-herring Amazon has employed to mask the show's real problem. It's just not very good.The dialogue is contrived, convoluted, and pretentious to the point of parody. Some of this is accounted for by the cast, which is lackluster across the board. But the lion's share of the responsibility must go to the writing. It's simply atrocious. The fact that so much of the script ignores, confuses and reinvents Tolkien's own creation is a factor. But even that isn't the real problem. The script is simply unhinged, be it from the source material or the vision the writers conjured up to replace it. What we end with is a convoluted mess grounded in nothing at all.I wish there was some redeeming aspect of the show I could point to, but there isn't. Even the CGI is becoming problematic. Every place just looks like a cheap video game imitation of the original trilogy. By the time we get to Numinor in episode 3, the place looks like someone tore down the shanty towns surrounding Rio and rebuilt them in stone.In summary, this show fails on every level. I suppose if you really wanted to find a silver lining, the sheer scale of incompetence surrounding this production will probably go down in history as record-breaking.

I really wanted to like this. After having read almost everything Tolkien wrote in my childhood and the promotional materials and the music, I was ready to dive back into Middle Earth. But on first watch, something seemed off.Visually, the series has the same brightness of the Hobbit. It's pretty, but doesn't feel real. Even the things that are old feel new. Costume design is okay, nothing special but not terribly egregious.The script and acting however, falls really flat. It's stiff, lifeless, and unimaginative in places and many conversations feel incredibly unnatural, both in text and delivery. It's frequently hard to watch.But my biggest gripe is with the in-world consistency. The glory of Middle Earth is in the world building which Tolkien meticulously designed and revised. I accept that any adaptation has to take a certain amount of creative license; the LOTR movies certainly did. The difference between the two is that the LOTR movies approached the story from the same angle as the book and made minimal adaptations in order to tell the story effectively. They also were reasonably faithful to the ethos of the world. This however, does none of this, instead having the arrogance to claim better knowledge of Tolkien's creations better than the author himself. This is a show centred on Galadriel. A Galadriel that bears precious little resemblance to the one in the source material save her name. Creative license lets you create new events, delete events, merge events, or modify events slightly to tell the story better. The problem with the way it has been done is that the original plot points will no longer fit.The thing is, as a stand-alone series, if Tolkien had never existed or the LOTR movies never made, this would actually be a half decent serial deserving 3-4 seasons to see the story through. But, in light of its origins, it really is a let down. For some reason, the only part with any life is the Harfoots.

ipc-title__text: How could they choose actors so badly?
ipc-html-content-inner-div: # How could they choose actors so badly?The casting choices in "The Rings of Power" are nothing short of disastrous. It's as if the producers deliberately set out to destroy Tolkien's carefully crafted world. The actors seem wholly unsuited for their roles, lacking the gravitas and presence needed to bring Middle-earth to life.The elves, meant to be ethereal and ageless, come across as mundane and unremarkable. Galadriel, a character of immense power and wisdom, is reduced to a petulant warrior with all the charisma of a damp log. The dwarves fare no better, with performances that border on caricature rather than the proud, complex race Tolkien envisioned.Even worse are the human characters, who fail to capture the essence of their mortal struggle. The acting is wooden at best, cringe-worthy at worst. It's clear that looks were prioritized over talent, resulting in a cast that's pretty to look at but painful to watch.This misguided casting undermines the entire production, making it impossible to immerse oneself in the world of Middle-earth. It's a betrayal of Tolkien's legacy and an insult to fans everywhere.

ipc-title__text: A dreadful vandalism of a great work of art by a greedy corporation.

ipc-title__text: The era has only just begun!
ipc-html-content-inner-div:
Tolkien has been a part of my life for almost 30 years, since I was 10 when I went off reading The Lord of the Rings and became enamoured by its author's mastery. I remember at 14 my friend told me emphatically, "They're making Lord of the Rings into a movie!" And I thought to myself, they'll ruin it. At 15 I refused to see The Fellowship of the Ring in cinemas because I did not want to spoil my vision of Middle Earth and all the characters I loved. It wasn't until The Two Towers was about to be released when I could resist no longer and I watched FoTR on VHS then went to the cinema that evening. From then I was hooked and I figired PJ and his crew were genius.Between TTT and RoTK, I became obsessed with LOTR internet forums and became somewhat of a lore master. I'd been deep into The Silmarillion, Unfinished Tales, and any literature by or about Tolkien I could get my hands on. I learned to replicate the Gollum/Smeagol voice exactly like Andy Serkis and all day spoke like this at school. I collected Lord of the Rings Warhammer miniatures and I spent what seemed like millennia painting them while listening to the LOTR soundtracks or with LOTR movies playing in the background on repeat. I was well and truly obsessed. It was my life.When ROTK came out, I was in the first session playing on release night. I was angry as hell they cut The Scouring of the Shire - something I will never ever be able to accept as a reasonable change by PJ. But otherwise I was very happy and I have watched those movies several times every year since.But I thought the era was over.No longer was the Gollum voice cool (was it ever?). Nobody wanted to discuss the movies any longer. All I had was internet forums.Then the Hobbit movies happened. I switched my brain off for a few moments during the films (any time Bard's children were on screen, and whatever Alfrid was supposed to be) but otherwise I adored them. Now I had 6 movies i could watch over and over.But the second era, that I was lucky to get, was ended. There would be no more. That part of my life was now definitely over.And some things that should not have been forgotten were lost. History became legend. Legend became myth. And for eight whole years, the Lord of the Ring passed out of all knowledge.Until, when chance came, it ensnared another bearer.It came to the creature Amazon, who took it deep into the tunnels of their film studio. And there it consumed them.Darkness crept back into the forests of the world. Rumor grew of a shadow in the East, whispers of a nameless fear, and The Rings of Power perceived, its time had come!Having invested many years in the Silmarillion and Unfinished Tales, I could not imagine how a TV show could possibly cover anything as grand and disparate as the tales of the creation and wars for the Rings of Power. Nevertheless, on release day I was there, Gandalf. I was there two years ago when the strength of my composure failed. I gorged myself on The Rings of Power.I was stunned by the first episode. A brilliant opener. But one episode a week drove me mad. I was always left thinking, "Is this it? Is this all you can conjure, Saruman?"
From the... Eruption onward, I was back to loving it. The final episode really impressed me. But in all I thought eh, 6 to 7 out of 10 as a rating. It was okay. I wanted a little more.But alas, I could not let it alone. Like Frodo's finger finding its way to the Ring, I could not, would not, not watch it again.This time I binged it it one sitting.Wow! Watching it in a single sitting was intense. I loved it so much more. The actors really grew on me. Harfoots grew on me. Numenorians grew on me. Galadriel grew on me. Almost everything that irked me I'm now okay with. Even love.I've now watched Season 1 five times through. Each time I have found new depth and nuance. Ultimately I see now how much Season 1 was setting up for whats coming later, and as I've since reacquanted myself with the lore, which I'd had a good decade away from, I've seen so many easter eggs in there that are going to make so much more sense in the following seasons.I went back and made a more concerted effort to rate each episode as I watched and my rating ended up as 8.5 out of 10.Meanwhile I've seen some of the backlash on the interwebs, and the 1 star review bombing that occurred. Frankly I've been disgusted by the racism, mysogyny, and pettiness of fellow (supposed) Tolkien fans. All I can say is: you can't please everyone. And not everyone deserves to be pleased. Even the original LOTR book has its haters. And to them I say Go back to the shadow!For me however, I'm extatic that the eras of my life that I thought would never be repeated have been reborn like the forges of Erebor! The Rings of Power is magnificent, and Aye! That's how it starts!The anticipation I have for Season 2 is more than I've ever had for any TV Show ever.So...If you haven't seen it yet, what are you waiting for!? Go!If you have seen it, see it again. I hope your second time is as great as my second time was.If you're like me, and you've seen it multiple times, Lan i Valaron arcanwar tauvar!

ipc-title__text: Amazon, in its hubris, has failed to deliver
ipc-html-content-inner-div: For the purposes of this review, I'm going to set aside the fact that this show is not a faithful adaptation of Tolkien's work. Enough has been said on this point by Tolkien's fanbase, and the show has already seen many understandably scathing attacks by Tolkien purists. Instead, I am going to review the show (as objectively as I can) for what it is- a modern fantasy series that licences some names and a few key plot points from Tolkien.Firstly, the good points. As you would expect, the CGI is impressive and many of the locations capture the 'essence' of Tolkien's world well. The music is pleasant enough, and some of the acting is convincing.Unfortunately, the show is badly let down by the writing and direction.I'll start with what was, for me, the first strong indication that the show might have gone off the rails a bit- the Harfoots. Tolkien's Hobbits were simple folk, yes, but not stupid. The Harfoots, on the other hand, are little more than a band of treacherous simpletons. They are not particularly likeable or entertaining to watch, and have little role to play in the story (besides babysitting a wizard). The way their accents lurch from Westcountry(?) to Irish(?) is also very jarring. I wont go so far as to say this caricature of Celtic peoples is offensive, but I'm not sure it is quite what Tolkien had in mind when he set out to capture the best of England's country folk!The dwarves are ok- no real complaints there.The elves on the other hand, are not very convincing at all. They are supposed to be wise, fair, and ethereal beings. Instead, they are just portrayed as aristocrats.And the men are just... men- disorganised, fallible, and easily bought.This brings me to the plot. The pacing is slow, and yet there are so many unnecessary characters and story arcs, it's hard to become invested in any of them.Many characters lack any clear motivation, and 5 episodes in, nothing has really happened to advance the plot that was set up in the prologue to the first episode. Most of the key decision makers change their minds on a whim, and at the behest of people they either don't know from Adam or have ample cause to distrust. This means none of these decisions carry any weight and the stakes just seem very low.Galadriel, who is arguably the main character, comes across as petulant and annoying. This is not a criticism of Morfydd Clark, but the script and direction. Again, you completely forget she is an elf (except in those moments where she single-handedly bests four or five men in armed combat, at which point the fact she is 'kind of magic I guess' can be the only explanation).Some of these things could be forgiven if it were the pilot of a low budget original series. But it's not. We're now five hours into the highest budget TV show ever produced.Amazon has once again demonstrated that you can't simply buy the rights to a beloved story and assume that it will be an easy ticket to success. Storytelling isn't pay-to-win.

ipc-title__text: After 6 episodes, I'm increasingly impressed. Ignore the haters.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: A key about this long-awaited series is the obvious thing: this is a Tolkien world we're watching. It's not a literal retelling of the author's Second Age stories, but very much to its credit it carries on the idiom and style of the Lord of the Rings movies. In this world the stakes are high, good and evil are both present in force, and the characters are in earnest. To get the most out of it, we have to take all our 21st-century irony and snark, and check them at the door. Settle in and get to know this big new cast of characters.Comparing this new RoP with the original Peter Jackson LoTR trilogy of 20 years ago might not be completely fair -- because those movies were a bloody miracle -- but I think what *is* fair is to judge RoP on its own merit. You don't have to have an encyclopedic knowledge of First and Second Age histories but knowing a certain amount of background from the Tolkien stories definitely helps. Better know the basics about Morgoth, the Two Trees and the Silmarils, the Valar, Feanor, Elendil and Isildur, among others. One thing I like a lot is what everyone seems to agree on, which is that it's visually spectacular. Epic movie-quality scenes and settings that show a lot of planning and craftsmanship. You can almost enjoy this by just taking it in visually.Another thing I appreciate though is that they are playing a long game. From the very first episode, we are plunged right in to about four different parallel storylines in different parts of world and entirely separate groups of characters -- Elves, Men, Dwarves, and Harfoots -- and they are all clearly going to continue while they intersect and interweave.And a third thing is that some real thought and care seems to have gone into scripting. The Harfoots talk differently from the Men, who are different (well, at least a bit) from the Elves, who are different from the Dwarves. The Elves are almost by definition noble, the Dwarves rather crude, and the Harfoots (pre-hobbits) lovably down to earth and comfy. That's what we expected, but doing it well and putting it across does count for something. Yes, there are some issues -- for example, the rank-and-file Numenoreans don't seem to be particularly noble here, and in a lot of cases the nature of the character conflicts and dialogs doesn't play out as anything new.The actors are an entirely new set of relatively unknown faces, and I'm totally fine with that. Who cares? It depends -- as it should -- on how good they are in their roles. Morfydd Clark in the uber-lead role of Galadriel isn't quite up to Cate Blanchett's perhaps-impossible standard, but she's good, they are putting her through a *lot*, and I'm happy to see more. Markella Kavenagh (Nori) is very good too, as are Lloyd Owen (Elendil), Owain Arthur (Durin), Nazanin Boniadi (Bronwyn), and Charlie Vickers (Halbrand) to name a few of the leads. They're all growing on me.Enough. It counts for a lot just to step back again into the Tolkienesque world once a week and see it being done seriously and well.But at the same time I hope we aren't done with movie versions of this immensely rich fantasy world yet. ipc-title__text: Might be the worst show ever made
An Unfortunate Journey into the Abyss: A Review of "Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power" TV Series
ipc-html-content-inner-div: As a devout fan of J. R. R. Tolkien's iconic fantasy epic, "The Lord of the Rings," it is with a heavy heart that I find myself writing this review for the "Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power" TV series. Having eagerly anticipated its release, hoping to relive the magic and wonder of Middle-earth, I can't help but express my profound disappointment with what can only be described as an awful adaptation that tarnishes the essence of Tolkien's beloved work.From the outset, it's evident that the creators of this series have opted for a misguided approach, straying far from the rich lore and intricate storytelling that made the original trilogy a timeless masterpiece. The fundamental mistake lies in the lack of respect for Tolkien's vision and the decision to take extreme liberties with the source material. In doing so, the show squanders the essence of what made "The Lord of the Rings" so compelling in the first place.One of the primary grievances lies in the poorly written and underdeveloped characters. The series introduces numerous new characters while mishandling established ones from the books. It becomes apparent that the writers prioritized shock value and superficial plotlines over genuine character growth. These caricatures lack the depth and emotional resonance that fans have come to cherish in Tolkien's creations. Additionally, the abundance of subplots and unending twists further convolute the narrative, making it difficult to connect with any of the characters or their motivations.Furthermore, the show's visual effects and production design are woefully inconsistent. While some landscapes and sets manage to capture the essence of Middle-earth's majesty, others fall flat, feeling like cheap imitations rather than the vibrant, immersive world Tolkien envisioned. Even the CGI creatures, which should have been a highlight, often appear unnatural and detract from the viewing experience.As if the lackluster characters and uneven visuals weren't enough, "Rings of Power" suffers from pacing issues that cripple the storytelling. The series drags on at a snail's pace in some episodes, while in others, it rushes through pivotal moments that should have been given the attention they deserved. This erratic pacing not only disrupts the narrative flow but also fails to create a sense of urgency or engagement with the audience.Perhaps most distressing is the mishandling of the themes and allegories that underpin Tolkien's work. The subtle, timeless messages of friendship, sacrifice, and the fight against evil are sacrificed for bombastic action sequences and unnecessary melodrama. "Rings of Power" misses the opportunity to delve into the profound depths of Tolkien's philosophical and moral explorations, reducing the series to a hollow spectacle.In conclusion, "Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power" is a colossal disappointment and a disservice to the legacy of Tolkien's magnum opus. This ill-conceived adaptation abandons the heart and soul of Middle-earth in favor of a haphazardly stitched together series that fails to capture the essence of what made the books so enduring. It is best approached with caution, especially by die-hard fans who may find themselves mourning the loss of the true spirit of "The Lord of the Rings."

I am writing this review after watching the first two episodes of the Rings of Power and as a self-proclaimed Tolkien "Superfan", I have read the main trilogy multiple times, and many of the lesser read books including The Silmarillion, Unfinished Tales, History of Middle Earth etc... I am a fan of Peter Jackson's original film trilogy, the BBC radio adaptation by Brian Sibley and The Hobbit stage production. I even taught myself a small amount of Quenya as a teenager. I have also read an amateur screenplay of the Akallabeth, the quality of which has so far, way surpassed the writing and dialog delivered in Amazons version.I am not a fan of this Amazon production.It was madness for Amazon to decide that a second age show was a good idea when they do not own the rights to the texts that most extensively cover this period of Arda's history, it was a greater madness and cowardice to condense the timeline to the degree that the showrunners have attempted.There are many, many changes to the established lore and cannon which have "subverted" Tolkien's works and I will not be able to cover all of them in this review, but understand that I am deeply saddened by the showrunners choices in relation to character.Their versions of Galadriel, Finrod Felagund, Elrond, Gil-Galad and Celebrimbor are confusing and rage inducing, character motivation have been swapped arounds so much that characters are now the opposite of how they were written. Some of the dialogue that came out of these characters mouths actually made me cry with disappointment, particularly the "you have not seen what I have seen" debacle. On my second watch of the first episode I cried during Finrod's little chat with Galadriel, what absolute bile, it was so bitter on a second hearing I dare not watch the episode again as I fear my heart will actually cease beating due to heart burn.I expected to hate the Harfoots, but did not. This was some welcome escapism from the butchery of language and character shown in the elven scenes. I thought the actress who played Nori gave one of the best performances, along with the Elrond, Disa and Durin trio. Although the Moria storyline is pretty anti-cannon, it was the highlight of the two episodes.I know every has been saying how beautiful and cinematic this show is, but I think it would be pretty difficult to spend the amount of money Amazon have done and end up with something that looked like trash. I also disagree and think that a lot of the CGI looked odd, especially the fading of the two trees. The CGI cities were pretty, but where was the individuality? Lindon looks like Peter Jackson's Rivendell, so did Eregion. There was opportunity for storytelling through design here and it was ignored.I would like to review the problems with pacing, not caring about three of the four storylines in the show, how people magically appear across the map wearing the same non-travel clothes, the uninspiring musical choices but I'm making myself angry and upset thinking about it too much.I was so hopeful when Amazon announced a second age show as there are beautiful and terrible stories that could have been told, unfortunately my hopes were dashed against the mountain with the first two episodes.

ipc-title__text: Very anti-Tolkien and not even good as fan fiction
ipc-html-content-inner-div: This show destroys so many of Tolkien's points. Ultimately it becomes anti-Tolkien, always trying to blur lines between good and evil, right and wrong and even between differences related to characters and peoples. Everything becomes blurry to the point where characters constantly change their mind without any clue to what prompted that change. The show ends up in complete confusion; perhaps telling of the writers and the time we live in.The show is some sort of fan fiction in the sense that it keeps a Tolkien facade while at the same time being far removed from actual Tolkien lore. Every 5 minutes a Tolkien fan will have to stop and say "that's not how it is". A lot of fan fiction out there is much more true to its source material - or very clear that the fan fiction is trying to create an alternative universe within a fandom. In that sense this show is quite deceptive; trying to appear Tolkien while being very anti-Tolkien. They use all the names and words from Tolkien, but they change the meaning to something that's not Tolkien at all.If viewers are willing to ignore the complete desecration of everything Tolkien, the show is still very bad. Some of the CGI and some of the music is nice, but that's about it. Almost all plot lines are illogical, stupid and boring. The dialogue is so fake, and many lines don't make sense when you stop and think about what is actually being said. The timeline is a big mess and people pop up and teleport to whereever the writers want them to be at a certain time. But worst of all, the characters are extremely unlikable. Galadriel, Elrond and the hobbits are probably worst, but most characters are unlikable: They lie, abandon innocent people to die and they generally seem like they have severe personality disorders. Flawed characters can be very interesting, but the problem here is that the writers didn't intentionally try to make the characters flawed. Instead, in an attempt to make the characters perfect, they wrote a bunch of totally inconsistent, wooden and sociopathic characters by mistake. It's almost like they want the viewers to root for the orcs and for Sauron.

The people putting this together are inexperienced and while currently that shows, lets all hope they gain skills and future series are more credible.

ipc-title__text: Very anti-Tolkien and not even good as fan fiction
ipc-html-content-inner-div: This show destroys so many of Tolkien's points. Ultimately it becomes anti-Tolkien, always trying to blur lines between good and evil, right and wrong and even between differences related to characters and peoples. Everything becomes blurry to the point where characters constantly change their mind without any clue to what prompted that change. The show ends up in complete confusion; perhaps telling of the writers and the time we live in.The show is some sort of fan fiction in the sense that it keeps a Tolkien facade while at the same time being far removed from actual Tolkien lore. Every 5 minutes a Tolkien fan will have to stop and say "that's not how it is". A lot of fan fiction out there is much more true to its source material - or very clear that the fan fiction is trying to create an alternative universe within a fandom. In that sense this show is quite deceptive; trying to appear Tolkien while being very anti-Tolkien. They use all the names and words from Tolkien, but they change the meaning to something that's not Tolkien at all.If viewers are willing to ignore the complete desecration of everything Tolkien, the show is still very bad. Some of the CGI and some of the music is nice, but that's about it. Almost all plot lines are illogical, stupid and boring. The dialogue is so fake, and many lines don't make sense when you stop and think about what is actually being said. The timeline is a big mess and people pop up and teleport to whereever the writers want them to be at a certain time. But worst of all, the characters are extremely unlikable. Galadriel, Elrond and the hobbits are probably worst, but most characters are unlikable: They lie, abandon innocent people to die and they generally seem like they have severe personality disorders. Flawed characters can be very interesting, but the problem here is that the writers didn't intentionally try to make the characters flawed. Instead, in an attempt to make the characters perfect, they wrote a bunch of totally inconsistent, wooden and sociopathic characters by mistake. It's almost like they want the viewers to root for the orcs and for Sauron.

As a lifelong fan of Tolkien's works and someone who adored Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings films, I went into The Rings of Power with cautious optimism. I fully understand that adaptations need to take creative liberties, but what I've seen in this series makes me question whether the showrunners even read the books.First and foremost, the storylines they've invented and the characters they've altered feel like a betrayal of the source material. I'm not against adding new layers to a story, but so much of what they've introduced feels disconnected from Tolkien's world. There are some saving graces, of course-Elrond's relationship with the dwarves was a joy to watch, and I found the dynamic between Sauron and Adar intriguing. These moments give a glimpse of what could have been.But then, there are the "hobbits." Or, should I say, the Harfoots. They're portrayed in such a grating and absurd way that they feel like a mockery of what we loved about hobbits in both the books and films. It's almost painful to watch them. The charm, the groundedness, the simplicity that made hobbits endearing is completely lost here.Considering the enormous budget, the years of production time, and the sheer size of the *Lord of the Rings* franchise, it's shocking to see how underwhelming this has turned out. Yes, the series has stunning visuals and occasional glimmers of hope, but the writing and character choices fall flat. If you don't compare it to the films or the books, it might be "okay," but for something of this scale, "okay" isn't good enough.In my eyes, they've failed to honor the spirit of Tolkien's work. It feels like a missed opportunity, and as a devoted fan, I can't help but feel deeply disappointed.

This series shocked and pleasantly surprised me. In many ways it's better than then the Peter Jackson trilogy and I never thought that would be the case. And, I love the fact that it is giving the back story to Galadriel and her sacrifice for so many humans and elves.

First, this isn't original Tolkien literature, so don't expect as such. It's more like a fan fiction prequel that has some Lord of The Rings characters and setting in the same world.Secondly, at the time it's being released, there's no other similar fantasy English TV shows that is family friendly and better than Rings of Power.With those points in mind I'll give it 10/10. In the long run comparing with all time great TV shows, maybe not so much. It is fun to watch, and the story builds over time. It's quite slow paced with not a lot of actions, but I like it that way. There's a vibe of serenity among all the chaos.

The costuming and CGI environments are gorgeous. They exceed the quality Seen in many blockbuster films.The writing is profoundly lazy and an insult to the richness of the Lord of the Rings universe, the source material, and the previous film renditions both acted and animated. Most of all, the writing is an insult to the audience.The plot holes are massive. Very little adds up, the contradictions are numerous, and key characters are undermined by half-brained dramatic twists that come at the integrity and personality of the characters.The casting is terrible. Anyone affiliated with its production should be embarrassed.

ipc-title__text: This is not Lord of the rings story!

ipc-title__text: All the pseudo-heroic dialogue sounds like it was written by Yoda
I expected to strongly dislike it but I LOVE it.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: After seeing so many mean memes and thumbnails and titles of videos on YouTube lambasting Rings of Power, I avoided anything concerning the series. However, my stepdad asked me to watch it with him because he was curious. Immediately, we felt the love and passion that was poured into this show. We got hooked. The acting, writing, costumes, set designs, special effects, soundtrack, and the use of deep LOTR lore are all overwhelmingly amazing.The cast delivered such compelling performances. You can't help but feel what some of the characters feel. Also, the script the actors were given was *chef's kiss*. A script really can make or break an actor's performance. No offense to the Star Wars prequel trilogy but "You underestimate my power," "Don't make me kill you," and "I don't like sand..." Need I say more? The prequel trilogy is a perfect example of great actors being hindered by subpar directing and writing. There is none of that in Rings of Power. Just about every line works and feels sincere.The special effects are great! Since many recent MCU movies have had CGI that clearly needed more time for polish but because the CGI studios have too much work to do in so little time, the CGI tends to look...unfinished. I've come to expect that look in most movies and shows that need heavy CG use. That is NOT the case here. The CGI actually blends so well with the actors, the sets, and environments. The use of lighting was also brilliant. They managed to create a seamless visual experience with the use of lighting and what's happening in the story.The overall writing is brilliant. The more you watch it, the more obvious it becomes how much they strived to be true to JRR Tolkien's stories. They clearly took great care to respect, celebrate, and create new stories to tell from within Middle-Earth. I'm truly grateful to witness such art.

ipc-title__text: Who is this show even for?

ipc-html-content-inner-div: It's probably not for everyone but it's a beautifully woven work of art. The story, cinematography, locations and characters made this one of the best TV series we've seen for a while.TV can get a bit lazy sometimes - hack and slash or big drama for example, but this cleverly removes much of the sex and gore we see in lots of other big screen pictures and proves you don't need to show heads rolling to get the story across.All in all, this just nails it and does things differently. It's refreshing and I've never seen anything quite like it. Perhaps that's why it hasn't done as well, or maybe you need a good setup to make the most of it (I doubt I'd have enjoyed it as much back when I was a student using a 16" laptop and laptop speakers!). We really, really enjoyed it.

Honestly, I am deeply disappointed by this series. What I was hoping to be an amazing journey back into Middle Earth has just turned out to be a very beautiful, but distinctly average, fantasy story, loosely based on the 2nd age.Amazon's "adaptation" is badly made TV with a nonsensical story built on wild coincidences, contrived plotlines and a blatant disregard for the various building blocks that make any story complete: logical character choices, a sense of time and place, and narrative tension-not to mention an overly large cast of mostly forgettable and uncharismatic characters, some wholly made up for the show and others changed entirely as to be almost unrecognizable.In every way that truly matters, The Rings Of Power fails from the writing to the acting to the presentation. It fails as an adaptation, neither enriching Tolkien's work nor remaining true to it. It fails as a good fantasy, giving us generic tropes and melodrama rather than blazing new ground. And it fails as a compelling story, filled with cheap mystery boxes and unsurprising 'twists.'I could go on, but it's honestly not worth my time.

ipc-title__text: Imperfect, but Definitely Not the Disaster the Fandom Want You To Believe It Is
ipc-html-content-inner-div:
I have to admit, I slept on Rings of Power for a few weeks, not really starting the show until it had almost wrapped up. While I had some reservations going into the show already, such as them not sounding very distinct from the Jackson film (shooting in New Zealand, using most of the same characters, etc.), most of my reasoning had been due to the negative reception online. However, the more I looked into it, I realized a lot of that negativity was stemming from frankly asinine reasons, complaints that the show was taking liberties with the source material (which all adaptations do) and the fact that the show was "woke" because of a female lead and POC characters (which is just stupid).So I decided to finally give The Rings of Power a shot, and despite a few flaws, I have to say that this show well exceeded my expectations, and is definitely not as much of a disaster as the rabid Tolkien fans on the internet would like you to believe.Visually this series is breathtaking to look at. When you hear that this series cost a billion dollars to produce, you expect this to look fantastic, and Rings of Power definitely lives up to that expectation. The visual effects, lighting, production design, costumes and makeup, and cinematography are absolutely astounding. This is exactly the type of production quality you need for a show as epic as this.There's also some great performances and character work here. I had some reservations about Morfydd Clark as Galadriel at first, but as the show progressed and she really came into her own. I bought her desire to track down Sauron and found her compelling enough to carry the show as a whole. Robert Aramayo was great as Elrond; I like their portrayal of him as a politician and found his companionship with Durin (another standout performance here) to be compelling. There are newer characters, ones who don't exist in the books (much to Tolkien fanboys' dismay) who are fine additions to the story. There's not a single weak performance here.The action sequences are solid and enjoyable to watch. If you go in expecting to see some of the more memorable moments from the Jackson films, like Legolas taking down an elephant or surfboarding down a flight of stairs while shooting arrows, you'll probably be disappointed, but on their own they are pretty enjoyable and engaging sequences.The biggest complaint that could be made comes down to the pacing. The story is deliberately slow, with many storylines going on at once. I didn't mind the slower pace because I was waiting to see what it was all building towards, and overall I think it all leads to a compelling climax. But the slowness is definitely felt here. Despite that, oddly enough, I felt as though the stuff involving the rings of
Power themselves to be a tad rushed, and would have liked a little more about it throughout the season. There are also a few lines of dialogue here or there that I was huge on, but they were far and few between.Overall The Rings of Power is a solid show that has the potential of getting better from here. It may suffer from a slow pace and a somewhat lack of momentum, but it makes up for it with its beautiful production value, compelling storylines, and likeable characters. I'm looking forward to seeing the following seasons and seeing where the story takes up and how everything will tie together.8/10.

ipc-title__text: Superb visuals, very good actors, interesting characterizations!
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Superb visuals. Numenor was splendid, and Khazad-Dum, awesome.Very good actors, especially Morfydd Clark (Saint Maud, for which she won a BAFTA Cymru for Best Actress), Joseph Mawle (The Passion), Lloyd Owen, and Robert Aramayo.Interesting characterizations, especially of Galadriel and Adar, but also of Elrond-Durin, Gandalf (the Stranger)-Nori, Galadriel-Elendil, and of course, Galadriel-Halbrand.I am very glad that the showrunners decided to make Galadriel the lead character of Season 1, if not of the entire series. After all, Tolkien called her the greatest of the Noldor. I understand that the show had to make Gil-galad appear more regal and powerful than Galadriel (despite her being much older and greater) in order to amplify her transformational arc.The show is far from perfect (dialogues were either insipid or cheesy at times) but is not bad! Looking forward to Season 2, especially to the further transformation of Galadriel (I won't be surprised if the showrunners will being her to Lothlorien during the Second Age, so that we can see her wield the Ring of Water), to the redemption of Adar, and to the introduction of Cirdan, who will wield the Ring of Fire!

ipc-title__text: Arguably one of the most confusing shows I've ever watched
VFX & Production Design worth the watch; writing not so much
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I have mixed feelings about LOTR: tRoP. The visuals are well done and the world feels epic, but the writing is lackluster and character development is poor.The most interesting storyline is that of Arondir the elf archer - it's grounded and he's relatable. Galadriel was a poor choice for a main character; trying to cram her primal-force nature into a human (or in this instance anthropomorphized elven) story-line simultaneously makes her over-powered and nerfed. She's a much better shadow-character whose motives and abilities are better left to the imagination.It doesn't help that almost every character spouts jingoistic phrases dragged from the worst tropes of fantasy writing. Between that and lack of good character development from which good drama can evolve, I think the show would best be served long term by making changes in the writer's room and holding on to the production team, VFX team and cast.It was worth a watch, but only for the visuals and some of the exploration of the Tolkien world from a fan-fic perspective.

ipc-title__text: Just watch the whole season first before complaining about silly things
ipc-html-content-inner-div: If you are going to focus on how the characters look, what they wear or how Tolkien wouldn't approve. Then your problem is with people in general and not really the franchise.Really ask yourself that question honestly. Why does it matter so much? Most people just watched the Trilogy and didn't even read the books. The books are for a very patient and intellectual mind, and I think the details are actually doing Tolkien justice. We are only 2 episodes in and it's stunning, so much work went into it and the details are captivating. Just give it a full season first before complaining about complaining. If you are unsatisfied then, go on then and be angry. But there is a difference between being legitimately angry and superficially spoiled...In the Game of Thrones books, Daenerys is without a single hair on her head and bald. Nothing like the character played by Emilia Clarke. She made it something that works very well for the screen and made The Mother of Dragans her own. Devoted fans also had a hissy fit about that in the beginning. Now we can't imagine her without hair. Only time will tell, but in the meantime... Give it a shot before shooting it down.

I have long loved lord of the rings, I find the fantasy realm of middle earth beautiful, engaging and inspiring. When the Hobbit movies were released, we heard the same hatred and bile from pretend fans who just complain because it wasn't to their expectations or imagination. Now again we see review after review from people saying this is the worst adaptation and how they've ruined the story.I believe that true fans of any story will be excited to learn more about it. Regardless of whether or not they truly expected It. We're the Star Wars movies that followed the original saga as good as the original trilogy and the completion of the saga, no possibly not. But did it add more to the star wars universe. Absolutely.I feel that many of these individuals would sooner ruin it for the vast majority, who do enjoy their favourite fantasy realm being expanded.Yes, there are things that you may not fully believe may have been in Tolkeins mind when he wrote any of the lore. But I truly believe that he would have been enthralled by the fact that even now, his writings inspire creativity and love for a world he created.On all the negative reviews, you will rarely see any suggestions on way things should have been done, it is merely complaining for the sake of It.Yes, the elves don't look like they are all in eternal youth. Elrond in LOTR didn't look like he was, yet the same people complaining about the appearance of elves in ROP won't say a word about that because they just want to nitpick and complain about anything they can think of.I firmly believe the people who are adamantly complaining about everything to do with ROP are the type of people who would put a hair in their food in a restaurant just to get a free meal. It is not so much that they hate the show, more that they wish to try and guide any future series or iterations, not realising that they could in fact ruin any chances of any future series being produced.I also think that if there was a story completely separate to the ROP, hobbit and LOTR, and was merely set in the same world, these people would still complain saying that It was not what Tolkien had in mind.I would say to any of these people, before complaining about what others have produced, demonstrate yourself what you believe to be accurate and produce something yourself for us to judge, before trying to ruin the chances of a show that many of us have thoroughly enjoyed. And I can say as a true fan of the story, if you were to do so, it would bring me an equal amount of joy as this has. Because anything that expands this amazing world is to be admired and cherished not spat on and destroyed due to a selfish sense of 'I thought it should have been done like this'.I cannot wait for more seasons to come. This has finally brought amazing characters and situations to life and helped to increase the amount of content available in this fantastic and beautiful world.Please enjoy this series with an open mind and heart, it does not subtract from any of tolkeins work and if he was around today he would be telling you the same. After explaining how nice a leaf was first obviously. But I do not feel he would be even slightly as negative as many of the comments posted.

Granted, I haven't read all of the literature, so I'm viewing this show from a separate lens from the diehard lore fans, but I thought they didn't really well for a first season. I would not rate season one a 10/10 when compared to the LOTR trilogy, but I do rate it a 10/10 when compared to all the other first seasons of television series out there. It's visually magnificent; has some great acting; I enjoyed the pacing for the most part; and aside from one or two short scenes that didn't make much sense, I thought they juggled the multiple storylines quite well.I can understand why diehard fans wouldn't agree with some of the delineation choices that were made, but I don't understand the sheer hatred I've seen directed towards this show. I took my time to get around to watching it because of all the negativity I heard about it, but I'm really glad I finally did watch it because I found there to be little merit to the gatekeepers' words.I'm really looking forward to season two!

Good story with amazing production. Middle-earth is as beautiful as it should be, stunning! They changed some points in Tolkien's legendary like Celeborn or the stranger, but his essence is there. Morfydd Clark as Galadriel was a great surprise and most of the casting is great, even when their stories are medium, they deliver good acting. I see what people say about the writing and I understand their point. They urgently need new writers that care about the show and understand Tolkien better. At the end my expectations were satisfied and I can't denied that I enjoyed it a lot. I'm really excited for the season 2.

As with many shows of today it lacks original thoughts, weak pacing or any meaningful and well-written scenes.Overall (arrived at episode 4), the show very much resembles the Hobbit films with somewhat over the top CGI action scenes and generally the look of the series is odd in a sense as it looks to clean and spotless to be real people living in a real world.Elves are basically humans with pointy ears, no superiority or any distinguishing features to them, I do like Arondir though. Galadriel and many other main characters act like they are living through their teenage years opposed to what they should behave by now. By focusing too much on too many different plots, completely overwhelms the audience and building up a genuine connection to either one of the characters is hard to attain.It seems like todays productions are mostly focused on easy money making through invoking stuff we've already seen and by very cheap and predictable writing processes. If you are going to spend a billion (!) on production hire someone with some writing abilities.Pictures and trailers looked somewhat promising but actually a total letdown.

Yes, Amazon spent most of the money for the rights, then another big chunk went into CGI, so it is definitely looking way better than the average TV show - but was getting money-pinching when casting actors and hiring scriptwriters. Admittedly, it is hard to write a prequel. People that are alive in the sequel - like Elrond and Galadriel - can't die and therefore you will never be afraid about them being safe. So usually you have to show some character development. Elrond is portrayed as some smooth talking diplomat and Galadriel as a warrior, which is definitely not the impression you get in "Lord of the Rings". It feels odd though that people who have lived for thousands of years would still do a character development. I did not know any of the actors, so they wanted to keep the budget for them pretty low and it shows. The pacing is also a bit slow to my taste.

ipc-title__text: 2 Episodes in and I am interested to see where we go

I hope to be able to come back and update my rating higher once the season comes to a close.

ipc-title__text: I truly do not understand the harsh reviews

Only because I didn't think they could successfully match the feeling I get when I watch LOTR or the hobbit series over again. I'm not the most knowledgeable about the series as a whole but I've always loved it and I still wanted to like the show a lot. And so far it's been really entertaining and visually stunning. While it won't ever be the same as the originals I think it gives me exactly what I was hoping for. There are several plots going on at once and I feel like it'll take a bit of time to understand and feel connected to the characters. I have no reason to believe that the series will not get even better. I love seeing this age of middle earth and the earlier beings (like the Harfoots). I think managing your expectations and understanding that this will not be the same as the others is key. I was surprised at the ratings still, I think it should be higher. Give it a chance it's enjoyable (even just for visuals).

"Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" has moments of great visual quality, especially the action scenes, but in between there are too many empty scenes and unnecessary dialogues that do not add anything to the story. The performances are good, the direction excellent and the CGI extraordinary. The only (big) problem is the script: it's not even remotely up to par with a major production. On the other hand, strange decisions have been made that provoke the anger of the fan base, for nothing. For example, what was the need to cut the elves' hair? I can understand other controversial decisions (which I don't agree with either), but unnecessarily altering the image of the elves, just for the sake of it, is totally incomprehensible.

ipc-title__text: Poor writing, even if you're okay with the bastardisation of Tolkien's work
This series deserves a better rating

ipc-title__text: Why This Series Fails to Capture the Magic: A Fan's Disappointment
ipc-html-content-inner-div: If you're a fan of the original books or the movies, I strongly advise against watching this series. As someone who has both read the books and seen the film adaptations, I found this series to be an enormous letdown. From the very beginning, it becomes evident that this adaptation fails to capture the essence of the original material. The story lacks any coherent flow in relation to the books, making it feel disjointed and disconnected. If you're expecting the same rich, immersive experience that the books and movies offered, you're in for a rude awakening.First and foremost, the plot is all over the place. It feels like the writers took a handful of key scenes from the books, threw them into a blender, and hoped for the best. There's no logical progression or development; instead, we're left with a series of events that feel random and poorly thought out. Important character arcs are either ignored or reduced to mere clichés, leaving little emotional investment for the audience. The depth and complexity that made the original story so compelling are nowhere to be found.One of the biggest disappointments is the cast. The actors, while perhaps talented in other roles, seem out of place here. Their performances come across as superficial, lacking the depth and nuance required to bring these beloved characters to life. It's as if they're just going through the motions, delivering their lines without any real conviction or understanding of their roles. This results in a series of flat, uninspiring performances that fail to engage the viewer.Season 1 was somewhat acceptable, largely because it had the benefit of novelty and curiosity on its side. It wasn't great, but it wasn't terrible either. At least there was some attempt to stay true to the source material, and it provided a few moments that captured the spirit of the books. However, any goodwill earned in the first season is completely squandered in Season 2. The writing becomes even more erratic, and the plot veers off into nonsensical directions that have little to do with the original story.

You cannot rely 100% on the media you are watching but have a take of your own, a history of your past whether it be literature, art or your own life experiences. To my mind if you have a desert in your own thought-stream, you're already absent of the multiplicity of meaning that a film/story points to. Tabla Rasa is a poor critic with nothing to compare to. I love the production values, acting as well as the depth of the writing. The only aspect of this that I absolutely cannot stand is the seemingly out of place Harfoot. Poorly drawn and definitely a distraction to the whole of the plot. If I could I would most definitely edit it all out from the rest of the story. Besides that I am a willing patron and can truly say LOVE IT! 8 without the Harfoot.

ipc-title__text: The Rings of Power - A Visually Stunning and Compelling Prequel Series
ipc-html-content-inner-div: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is an exciting new prequel series set in Middle Earth, based on J. R. R. Tolkien's beloved books. The show is produced by Amazon Studios, and the first season has already been released.The series takes place during the Second Age, thousands of years before the events of the original trilogy. It explores the rise of Sauron, the forging of the Rings of Power, and the epic battles that took place during that time.One of the standout elements of the series is the world-building. The production design is top-notch, with stunning landscapes and intricate details that bring Middle Earth to life. The costumes and makeup are also impressive, with a wide variety of creatures and characters that feel both familiar and new.The writing is also strong, with a talented cast bringing complex characters to life. There's a good mix of familiar faces and new characters, and the show does a good job of balancing multiple storylines without feeling overwhelming.The action and battle sequences are also impressive, with choreography and special effects that create a sense of epic scale. The show doesn't shy away from violence and brutality, but it never feels gratuitous.
