ipc-title__text: Why This Series Fails to Capture the Magic: A Fan's Disappointment
ipc-html-content-inner-div: If you're a fan of the original books or the movies, I strongly advise against watching this series. As someone who has both read the books and seen the film adaptations, I found this series to be an enormous letdown. From the very beginning, it becomes evident that this adaptation fails to capture the essence of the original material. The story lacks any coherent flow in relation to the books, making it feel disjointed and disconnected. If you're expecting the same rich, immersive experience that the books and movies offered, you're in for a rude awakening.First and foremost, the plot is all over the place. It feels like the writers took a handful of key scenes from the books, threw them into a blender, and hoped for the best. There's no logical progression or development; instead, we're left with a series of events that feel random and poorly thought out. Important character arcs are either ignored or reduced to mere clichés, leaving little emotional investment for the audience. The depth and complexity that made the original story so compelling are nowhere to be found.One of the biggest disappointments is the cast. The actors, while perhaps talented in other roles, seem out of place here. Their performances come across as superficial, lacking the depth and nuance required to bring these beloved characters to life. It's as if they're just going through the motions, delivering their lines without any real conviction or understanding of their roles. This results in a series of flat, uninspiring performances that fail to engage the viewer.Season 1 was somewhat acceptable, largely because it had the benefit of novelty and curiosity on its side. It wasn't great, but it wasn't terrible either. At least there was some attempt to stay true to the source material, and it provided a few moments that captured the spirit of the books. However, any goodwill earned in the first season is completely squandered in Season 2. The writing becomes even more erratic, and the plot veers off into nonsensical directions that have little to do with the original story.

ipc-title__text: A true masterpiece of scripted drama. Love, love, love it!
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Not going to waste too much space refuting the obvious troll reviews, but to say if you're a "Tolkien purist" who is going to nit-pick every detail not aligning "accurately" to the lore, this isn't the show for you. Firstly, the showrunners were restricted to the Lord of the Rings books and appendices and did not get the rights to anything in the Silmarillion or the other post-humously published manuscripts and notes. If you are upset at that, blame the estate for keeping such a iron grip on the expanded lore. Secondly, any mature adult recognizes that adaptations are going to have make a lot of changes to translate text to a living performance, and have to work with a lot of constraints.That being said, this show has absolutely blown me away so far. I have watched the first two episodes 5 times now and just watched the third last night. Everytime I rewatch the episodes, I notice some new little details. There is SO much information being conveyed in a few short scenes, that you will likely miss most of it the first time you watch. There are also a ton of easter eggs for references for lore junkies and fans of the Peter Jackson films.The sets, the costumes, the props, aren't just gorgeous to look at, they are extremely detailed and convey so much and truly bring middle-earth to life.The score by Bear McCreary is pure beauty. Unlike the triumphalist Wagnerian epic score from Howard Shore that helped make the Jackson trilogy so popular, this has a huge range of emotion, while conveying feelings of tragic beauty and loss in subtle way that Shore's music never could.So far, I love the characters and how they have been potrayed. The elves, southland men, dwarves, numenorians and harfoots all have been introduced with their own unique culture, accents and way of life. Galadriel, by Morgynn Clark, is shown as a haughty, arrogant elf who is obsessed with her mission. She is NOT the Lady of Lothlorien yet, but watching her develop over time will be really interesting. Elrond is done wonderfully, but perhaps my favorite is Nori of the Harfoots. I love every second of the harfoots.With the exception of the prologue in episode 1, which quickly explains the events of the first age, the story itself takes place during the 2nd age, when the rings of power (as the title suggests), are just being forged, and Sauron has gone into hiding. There are a lot of new, original character and locations created just for the show, that gives the writers a lot of liberty to craft new stories, and show us more of the world of Middle Earth. The timeline is going to be siginificantly altered from the books, and many parts will be compressed or happen in different order. I think that makes perfect sense, otherwise, we would have to sit through centuries of just elves talking. The has been a lot of discussion of who is secretly Sauron in disguise and what some of the other "mysteries" are. While these are fun for the audience to keep themselves busy with fan theories, the real essence of this story is mythology and destiny, and morality.I think that's what this show does so right. They could have made this a typical gritty, intrigue-laden telenovela or soap opera that had fantasy elements in it for show, but they made the right choice by bring to life Tolkien's mythical world. This is NOT some low-brow teen romance drama, or shock-value violent fantasy show. I think a lot of people looking for "plot holes" or whether what this character or that character did "made sense" fundamentally do not understand mythology and folklore or religion-based literature. There are so many layers of depth to this show, that will keep you re-watching over and over, each time seeing something new or having a new perspective. This is storytelling at its best. This is a work of art. It's poetry and opera rendered in ultra-high definition.I am so glad I didn't listen to the trolls and watched this show. There's only a handful of shows that captured my attention this much, but this is the only one that has moved me on multiple levels. I am giving this a solid, well-deserved, 10 out of 10. Bravo!

ipc-title__text: The Rings of Power: A Disappointing Attempt
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Amazon's The Rings of Power presents a disappointing departure from Tolkien's works. The series suffers from significant writing issues, particularly in its dialogue. While aiming for sophistication, the script often feels empty, failing to effectively drive the narrative or develop characters.Evidence of a series in trouble emerged within the first several minutes with the introductory monologue: "Do you know why a ship floats and a stone cannot? Because the stone sees only downward. The darkness of the water is vast and irresistible." The writers in their attempt to sound "Tolkienesque" without actual source material produced dialogue that is pretentious and devoid of meaning. I remember thinking during that initial scene: "uh-oh, this won't end well for Amazon".The series does not develop an audience affinity for any characters, or develop characters altogether.The plot meanders through numerous subplots without building a compelling central story.Overall, it was a chore to watch.Sometimes it takes an initial season for show runners and writers to find their footing. Given the substantial monetary investment Amazon has made, perhaps Season 2 will demonstrate improvement.

ipc-title__text: The Directors and Writes copied bad 90's/2000's Sci-Fi and Fantasy Shows
ipc-html-content-inner-div: As the season drags on, the quality of the show fails to meet the standard most people attribute to the LOTR world building or the budget Amazon threw at the show.The special effects, landscapes, scenery and musical score are really the only thing that is better than any other run of the mill fantasy show. The casting falls in line with current film trends of diversifying the cast to reach a wider audience which is nothing new and can be easily accepted in spite of the source material (the writing of the characters not so much... see below). It has a few stand out actors and a few that are just there which is normal for a large cast on a TV show. Over all, the set up is good.However, the writing decisions and scene decisions are what I would expect from a regular, soon to fail, one-season and done, generic show that SYFY channel produced on an even smaller budget. It is plagued by flashy scenes that don't do anything for the plot, events occurring because the need to happen and not because they are plausible or well written, the main characters survive only because of plot amor and not because of well written explanations, character development that is either predictably bad, contradictory, or just bland. This show also has all the typical tropes and cliches you find in fantasy films and TV but they feel out of place, misused or there just their for the sake of being their.I thought the writers would have learned from all the 90's and early 2000's TV shows that made all these tropes obvious and some of which actively made fun of them for how bad they are.

This show is incredibly well done & it is obvious that the writers, directors & actors fully embraced & preserved the spirit of Tolkien. A+ production value as well, an instant classic. Ignore the naysayers, for they are not true Tolkien fans if they're caught up in pettiness & hate, which so many of them are, sadly.Galadriel's ferocity & single minded purpose is well acted, Elrond's curiousity & love of the world is also well conveyed. The locations they play in as the story unfolds are magically interwoven & it's clear they relied on the visual artists who've painted Tolkien inspired art for decades. #kudos.

ipc-title__text: Would've been a fine fantasy show had it been an original story; but this is not Tolkien
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I get that Amazon does not have the rights to The Silmarillion, and I fully understand that a 1:1 adaptation is impossible. However.There are simply too many lore and character changes. For instance, Galadriel. Other than the fact that the actress is so far the weakest of the cast, her motivations for going & staying in Middle Earth are wrong, her husband Celeborn and their daughter are nowhere to be seen, and they're portraying her as this rebellious "there's a tempest in me" young Galadriel, when in fact she's one of the oldest elves in Middle Earth at the moment, she's already +5'000 years old... it just doesn't make any sense.Then you have small yet weird lore changes such as Gil-Galad being the one to tell Elves to go to Valinor, Celebrimbor looking old, Isildur being born before the forging of the rings, the hobbits having a prominent storyline in the Second Age...There are some positives points though: The character Nori so far is the most interesting, I think the actress is the strongest of the cast she really captures that sense of wonder and adventure; the Disa-Durin dynamic is interesting and the diner with Elrond was so far the best moment in the series (as of episode 3). The visuals of the series are amazing, you can see that the budget went into making the show looking good.Unfortunetely, looking good is not enough when it comes to TV, especially when one claims to adapt Tolkien. The writing and the pacing are a real problem in this show. The fact that we have several POVs can work, but here we switch too quickly from one to another, not having enough time to connect with the characters. I'm still invested to continue, because it's still based on a story that is very dear to me and I will hope until the very end that it will get better.

ipc-title__text: Fair enough by itself, but doesn't worth its hype and production cost
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Well, what should we expect from childish story based on such brilliant but still child fairy tales as Mr. Professor overhyped novels? Especially with the tons of $ poured by Amazon?Definitely - gorgeous picture, the simplest good/evil dichotomy, beautiful men and women, silly but funny swordplay, ridiculous and pretentious monologues, basic but still attractive race archetypes - all these Elves, Dwarves, Orcs, Humans...Well... we got all this. Nor less, nor more.It was always amusing for me to observe endless attempts of infantile adults to approve that Tolkien tales could have some value for 20+ people. Of course, all that attempts failed pathetically by very simple reason - u shouldn't have some higher purpose to have fun from child fairy tale. Bright, basic, slightly stupid tale - that's what we love Tolkien world for. After all, contemporary art (its both mass and elitist culture entities) is too demanding and even exhausting sometime. Short relax wouldn't harm - and contrary to typical superheroic movies or remastered classics, Tolkien's stories are really safe choice and stillwater port in the storm.Typical claims for this series like poor character development, weak story, boring dialogues - all are irrelevant. Because all of it are the same in the book source material - and if we're speaking about The Silmarillion, also boring as hell. The demands 'follow the source material to the letter' not just irrelevant but ridiculous - it's The Second Age, the time period almost NOT covered by any novels (and even that tiny pieces of information we have was post mortem publications - the veeery questionable source, indeed). So, all recited issues aren't issues at all.The main problem with Rings of Power series is its... ordinariness, let put it this way. According to world-range hype and insane budget of the show , we have rights to expect absolutely breathtaking visual and unmatched epic level of Good vs Evil struggle.Instead... we got very humble scale of conflicts, acceptable but very cheap CGI, ridiculous outfits, no beautiful heroes nor disgusting villains, no true love nor primordial hate, stupid fight scenes, et cetera, et cetera...Series are pretty good as standalone product, but as a door to Wonderland of our childhood it doesn't stand any criticism. It's like dive into magic pool and instead of picturesque kingdom with dragons, fayries, sorcery and princesses find yourself in a respectable private middle school. Everything is ok, no real danger around, landscapes and people are pretty nice... Just no magic.I definitely don't drop this series and will watch Season 2 with pleasure - but Rings of Power definitely won't take place in my list of top 10 fantasy shows. Enjoyable, but nothing special. Fair 5/10.

The plot is really slow to develop. Few characters draw any interest (Arondir & Isildur mostly). The acting is stiff and there's lots of pointless dialog. The female leads are (probably) supposed to be strong but come across one dimensional and self serving. The male leads are weak, uninteresting, and easily displaced by women or villains. The most annoying character is Galadriel who, sadly, gets most of the screen time. She is a two dimensional actress and doesn't care about anyone but herself. This plays like a bad MCU movie, and bears no resemblance to Tolkien's world. This should not be linked in name to the Lord of the Rings books.There are many distortions, but here's one. Why is Galadriel in armor, fighting with a sword? She's a caster, not melee. Tolkien wrote her with magical super-powers which made her a truly awesome & powerful female character (maybe the most powerful among all elves). Why rewrite her to be more physically strong and adept with swords than her male companions, when she could have dominated using her magical powers and remained true to the essence of the character Tolkien created? Instead they replaced Tolkien's powerful female, diminishing her into what feels like a generic 'action hero' cookie-cutter 'strong woman', assembled from stylized clichés brainstormed in focus-groups whose frame of reference is Marvel, not Tolkien. The result is a formulaic debasement of the original Galadriel.Change the names of all the characters, give the series a different title, so it doesn't offend Tolkien fans; and you'd at least have an average-to-poor fantasy that might appeal to some kids who haven't read Tolkien. To call this Lord of the Rings is a travesty of a canonical text.

ipc-title__text: The Rings of Power is not supposed to be the universe of the Trilogy.

ipc-html-content-inner-div: The Rings of Power" is a show that promises much but delivers little, feeling more like a telenovela than an epic fantasy series. The narrative is disjointed and relies heavily on coincidences, making it difficult to invest in the story. Those hoping for an exploration of the rich lore surrounding the Rings of Power will be sorely disappointed. Instead, the series introduces a host of new characters and storylines that have no basis in Tolkien's works, consuming valuable screen time that could have been better spent on the actual tale.The show underestimates its audience's intelligence, spoon-feeding them every detail as if they were incapable of following a complex plot. It's clear that Amazon anticipated a distracted viewership, designing a series that one can watch while doing household chores. Sadly, this approach strips the show of any depth or engagement, leaving it as a hollow, unremarkable addition to the fantasy genre.

ipc-html-content-inner-div: "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" is set in the world of J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth. The show has garnered attention for its grand storytelling, which unfolds long before the events of "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings." It's a tale of the emergence of great powers, kingdoms rising to glory and falling to ruin, unlikely heroes being tested, hope hanging by the finest of threads, and great villains threatening to cover all the world in darkness.The series has not been without its detractors, criticized for: pacing issues, at the halfway point of the series, there had been little action, which contrasts sharply with the dynamic pacing of Peter Jackson's film trilogies; a lack of depth in character development compared to the source material; characters and cultures portrayed as uncharacteristically harsh; the dialogue attempts to deliver elegant similes or use metaphors, but often fall flat, the show over-extend itself to create unique idioms; the costume designs, particularly for characters like Galadriel and her elven soldiers, have left much to be desired.It is a reasonable assumption that the show will be forgotten soon after it's final episode has been published.

ipc-title__text: A harrowing disregard for the source material
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I don't write reviews often but I truly just need to express how much this series pained me. The original trilogy is something that has always been a beacon of comfort and a reliable source of entertainment for me over the years. Upon hearing that there was going to be a new TV show, I had high expectations. Amazon however has disappointed me immensely, choosing to desecrate Tolkien's works with unrealistic ethnography and ironically sexist depictions of female characters. I can understand a show being boring, each work is enjoyed by different people, but boredom is the least of my concerns with this show. The dialogue is abysmal, the characters aren't compelling or even logical, the amount of plot holes is absurd and the scaling of middle earth doesn't even come into it. Tolkien's world is a depiction of what a fantasy-medieval would look like and thus provides comfort and engagement for the wider audience. This show is not that. This show is a reflection in a dirty mirror, one which displays all the most irrelevant social issues imaginable. That is 'irrelevant' to the world of Tolkien, not to our current society, we are still very much burdened with gender and racial discrimination. This show does nothing to solve that, it doesn't even make sense. A pitiful disgrace to the life's work of Tolkien and a great disappointment to his fandom.

ipc-title__text: Naysayers be gone, RoP is Excellent
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I'll give this the only praise a show or movie needs: this show got me into all of Lord of the Rings. Fellowship came out when I was in junior high, and for one reason or another, movie and the trilogy it belonged to didn't hook me. Granted, I was 13 at the time and I thought that LotR was competing with The Matrix trilogy for reasons only a 13-year-old would understand, but that's another subject.From the onset of The Rings of Power, I was captivated by these characters. There's something about an origin story that I truly love. Knowing where the ship is headed somehow makes the journey getting there more enjoyable to me. It felt like diving into a rabbit hole where this universe had the space to breathe and expand. To take its time telling the story. It's like the show has slowed the speed of the story down and delved into fine details in a way that makes all of it feel real. Don't get me wrong, I love a good Spielberg movie with John Williams dropping the beat, but there's also something to the style of The Walking Dead that makes the unbelievable seem believable.Do I know all the lore about LotR? No, I do not. Have I read the books? Sure haven't. Did I binge watch the original trilogy, the hobbit trilogy, replay Shadow of Mordor, start Shadow of War, and dive deep into Wikipedia to understand the lore and timeline of this story after watching 3 episodes? Sure did.This show got me into Lord of the Rings - all of it and all of the wonderful things that are Lord of the Rings. That's the highest praise I can think to give. Unironically, ten out of ten, highly recommend.

It fair to say, this show has been deliberately targeted by SocMed trolls to reduce the ratings score. I've literally no idea why anyone would do such a thing. It smacks of wanton immature vandalism. I have no problem with reviews that don't like one thing or another with a production but to then score the review with 1 or 2 stars indicates to me that the body of the review is made to throw people off the scent. I would probably have scored the show an 8 but to counteract the review bombing I've give it a 10.So what to say about the show?Well, the casting is exceptional and acting is Royal Shakespeare Company standard. Many of the actors will be unfamiliar to US, & indeed UK, audiences but don't let that put you off. Most shows that have a story to tell and don't want a celebrity to get in its way will cast relative unknowns. For UK audiences a number of faces will be familiar, in particular Sir Lenny Henry. For those who don't know Lenny is a comedian by profession but for the last 20 years he has taken on more an more straight acting roles. His most notable acting achievement was playing Othello on the West End. The other actors give faultless performances, and all of them a very belivable in thor roles.The costume design is beyond belief for a TV show. There is literally no distinction from the LOTR & Hobbit movies.The set design is of equal; stature. The quality of the filming is off the chart. We've talked about how superb some TV shows are these days, barely a difference between their production standards and that employed in film making. Well, I'm also watching the latest GOT: House of the Dragon, which falls into that category. It has a definite movie feel about each episode. However, when I watch TROP the level of production is mind blowingly good. Again, there is no discernable difference to the movies. If anything TROP is far far better.The first two episodes have started to plot out what will be a great story, that by season 5 will have spanned 3500 years. So assuming there will be 40 episodes it means each show covers about 90 to 100 years. Expect the story to skip along. Also bear in mind that Elves don't age very quickly and most other people of Middle Earth live somewhat longer lives than we humans. That said, characters will come and go. The story so far has been about setting the scene and establishing the premise of the season, which appears to be about searching for Sauron, even though many Elves think he has gone, and starting the work to create the rings of power. All in all we're 2 hours in and we know what motivates people, what their objectives are and who we can't really trust. I'm all set for the next episode but I have re-watched S01E01 & S01E02 already. It was well worth it.The music is by Howard Shore so you can expect it to be of the same quality of the movies and indeed it is. There are times when no background music is needed and they use it anyway and that did seem a little over the top. But then again Shore does use leitmotif to good effect, which all adds to that high quality dramatic feel. However, he hasn't reprised them from the movies. He's created new ones for this production, though it has a very similar tone to the original soundtracks that we all love so much.In terms of direction the show is faithful to the character traits defined by Tolkien and brought to life by Jackson. There are 3 directors for the season, with Wayne Yip bagging 4 episodes. He has a great pedigree having directed shows on a huge range of top class sci-fi & fantasy TV dramas over the last 10 years.Many Tolkien Pedants insist the show isn't faithful to this or that and some of it is true. There is artistic licence taken when introducing new characters and new story lines. However, none them undermine the work of the novelist and if anything, I'm sure Tolkien would not have minded. He created Middle Earth as a possible mythology for the people of the British Isles separate from the mythologies we inherited from our ancestors. Those mythologies are interpreted & reinterpreted all the time. No one in Sweden or Denmark complains if Thor is in a Marvel movie fighting Thanos. So to criticise this production as being unfaithful to Tolkien (which it isn't by the way) is to treat his work as a religious text and the shows producers as apostates. My take is these pedantic trolls would never be satisfied and should be ignored. I will confess, I can be very critical of shows that leave important things out. I still get annoyed at Jackson for not putting Tom Bombadil in the LOTR:TFOTR, either in the theatrical release or the extended edition. That said, I didn't go out and slag the whole movie off, I reviewed it on its merits as they appeared and not as I wished them to be. If I had been the director I'd have made different choices but I'm not and to judge something as if I was seems immature and petty.So, overall I am extremely pleased with the show so far and can only expect it to get better. If I was Amazon I would consider presenting it in cinemas as an 8-hour bingefest, in the run up to Season 2. It will be a sell out, I'm sure.

Rather than realize this, the show jettisons any sort of fidelity to lore and common sense by blending elements from throughout the second age into scrambled narrative that doesn't make sense on its own terms.Characters do not understand the world they exist in and struggle to make logical decisions. The dialogue in the show is best described as a cheap imitation of weighty and meaningful dialogue. Characters attempt to convey the importance of events by how they speak, and not what they say.Visually the show can be appealing, but the impact is blunted by some of the design choices and the poor execution of other elements throughout the show.This show fails on its own merits. It is all the more tragic when the source material is Tolkien.

I had to check Twitter after watching this episode and I wasn't surprised the consensus was that this was maybe the most epic piece of cinema people have seen in a series..So, this show gives it an A++ on effort. ipc-title__text: So horribly boring, almost every aspect is wrong just in the first 15 mins.

ipc-html-content-inner-div: Rings of Power is pretty good, but not great. It has some really good visuals, some parts looked like they were shot on film, and there's going to be more great visuals coming up. The opening explanation of the world and subsequent scenes have great fantasy imagery that people are going to absolutely love.I am not here as a Tolkien lover, I love a lot of Tolkien but haven't read much more than the fellowship. I am here as a lover of film. The pacing and writing of the show is pretty lacking for my taste. The opening paper boat scene didn't really act as the "hook" that most films immediately need. What the scene really did was set up my lowered expectations. It set up Galadriel's character arc in 10 seconds, going from an innocent child to vengeful. And it also set up the quality of the writing. Her brother sits her down and says "Why do boats float but rocks sink to the bottom? It is because a ship looks up to the light while the rock only looks down to the darkness." This made me let out a cow-like moan as I rolled my eyes.Moving on to the snow area, a party member gets hurt and they must help him, but Galadriel says "No we keep moving." The party gasps and explains a member needs help. Galadriel turns around and gives them the stink eye. This made me laugh. What was once a race of proud, noble, perfectionist elves, are now dramatic soap opera characters. The scene could have been Galadriel turning around and kneeling down to the wounded party member as she notices the landscape around her and says "we're already here." But instead she just gave them the stink eye and got mad. It didn't feel right. And then her party didn't respect her anymore. And it didn't feel right.All in all, I think the writing is very mediocre and almost unbearable. Galadriel being a strong action hero could work, but this version does not work well. Let's look to Eowyn in the Lord of The Rings films. We build her character for a long time, and when she finally decides to go to war, it's incredible. It's emotional. She has gone through so much and we understand her actions. Maybe Galadriel's arc will feel incredible and well earned as the show progresses, but with what I've already been introduced to, I don't think there's much more to expect.It's not that "The show doesn't feel like Tolkien." or "The show doesn't feel like Peter Jackson." It's that the show DOES feel like a mediocre soap opera with above average visuals. Good writing is good writing, plain and simple. A lot of people are going to love the show and thats great! But there are valid complaints and criticisms with its quality. It's not horrible, but its not incredible. I didn't love it, but hopefully you do!

ipc-title__text: A rocky start but a thundering finish
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I would take with a grain of salt any reviews that are only based on a couple of episodes. The start of Rings of Power is, to be completely honest, rocky. You're left wondering who various people are, or what their significance is, or why characters are doing what they're doing. There are also events that just plain don't get expanded on, which leaves you scratching your head. But just like the first couple of books in the Wheel of Time series, you really have to give the first few episodes of this show a chance. Once you do, the last half of the season builds and builds and the final episode is a masterful crescendo.I can't wait for season 2, now that characters are cemented and there's understanding about the events taking place, it will be great to see *how* they tell the story from hereon in.To be clear, that doesn't excuse some of the mistakes of the early episodes. Some of the portrayal of elves is odd - they are shown doing acrobatics at some points, yet when walking around in heavy armor some actors/actresses seem wooden rather than graceful. Some of the scriptwriting is terribly cliché and not very clever. Some of the battle scenes are disjointed, with gaping holes in the action that seem engineered ("all the assailants, go have a five minute break so we can cover this other important point!").Yet there are also gems; Aramayo is a fantastic Elron, and masters the tricky job of portraying a character living several thousand years prior to someone else's portrayal. The CGI and atmosphere is incredible, and easily does the film's style justice. The music works well especially toward the end of the season - hints and suggestions at earlier themes, without a straight rip-off of melodies.All in all, if you've been on the fence about watching this series, or watched an episode and didn't like it - give it a fair shot. Season 2 is coming one way or another, and I'd rather have a series going from bad to good than the other way around (GoT style).

ipc-title__text: A rocky start but a thundering finish
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I would take with a grain of salt any reviews that are only based on a couple of episodes. The start of Rings of Power is, to be completely honest, rocky. You're left wondering who various people are, or what their significance is, or why characters are doing what they're doing. There are also events that just plain don't get expanded on, which leaves you scratching your head. But just like the first couple of books in the Wheel of Time series, you really have to give the first few episodes of this show a chance. Once you do, the last half of the season builds and builds and the final episode is a masterful crescendo.I can't wait for season 2, now that characters are cemented and there's understanding about the events taking place, it will be great to see *how* they tell the story from hereon in.To be clear, that doesn't excuse some of the mistakes of the early episodes. Some of the portrayal of elves is odd - they are shown doing acrobatics at some points, yet when walking around in heavy armor some actors/actresses seem wooden rather than graceful. Some of the scriptwriting is terribly cliché and not very clever. Some of the battle scenes are disjointed, with gaping holes in the action that seem engineered ("all the assailants, go have a five minute break so we can cover this other important point!").Yet there are also gems; Aramayo is a fantastic Elron, and masters the tricky job of portraying a character living several thousand years prior to someone else's portrayal. The CGI and atmosphere is incredible, and easily does the film's style justice. The music works well especially toward the end of the season - hints and suggestions at earlier themes, without a straight rip-off of melodies.All in all, if you've been on the fence about watching this series, or watched an episode and didn't like it - give it a fair shot. Season 2 is coming one way or another, and I'd rather have a series going from bad to good than the other way around (GoT style).

ROP does this well.The other challenge is properly depicting the high moral character of Tolkien in the tension between good and evil. Here one has to be so careful, its like making a Biblical movie, take too much license and you'll pay a high price. Tolkien was a Christian and friend to C. S. Lewis. He had no grey 'wokeness' about good and evil.On this score ROP is doing ok but must take care not to let modern political correctness taint this world, there simply is no room for it, it only muddies the water. ipc-title__text: Mediocre with some really poor writing
ipc-html-content-inner-div: The show is fairly mediocre so far, feels more like a Saturday night BBC family show than a $1 billion fantasy epic.Positives are: the visuals are mostly impressive, there are some likeable characters (Nori, Durin, Disa, Elrond), the bare bones of the plot are fine albeit we still haven't moved very far, the orcs use practical effects which is better than the Hobbit at least.Negatives: the dialogue is very hit and miss (leaning more towards miss with some extremely clunky lines that completely take you out of a scene- it often feels like something a high school student would write), some of the costuming and aesthetic feels too fancy dress especially when compared to the lord of the rings trilogy, the dialogue is extremely repetitive and many of the characters feel lifeless (there's been little if any character development and I still feel like most characters can simply be characterised by their plot purpose rather than who they are, I.e. Arondir is just "the Southlands elf who loves the human", Galadriel is still just "The elf woman who's looking for Sauron"- they don't feel like real characters and it's hard to care about them. The plot moves the characters instead of the other way around. It also feels like the plot is in fact stalling/stretching which is why we get repetitive arcs while we wait for plot points to catch up, it means the episodes move quickly with strange mini arcs but then at the end of it we haven't really gone anywhere with the main plot. I'll probably see where this season goes but I doubt I'll bother with the next season unless there's some significant improvements.

5 episodes down the line and the plot is so boring. Random scenes, random dialogues from people we don't even care about. In fact it's so badly written that the show runners have kept some characters, like Adar or "Gandalf" a "secret" to increase anticipation without success.Being a huge fan of PJ trilogy, the scripting is pathetic. The fact that the writters try so hard to make some stuff sound poetic ("The sea is right"....) is even funnier. If you're not going to use any of Tolkien's writing in the script, then you might as well not call this Lotr but some generic fantasy thingie. Had low expectations even before this show kicked off, but now it's just unbearable.

ipc-title__text: Amazing, depending on what you want
ipc-html-content-inner-div: For me, this is an absolute banger of a series.I love Tolkien, I love beautiful music and seeing the amazing landscapes of middle earth, I love watching elves talking about sailing west, I love watching Galadriel trying to find evidence that Sauron is alive, I love watching hobbies talk about wandering un-known paths. I see nothing so far that conflicts with Tolkien's works (although there is certainly much invention in this series but it's invention that fits and has its place).If you don't like these things, you won't like the series. The only thing I didn't love was how mundane the elves seem. Although all of them acted very well I think, there is something disappointing in how much the elves are made to resemble people. The elf Gil-Galad, the elven king, who is literally the name Aragorn cries sometimes when rushing to battle, seems a bit petty and mundane here.On the other hand, the vistas and cities are breathtaking and I just want to spend more time there. I wish the series never end and I haven't been this excited over a TV series in years. I find very little to fault and I feel the series isn't getting the credit it deserves.

ipc-title__text: I am thoroughly enjoying this show!

ipc-title__text: It's just not very well made
ipc-html-content-inner-div: This is supposed to be this ripe cinematic product that took a while to get done, got reworked and then reworked some more. We're given a promising start with beautiful visuals and imagery and words that appeared like the series might be deep and allegorical. And then, these hopes fade all too quickly and the series turns into this Troy-type modern peplum series with cued Hollywood-style transitions and stereotypical dialogs. In just a couple of episodes, already it doesn't feel like the Tolkien universe. The worst thing is most of the subplots aren't interesting. One of them might convey a sense of intrigue, but most of the time the characters go on about their quests, and they're not engaging simply because they're introduced too quickly before any affinity has had the time to bloom between the audience and those fictional characters. It's like they go on these tirades, but no one really cares. The characters' plights are too sudden, or too standard and rehashed, and it's difficult to really care. As the audience we're supposed to be treated to cinematic excellence, to just have to sit back and be genuinely entertained, but instead it takes a lot of work to even come close to wanting it.

ipc-title__text: The CGI is very good but the acting and directing is uninspired.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: It's hard to screw up Tolkien and there are exciting ideas in here, like how was Mount Doom created. It seems like they spent so much money on the CGI that they had little to spend on good actors, writers and directors. You can't stick on a pair of elf ears and expect Peter Jackson level of character development, and that's really what is missing. I am struggling to find characters that I care about. I will continue to watch purely on the the chance that I will learn more of the back story that Tolkien developed for TLOTR trilogy, and that may be enough for many of us.

Not in my wildest dreams, almost 40 years ago when I immersed myself in the world of Tolkien beyond the LOTR and into the Simarillion could I have imagined that they would actually make this. Aside from the awesome production, the acting is brilliant and the story is intriguing, and we can be sure that what is coming is going to be even better. They should relax and enjoy and if they are Tolkien fans they should count themselves lucky.After two episodes I'm wondering how Sauron will deceive Celebrimbor, because this is the crux of the whole story which extends thousands of years to the end of the return of the king, when Galadriel is finally allowed to take ship to the west.

I'll review this on its own merits, rather than in relation to any other Tolkien-related media.The plot is utterly nonsensical. Without spoiling, should you be masochistic enough to watch this billion-dollar mess, the plot relies on a series of contrivances and out-of-character actions. One example which will not spoil anything.A group is under threat. They go to a safe place. They then destroy the safe place because the plot requires them to be in danger later in a different place in order to be saved by another group.Every episode is like this. There is never foundation laid that lasts multiple episodes, rather tension is built and released within minutes, sometimes immediately, so that there are never any real stakes. If you watch the first 20 minutes after the scene setting of episode 1 (the cold bit, you'll know what I mean if you watch it) is a good example. Again, every episode is like this.There are numerous plot threads, of which roughly half are irrelevant to the overall story, and could easily have been cut. This is even more obvious when tonally deaf editing decisions cause scenes that might carry some weight are immediately undercut by comedy relief.Further on the plot, a lot of plot points happen off screen, with the audience required to perform mental gymnastics to piece the disparate events together. The driving action is never properly fleshed out and the result is a series of 'and then this happens' until the credits roll.In terms of character writing, very few characters are believable. I would be fine with characters being unlikeable, but in order for the plot to progress the characters have to act against either their interests or their character goals. There are barely any moments of true characterisation, by which I mean a character doing something because it is established in the character. Rather characters do things because the plot requires them to, and the abilities of characters are repeatedly forgotten about by the writers for plot convenience. This ranges from characters with super senses being suddenly deaf for a scene, to characters magically gleaning information they have no way to know, to characters flip flopping on their morals as the plot requires. This is possible because basically no effort or time is spent on characterising them.The main character is utterly unlikeable, if only because of a complete lack of self awareness and critical thinking skills. Bear in mind that this character is meant to be very, very experienced in life, war and politics. When you watch the show, ask yourself what an average person would do whenever this character does something. You'll find shortly that the main character is deranged by any metric. Again, this would be fine, but many other characters act as if the main character can do no wrong. There is no consistency whatsoever in this regard.The main villain is the most sympathetic character in the show, and this is a serious problem with the writing. The main villain can be sympathetic, understandable even, but should always be the character the audience likes the least. The reason for this, without spoiling, is because the characters actions are motivated by somewhat consistent character traits. That's the bar.For the good. The clothes look pretty good, and are fairly distinctive (except the armour, thats awful). The visual effects are good, and the music, while not placed over appropriate scenes, is also good. Some of the actors also do a good job, and its a real shame to see their talent be wasted on such a poor script. I only hope it doesnt damage their careers in the long run. That's the three stars. VFX, music, some actung and (some) costume design.I could go on, but for the sake of the length of this review, I'll leave it more or less there.The short version - neither the plot nor characters are constructed in a way that makes narrative sense. Characters do things because the plot requires it, and when the plot obviously makes no sense then it just happens off screen as a cliffhanger. There are no stakes, and the plot consists of a series of mystery boxes, trailer scenes and callbacks to better LOTR media.For funsies, before watching the show, have a look at how many credits the two writers had before putting pen to paper in this. It explains a *lot*, and remember too, it cost 1 *billion* dollars. Good luck.

ipc-title__text: Doesn't matter if its lore accurate, its still a bad show.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: It gets 2 stars only thanks to some decent visuals.The show is terrible. Clean and simple, if it you rate it as a standalone show that has nothing to do with Lord of The Rings its a 2-3 star show. If its to be considered tolkien or based on peter jacksons its a 0-1 star show. Why the difference? Well thats simple, you dont get to butcher the lore all while pretending to appeal to a big fandom.To put it simply, Rings of Power is boring and terribly written even if you consider it, its own show. The writing is laughably bad, the acting is terrible (tho that could also be in part bad writing and on-site directing). The show logic is missing, and the choreography is horrible.It does have some few visuals that are good, but that gets ruined by poorly cast baby face actors, horrible costume designs and that god awful slowmotion horse goblin face scene, the hell where they thinking.Show is slow, nothing really happens. When it does happens its devoid of logic and poorly executed.If it was a show with a 50 mil budget i could forgive it. But its the highest budget show of all time. And for that reason alone it deserves to be a 1 star show. Truly the worst show ever made, once you factor in the price vs the result.

ipc-title__text: It's not better than the Peter Jackson movies, but the story serves as a prequel
ipc-html-content-inner-div: It's not up there with the movies made by Peter Jackson, but it's an interesting prequel. The production and the story are good, and at least they had the decency to include Howard Shore to compose the main theme which is amazing. The inclusion of black people does give a strange feeling, but that is something that can be ignored and that every viewer should do. The black elf actor is not bad. Too bad the pigmentation is somewhat questionable, but the character is not bad. The truth is very difficult to say that this series is inclusive, since no matter how much they say it, in the end they are minor things that can be ignored. Galadriel becomes quite hateful in some ways. But that's because after losing her brother, she was consumed by revenge, and it's no wonder she's become so defiant, neglectful, and even obnoxious. Since she is willing to fulfill her goal no matter who she puts at risk, she therefore has a long way to go to become the Galadriel seen in Jackson's films. Another point against it is that it is not a very epic series, since there is not much action and it can be boring. But being the first season, it is nothing more than the first chapter of a journey that is supposed to be 5 seasons to learn more about the events that lead to the Peter Jackson trilogy. From that aspect it is an interesting series, although it is difficult to see it since with all the nonsense that Amazon has said; But considering that he lied to the public and decided to take creative liberties, Tolkien's fans are now blinded by anger and the decisions Amazon made afterward didn't improve matters. On the one hand, Amazon condemned its own series, but the fans are either too demanding or are immature children who don't know how to be adults. The Rings Of Power is a fairly decent series whose only flaw is taking creative liberties that derive it from Tolkien's works. In that respect it falls short of the third installment of The Hobbit, but it is a fascinating prequel to learn a little more about the events that led to the Peter Jackson trilogy. My final grade for this series is 8/10.

ipc-title__text: I Loved It!! But Not Until I Watched the Beginning Again

I then wondered what I was thinking when I first watched! Did I fall asleep?? I loved it and got so much more out of it. I got excited about finishing the first season and wasn't disappointed! It was tremendous! Excellent character development and excellent story!! I can't wait until the 2nd season!

This series is, quite frankly, a mess...
It has some visually pleasing moments and nice scenery but the writing is extremely poor and each characters looked bland and inexpressive, with embarrassing lines of dialog. I simply didn't manage to build a connection with a single one of them.Worse than that, the show is not particularly entertaining, being downright boring at time. There is very little build up, ridiculously obvious plot twists, vague stakes and it's just hard to get hooked to what little story it offers. I'm not really sure what is going with the writing team but some serious self-reflection is needed here and perhaps a return to the basis. For the most expensive series of all time, taking place in the beloved LOTR universe, to say it was disappointing is putting it lightly.

ipc-title__text: I love this series so much! Can I work on it?
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I am a Tolkien fan, but I have never read The Silmarillion. I tried when I was fifteen and was so bored I gave up. I have no idea what happens prior to The Hobbit. Therefore, I had no expectations when it came to the storyline of this series.From the first episode I was hooked. I was hooked by the story (I've always been a fan of Galadriel) and the direction and cinematography of this series, costumes, the sets - visually it is probably the most beautiful fantasy series I have ever seen. I like the aesthetic much more than what is shown in Peter Jackson's movies (which were amazing, but I am not a fan of color filters). I love this series so much I wish to work on it! I'm a Story Artist. Can I?I love that there are so many ladies leading the show. It always bugged me that there were so few women in Tolkien's stories and they were always the ideals. I love the diversity (I remember Gimli mentioning that dwarf women had beards?). I love that the characters are not perfect and therefore have room to grow. The costumes for this show are insane! How? So beautiful. Elrond's and Durin's friendship - love. I love that they show Durin as as a real man with emotions...It does make me feel uncomfortable that the human race is so flawed, but maybe that is the point? It intrigues me that the elves are not perfect.As far as story being all over the place and difficult to follow, I personally had no such difficulty. This entire season feels like ACT 1 and it did what it needed to do - establish all the primary players and their goals. The show even manage to surprise me a few times and by this time in my life that is NOT easy.I don't know how accurate this is compared to the original books, but I don't care. I can't wait for the next season.

Now, when I initially saw the trailer for the 2022 series "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power", I wasn't exactly won over. But I figured that I would give the series a chance, as I do enjoy a proper fantasy tale or two.And I am glad that I opted to give "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" a fair chance, because I found it to be just as enjoyable as the two trilogy movie series were and as the online role-playing game is. So "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power", from creators Patrick McKay and John D. Payne, definitely was something that fitted right into the franchise of "The Lord of the Rings".Personally, I don't understand all the grief and hate that the series have gotten online. ipc-title__text: It's not better than the Peter Jackson movies, but the story serves as a prequel
ipc-html-content-inner-div: It's not up there with the movies made by Peter Jackson, but it's an interesting prequel. The production and the story are good, and at least they had the decency to include Howard Shore to compose the main theme which is amazing. The inclusion of black people does give a strange feeling, but that is something that can be ignored and that every viewer should do. The black elf actor is not bad. Too bad the pigmentation is somewhat questionable, but the character is not bad. The truth is very difficult to say that this series is inclusive, since no matter how much they say it, in the end they are minor things that can be ignored. Galadriel becomes quite hateful in some ways. But that's because after losing her brother, she was consumed by revenge, and it's no wonder she's become so defiant, neglectful, and even obnoxious. Since she is willing to fulfill her goal no matter who she puts at risk, she therefore has a long way to go to become the Galadriel seen in Jackson's films. Another point against it is that it is not a very epic series, since there is not much action and it can be boring. But being the first season, it is nothing more than the first chapter of a journey that is supposed to be 5 seasons to learn more about the events that lead to the Peter Jackson trilogy. From that aspect it is an interesting series, although it is difficult to see it since with all the nonsense that Amazon has said; But considering that he lied to the public and decided to take creative liberties, Tolkien's fans are now blinded by anger and the decisions Amazon made afterward didn't improve matters. On the one hand, Amazon condemned its own series, but the fans are either too demanding or are immature children who don't know how to be adults. The Rings Of Power is a fairly decent series whose only flaw is taking creative liberties that derive it from Tolkien's works. In that respect it falls short of the third installment of The Hobbit, but it is a fascinating prequel to learn a little more about the events that led to the Peter Jackson trilogy. My final grade for this series is 8/10.

After 5 episodes, I can conclude that the main purpose of this show was to destroy the source material, a labour at which the showrunners performed flawlessly.That is usually a terrible purpose to begin with, but we've seen it working many times in the past. Apocalipse Now is but a reimagination of Joseph Conrad's HOD, after all.It's obvious, however, that In order for this kind of experiments to succeed, the resulting product HAS to be superior (or at least, on the same level) to the source material. Bloodborne is basically a japanese man trying to reimaginate Lovecraft and succeding in creating something of equivalent value.However, Rings of power is so full of itself to even consider providing anything of value in return. It seems to take pride in the mere destruction of the "archaic" legacy of Tolkien.In the end, the main sin of this show (and the one that will get it cancelled more sooner than later) is that it takes pleasure in destroying something for the sake of it (or, to put it bluntly: for political reasons) while considering that the audience does not deserve something of the same quality in return.Fans will not support this nonsense, and the random person won't find anything of value here to feel attracted to swords, dragons and stuff.This is also, apparently, the most expensive show in Earth. A quality that not only does not help, further adding to the injury. Was it neccesary to spend so much money in destroying something?

ipc-title__text: Better have a copy of the Silmarillion handy if you want to say I'm wrong
ipc-html-content-inner-div: When Neil Gaiman said that he loved the premier, I knew it was going to be worth giving a chance despite over a year of knee-jerk reactionary hate among the "Purists" of the Tolkien fandom. You don't question the guy who wrote Sandman when it comes to good storytelling.Rings of Power is set in the Second Age. By and large there's probably not even 100 published pages of content regarding the events of this era in the history of Middle Earth. In the Silmarillion it accounts for not even 50 pages, Akallabeth is less than 40 total. We have largely no idea what day to day life was like nor what relations between the people of Middle Earth was like, except in the broadest brush strokes. This gives the creators tremendous creative freedom to add meat to a bare bones skeleton of the setting at within this time frame. As long as all the principal characters are where they need to be at the end of the Age, then I am all for however they want to portray these characters.Morfydd Clark is crushing it as Galadriel. I need people to understand their impression of Galadriel is mostly wrong. Galadriel in the Fellowship is a very different person than Galadriel in the Silmarillion, and Morfydd is playing the character from the Silmarillion exceptionally well. Keep in mind that Galadriel is described as the sole woman among the Noldor to stand up and call upon her people to leave Valinor for Middle Earth because she too wanted a kingdom to rule. She's also described as being second only to Fingolfin among the Noldor who migrated to Middle Earth over the glacial Helcaraxe. All this nonsense about her being a sorceress who spends her free time being dainty at home, like Elrond, *do not know* what Galadriel has seen.All the original characters are interesting, Nori and Arondir stand out to me as particularly exceptional without really trying. The dialogue is VERY Tolkien, and there aren't any wasted scenes. Every scene is doing something with regards to revealing information about the characters, helping us connect with them (as long as you're not going into it with an intentionally contrarian mindset). Production value is through the roof, you know you're back in Middle Earth.Honestly, I think it's funny people argue this "isn't Tolkien". I'll give you a challenge, Review Reader. Find the Dragon Helm of Dor Lomin in episode 2, and when you do take in the context where you see it. The attention to detail which goes into that moment is all you need to know about how faithful they are to Tolkien's world.

I watched this with no knowledge of this world from previous movies, nor have I read the books. Maybe this helped me appreciate it and enjoy it for what it is - a visual beauty with charismatic, engaging characters, and an interesting story line. I could not do that with this one. I had to WATCH it, so very beautiful, something a series hasn't done for me since this first 4 seasons of Game of Thrones. I'm looking forward to the rest of the series! Bravo!

Let me state up front I don't care how closely a show sticks to the source material. At the end of the day I just want to be entertained. That's why I turn the TV on. I couldn't be bothered to tune in to see if Amazon was faithful to Tolkien. Who cares?I will also add I don't care about the ethnicity/skin color casting "controversy". Put it down.The problem with the first two episodes is they aren't entertaining. A lot of characters are introduced, but they aren't interesting. The scenery is gorgeous, but nothing is done with it.Elves. They're presented as immature human teens. These are immortal beings. Even as teens they would have an entirely different perspective from us. It's one thing to make dopey decisions when you know won't be alive when the bill comes due (think US politicians), and quite another when you know you will have to live an eternity with the consequences of your actions. Entertain us with a different perspective on life.Supernatural elements. If you're going to have a guy swim across the ocean, you must consider the implications of these capabilities. "I'm going for a swim" would take on a new meaning. All land on the planet would have been discovered within the first few years. Entertain us with meaningful supernatural implications.Good vs Evil. For one thing, you can't apply human standards to decidedly non-human beings. For another, what even are human standards? They evolve over time and there has never been consensus at any given time. Yet all of these groups are operating under a twenty-first century western ethos. It's a lost opportunity. Entertain us with these groups presenting alien takes on the concepts of Right vs Wrong.Stakes. The stakes couldn't be lower. Virtually none of the characters care about the overarching Good vs Evil plot. If the characters don't care why should we? The characters operate as if the outcome is preordained and that it'll all work out in the end. Entertain us with stakes we are deeply invested in where the outcome hangs in the balance.Rising action. As there was essentially none in the first episode, one might think it could only go up from there in episode two. It didn't. Entertain us with action.Hobbit AKA Harfoots. Soap. Invest.This is a very pretty show where nothing entertaining is happening. I didn't watch another episode as I've put enough time into this.Two stars for the production values. No stars for not being interesting or funny or exciting or emotionally fulfilling or... entertaining. Two stars.

**Title: A Disappointment in Middle-earth: "The Rings of Power" Review***Rating: 2/10*"The Rings of Power" was supposed to be a triumphant return to Middle-earth, but instead, it delivers a hollow, frustrating experience that strays far from J. R. R. Tolkien's rich legacy. The series is plagued by poor acting, terrible dialogue, and a storyline that feels more like poorly crafted fan fiction than a faithful adaptation.The acting is one of the most glaring issues. Many performances are wooden and lack the emotional depth required for such an epic tale. Characters that should be commanding and memorable, like Galadriel, are reduced to bland, one-dimensional figures. Galadriel, in particular, is portrayed as impulsive and shallow, a far cry from the wise and ethereal presence in Tolkien's original works.The dialogue is another major flaw. Tolkien's language is known for its beauty and gravitas, but the series' lines are awkward, clunky, and jarringly modern. The lack of the poetic, lyrical quality that defines Tolkien's prose is palpable, leaving the characters sounding more like actors reading scripts than inhabitants of Middle-earth.Perhaps the most disappointing aspect is the story itself. The showrunners have taken significant liberties, inventing characters and plotlines that feel disconnected from the core of Tolkien's mythology. These deviations are poorly executed, making the narrative disjointed and difficult to engage with. Important moments are rushed, while unnecessary scenes drag on, resulting in a story that feels shallow and uninspired.Visually, "The Rings of Power" is stunning, with beautiful landscapes and impressive sets. However, the visual splendor only highlights the series' shortcomings. Despite its grand appearance, the show is ultimately an empty shell, lacking the depth, emotion, and authenticity that make Tolkien's world so beloved.In summary, "The Rings of Power" fails to honor Tolkien's legacy, offering a disappointing and hollow interpretation of Middle-earth that will leave fans yearning for something better.

It didn't need a mystery Sauron, it didn't need to make up a back story for Mithril, or the Balrog, or to make Galadriel an idiot who singlehandedly brought evil back into Middle Earth.The show writers butchered Galadriel, Elrond & Celebrimbor. It is very difficult to follow up on the LOTR and The Hobbit movies. They were an excellent interpretation of books the were long considered impossible to make into movies.ROP is a good effort to make something out of the other tales around middle earth, Tolkien wasn't able to finish. But it doesn't really match up to the previous movies. I can not really put my finger on it. Is it that the background actors sometimes move very wooden? Is it that the elves look like pointy eared humans, rather that the elves from LOTR and The Hobbit? Is it that the dynamics of the story is much slower? Is it that the details of the scenery sometimes look more simple? Is it the very poor character and acting of Arnodir? I really can't tell.It is good and very worthwhile to watch, but you, or at least I, can not stop comparing it with the earlier movies and then it is just doesn't match up.Additionally while season 1 is acceptable, season 2 goes down the drain. ipc-html-content-inner-div: There has been so much controversy leading up to this series I was half expecting something awful.There is so much depth to Tolkien's work and I have read much of it. In the end it is a hard balance to achieve in a TV adaptation. Stories need to be laid out and not rushed so the complaints about it being slow are unwarranted, this not some trivial genre like Marvel Universe. The foundation of stories have to be laid and I think so far it has been done well.The atmosphere is great, the visuals are wonderful. The storyline works so far, but of ourse it is abridged and not every tiny detail is written in the history of the second age, so I guess some artistic licence is warranted and has not been unacceptable. The balance of jovial humour and darkness of the storyline is ok so far, but I just hope it doesn't go the way of The Hobbit adaptation which just came across as too silly at times.The big issue that people seemed to make was the use of racial diversity. While I understand some of the concerns I did not find it bothersome at all, perhaps because I had already expected it, but it wasn not a source of distraction for me.So far I am pretty impressed, but it is still early in the season.

If you are into Tolkien, you won't be put off by pseudo-religious, esoteric bombast and angel-like sing-song-soundtracks. The Rings of Power naturally have all that, but if you are able to get through such things without allergic reactions this is a good-looking show. Entertaining, with good production values and a promise of more good stuff to come. Fantasy never is a thing for people with an allergy against pathos. So do expect an overdose of heroism, sword-swinging grandeur and very foreseeable character-shaping: Galadriel and Elrond will prevail heroicly, the king will be challenged by dark seductions but show his decency in the end, the not-yet-halflings will show heart and bravery although being small and otherwise more responsible for the necessary comic relief, the elbs will be angle-like, superior and slightly arrogant creatures and the numinors will show us to what heroic highs and lows mankind can aspire in extreme conditions. No one will be surprised by the general direction this will take, but I think we can trust the makers that they will provide an entertaining ride getting there. Not bad.

Furthermore of which is also leads to pointing out a flaw with the series; scenes do not get portrayed to their middle-earth location and for the average viewer or someone fresh to middle-earth would have no context as to who is where and what that represents to the bigger plot (probably less so at the end of the season).Little plot questions I would of liked more depth of explanation is to whom the White Cloaks are, rather than leaving any answers until season 2.Overall it was an enjoyable watch by the whole family and we look forward to any future installments, even besides myself dissecting each episode in my head, it was well made.

While being a huge fan of the books and films, I'm by no means a Tolkien die hard or geek. As a piece of work that delves deeper into what I've both read and watched before, I think the show pays excellent service to the Tolkien legacy. It feels familiar through and through. Maybe the characters aren't as well rounded or colourful, but the charm, spirit and energy shines through enough to make it very worthwhile. I must say, though, above all else, it's the visual splendour that shines the brightest. It's a work of art from frame to frame. By far the most magical and beautiful TV show I've seen. It leaps off the screen. From golden cities to magical forests to labyrinthine mines, the show is an absolute feast for the eyes. All lending itself beautifully to the narrative of the many characters that bring it to life. And the effects and scale are nothing short of breathtaking.Where it falls down is some of the characters could use a little more depth and engagement. The dwarves were great fun and I loved the wholesomeness of the Hobbits. The elves were characteristically stiff and regal and the orcs were characteristically snarly and feral. Ticked all the boxes. Just could use a little more punch to the characters beyond the well-constructed dialogue. There's also a couple of misfires with casting, but for the majority, the ensemble were great. The Hobbits and dwarves especially well played. Nori and Durin are superb!I realise there's a great deal of bad will towards the show for personal biases from the target audience, hence my 'perfect' score. The outspoken few can be extremely vile. Its not perfect, but it's up there with the best TV and I'm eager to see where it could go. It's just such a rich and engrossing show that it has real potential for greatness. More, please. More action, more beasts and a touch more sparkle to the leads and it could carry the Tolkien legacy high on its shoulders for years to come.

ipc-title__text: Refreshing watch Disney should pay attention

The most expensive show ever made, and it definitely looks like it. I can see a trend already.this was filmed beautifully, from the locations to the sets to the clothes and even the props, all of it has been the best I have seen in any tv show.about there being black actors playing certain parts, who cares? Looking forward to more episodes, the CGI is beautifully done so far!

How others vote this so highly.I had to turn off after part of episode 1, it's pretty, but that's it. Galadriel isn't on screen, it's someone else called by the same name. There is no ethereal character on screen, the elves aren't elves, just people with pointy ears, more akin to Vulcans than Elves.So i just don't understand, i've given 2/10 for visuals alone. Beautifully shot, stunning score, top tier acting and amazing visuals. Couldn't ask for a better show. Every episode had the feel of an entire film. No filler, no pointless violence or sex scenes that seems to plague fantasy shows.Every character felt deliberate and real. No bad one liners or silly comic relief, and thankfully no sketchy CGI. Having real costumes/prosthetics as well as real sets and location makes all the difference. I'm not going to lie i do still watch lotr and hobbit from time to time.I've never read the books. But i remember buying VCDs DVDs and digital versions of these movies. ipc-title__text: Understand the hate but found it enjoyable & worthy of my time

ipc-title__text: Looks outstanding, but under the surface it's a mess.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: The show looks absolutely outstanding with pretty great cinematography, set design and materials that look expensive. Here the budget truly shines, but when the actors to their part and deliver their lines from a lackluster script, following a story that bleak and boring. It's easy to see through the beautiful landscapes, and realize how horrible the writing and actual story is.The show didn't have to replicate the Peter Jackon trilogy, but still capture the magic of what made that world and atmosphere feel so special. Take inspiration from both books, the movies and lore surrounding the world of middle earth and beyond. Personally I have read the hobbit and the LOTR trilogy, so I do have some inside knowledge, but as the show is set many years before these events, I was excited to see Middle earth and the lands far away in a new light. I was pretty disappointed though as the show falters in so many aspects, where other fantasy shows and movies shine. Maybe in season 2 they will expand and hire new writers, but for now I was left with an empty feeling for the show's future seasons.The production value is extremely high and the set designs, clothes, materials and cgi look pretty outstanding, but they should have spent some of that money on developing a better story and hiring better writers that truly understand the source material.6/10.
