I thoroughly enjoyed the experience and I am really looking forward to the season which I have feeling will be even better. Give it a full try before you judge it.

ipc-title__text: Butchered Lore: A bad D&D film
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Probably is great if you've never watched a lord of the rings movie before and know absolutely nothing from the lore (like the script writers).The elves don't look or feel like Lord of the Rings elves, in fact they are hardly distinguishable from humans. Female dwarves don't have their iconic beards, and despite the high budget of the series the forced perspective shots that made the hobbits and dwarves appear diminutive in the Jackson films are sorely missing. The dwarves and elves are missing their iconic "crunch" - eleven elegance, slender height, and enchanting seriousness & the dwarves obstinance and craggy demeanour. Tolkien wrote greed and addiction wonderfully, as a cold slow burn, which would eat away at the characters over time... RoP's greed isn't sown throughout the series, instead it is simply flat, and appears as immature writing. In fact there is little subtle writing at all. It's obvious the writing and film crews were simply outclassed by the ones in the Jackson films.From the character side of things, Galadriel truly isn't even a whisper of the powerful sorceress who felt like she belonged amongst the like of Sauraman, Gandalf, and Elrond. She's reduced to nothing but a rebellious teenage Karen Mary Sue who has plot armour so thick that she carves through trolls like butter and can swim across entire oceans. Lots was moved and proxied due to incomplete copyright coverage, and it's unbearable to watch.On the only bright side, the visuals were nothing short of stunning and beautiful. Less importance was placed on film work, script writing, casting, and more given to visual effects, that much is clear. Unfortunately, the immersion gifted by the wonderful visual effects are undone by the above mentioned. The series also struggles with the same "power creep" as the hobbit movies, wherein everything is so large, opulent, violent or grand that nothing is... really.Didn't mind the forced diversity, as the actors and actresses who were diverse blended in with their peers in terms of talent and it does make LotR more accessible to modern audiences.Overall, the series watches like an over budget dungeons and dragon sitcom, and definitely is not lord of the rings. I cancelled my Amazon prime in disgust.

Where do I start with this totally clear example of IP thieves!!!I think when Galadriel was brought out of her cell to see the Queen and she grabbed THREE guards and pushed them into her cell in the fastest edited "nudge" I've ever seen in my life it highlighted how lazy some writing and filming was, along with the "rocks look down and sink and boats look up and float" lines of wisdom and philosophy.........It was ALL over for me! Super super forgettable garbage. Talk about unworthy people taking hold of an IP and simply ruining it.Hollywood needs to step out of its own bubble and go back to drawing board!

ipc-title__text: Great mystery-style plot in a Tolkien setting. Perfect.

ipc-html-content-inner-div: The writing is so horrendous that it's impossible to watch. It feels like a school project where a class of grade 4 students are told to get together and write a story. Whomever made this tries to pass it off as a Lord of the Rings prequel, but c'mon, anyone who's read anything Tolkien can clearly see this has absolutely nothing to do with Middle Earth other than in name.I really wish this project would have been put into competent hands. Will not be watching any more seasons. Now I'll need to dust off the books so I can wash this bastardization out of my head.At this point, the show is unsalvageable. Only a complete reboot could bring my interest up again as long as it's put in competent hands.

I do not have much good to say about this TV show. But let's start with relatively good thing - I really think that the budget shows here - cinematography is good. The rest seems like a poor joke. Starting with "mary sue" type of main protagonist, ending with very poorly written and executed story. Also... quite predictable.I felt dissapointed as well in the acting (how this is possible in such expensive show?), and characters themselves.I wish I did not see this TV show. I wish I gained this wasted time back.BTW. Not being a Tolkien's lore fan (just an average Joe), it still felt like a slap towards his legacy. The only thing that makes this show close to original Tolkien's creation is the show's name and names of some characters.

If you're going to stand on the shoulders of giants, do something other than deface the giant.I will openly admit I bailed half way through episode 2, but bare in mind that this is 1.5 hours into the show. That is longer than some films, if you can't be interesting in one and a half hours, I am out.The casting for this is very odd, firstly the Elf King looks like he'd be better playing a detective and Elrond has the hair cut of an 80s wall street banker. Gone is the idea that elves are beautiful elegant and ephemeral beings, now your mate Barry from the pub could be an elf.Where did the money go? It wasn't on big named actors / actresses... Honestly, the production values are pretty bad for the price. Some scenes are so obviously green screened its embarrassing. For all the beautiful landscapes, they just shove this stuff down your throat. You're not lead from the quiet Shire to a small town to Rivendell, etc.The disjointed way it introduces so many characters, so quickly, you just don't have time to care. It's all very cliched and rehashed tropes we've seen before. I found I am not interested in any of the main characters that it flips between.The script is also such a pale, pale imitation of Tolkien that it is unrecognisable as an extension of his work. The idea that anyone was able to pick up the pen Tolkien put down is pretty ambitious, but how you could be happy with this is incredible.If this didn't have LOTR plastered all over it, not one person would care. It has nothing of the magic, charm, skill or gravity as the PJ films. It's on a par with lame fan fiction when compared the books.Any points this film earns in cinematography, etc it loses for being boring. You can't get better than a 2/10 if the show is unwatchable. The Show No One Asked For: The drill bits of boring.

I have to say we agreed with the initial disappointment about this series as the first couple of episodes did not grip us. We also struggled to follow the various storylines and engage with the characters. It is true that Galadriel seems rather aggressive but I do think that the actress is brilliant and she grew on me over time.Elrond was also a character that won my heart in the end, having initially thought that he's no Hugo Weaving. The friendship between him and Durin was brilliant and really captured our emotions in the end. Durin himself was a cracking character!We have just watched the last episode and it blew us away with some big surprises and fulfilled our hopes in the end with a hint towards a certain character from LOTR.We now look forward to series two and expect they will hit the ground running now that we are engaged more and familiar with the characters, as well as the story moving along better.

I really enjoyed this series. There are many complaints about how this is not true to the original books and movies but this is a reboot and should be treated as such.The story grew slowly so you could get to know the characters. Which is good.I look forward to seeing what's next for this series.The filming of this series has been done exceptionally well. Great use of the music being used to engage the viewer. I encourage everyone to watch this series with an open mind and don't condemn it because it doesn't stick to the books and movies 100%. A little variation can be a great thing. Give it a go and you may find that you will enjoy it as I have.

I've read a good number of the histories of Middle Earth, The Silmarillion and Tales of Numenor amongst others.This whole series only superficially "feels" like it reflects Tolkein's imagination and scope.The CGI for the most part was decent and the costumes and sets spectacular, but the script "writing" and acting for the bulk of the show was dire.I have great respect for the WETA filmmaking and Peter Jackson's attention to detail, but this series, as with both LOTR trilogy and The Hobbit suffers from too much ego. The filmmakers did things to enhance the story which were inconsistent with the Tolkein canon and in some cases just outright ruined my enjoyment of the show.Casual Tolkein fans will probably enjoy this for what it is.Purists will detest it.

Visually a striking show throughout, I assume that's what the vast majority or the budget was spent on. Unfortunately the positives end there, borderline laughable acting to couple with a script so wooden is not a great combination. The storyline is just straight up boring yet also incredibly disjointed and I just don't care about any of the characters who at the end of season 1 most are still not explained or linked to the others. Somehow they made it so there's just is no tension in any scene, at no point was I wondering what was going to happen or at the edge of my seat in any way. Very disappointing.

ipc-title__text: Really Boring... Nice to sleep to
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I was hoping that this show was going to be as good as the previous Lord of the Rings movie and was really looking forward to watching it. After finishing season 1, I only remembered how many times I fell asleep in the middle because it was so slow, how many times I looked at my watch while watching, and how many times I ran off to check something and never returned to finish the episode because I didn't really care how it ended. The great reveals weren't so great, I wasn't invested in the characters, and I was disappointed that it wasn't near the show that the LOTR had been. I had loved Galadriel in the LOTR, and here she was portrayed as mean and obsessed to the point I wasn't sure how she connected to the LOTR movies. It was like she was two different people. I did like the scenery, but the costumes did not convince me. The music seemed misplaced - it didn't match what was happening on screen, and it confused me. All in all I felt like it was a waste of my time, and I was not excited to come back for the next season. I wanted to like it and was willing to wait for it to get better, but after a whole season I have not decided to invest more time hoping it will.

Watched the whole season. Was fearing the worst, and was very pleasantly surprised.The cinematography is incredible - and the overall ascetics are amazing - it's well worth a watch, just for the visuals.I really like the fact, that they've taken some liberties in terms of the storyline.I, however, was not the biggest fan of Morfydd Clark's portrayal of Galadriel. In terms of looks, i get it. But, in terms of acting, i never really felt it.Overall, it's well worth it, and recommendable. I've missed the LOTR universe, and this show satisfied my thirst. I'm looking forward to more in the future.

ipc-title__text: I tried to like it, but...
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I feel like the writers are insulting our intelligence. There is a lot of flowery language that is supposed to sound 'Tolkienien' but unlike something he would have written is utterly devoid of meaning and falls flat.None of the canonical characters behave the way they should or are as we know them from Tolkiens writings, Galadriel in particular is painful to watch and has a mean case of RBF.I'm not usually one for falling asleep while trying to watch films or tv but this caught me snoozing like never before through sheer boredom.Last but by no means least, the timeline is completely out of whack!Scenery is pretty though...Listen to the books on Audible instead 😉

Sadly, the Rings of Power falls well short of my hopes.Far too many characters are introduced far too quickly and the show struggles to decide who its protagonist really is. I guess there are several, but why anyone thought that was a good idea is beyond me.The characters that are there range from invincible to unlikeable. Watching someone effortlessly kill a major (and enormous) monster when several others didn't stand a chance is boring. There are no stakes and no reason to root for invulnerable characters.Another major problem is the dialogue. Why is it filled with exposition? To me it's very lazy writing.Very sad, really, because I was hoping to love this show and I just don't. They really dropped the ball with this one.

ipc-title__text: The problem this show has its just good
ipc-html-content-inner-div: The show is good, no doubt about it. It looks great and over the whole its a great prologue to the events in Lord of the Rings. The only way however is that it could only have been a succes if it was the best show ever made. It is not of course.For me the inconsistencies with the original lore are not a problem. They mixed up the timelines a bit to be able to tell "what came before" simultaniously and in a interesting way. If you are the type of guy that says "BUT HOBBITS DONT EXIST IN MIDDLE EARTH IN THE SECOND AGE" then well... Its a Tolkien show, it just got to have Hobbits. In way the LOTR did the same thing with Arwen of course replacing Glorfindel, the complete absense of the Old Forest and Tom Bombadil and many more smaller changes.A problem I do have is with the characters and how they are written. People have an issue with Galadriel and I somewhat agree. She is just angry all the time. Now I understand that she suffers a bit from the Cassandra complex and that makes her anger understandable. However, she could show other emotions other than anger and determination from time to time. And this counts for other characters as well, the show is not especially deep in that regard, almost cartoony in a way with stereotypical roles.Although the show certainly looks very pretty, it looks a bit too much like pure CGI at times. I would have appreciated a more gritty realistic look here and there. Music does its job with a nice fantasy score but it hardly stands out, pretty forgettable. Even when I write this not a single tune comes to mind.All in all, while flawed, its good and entertaining. I once learned that when you review a product, you got to review the product as is, and not what you wanted it to be. Thats what most people seem to be doing and probably the best people in the world with an unlimited budget couldnt make what people want it to be.

I'm very irritated with how low the ratings are on this show so far. It's STUNNING, the acting is great, the characters are great, the story is interesting. What's not to like? I would recommend this show to anyone. The storytelling has a nice pace, they do well to explain lore as it comes up, costumes are gorgeous, settings are gorgeous, I really love it so far and I can't wait to see where it goes!I think it does a great job of capturing the scope of middle earth and everything that's in it. We get to see many different locations and different types of characters. There's multiple storylines that blend together to tell the full story and that's what's so cool about it - seeing the different perspectives of how the coming of this great evil is affecting all of middle earth, and how they're each choosing to handle it, whether it be fighting it, hiding from it, or joining it. They also use maps to help the viewer understand where things are which I love. There are so many small details like that that make the story easy to understand yet keep all the nuances that make it Tolkien's world. Again, overall, the people that gave bad reviews need to chill out. This show is really great and as a fantasy genre lover I'm looking for many more seasons.

I really wish I was enjoying this series and I really hoped the series would be great, but I'm disappointed. The script is weak and is sometimes amateurish, most of the characters are very superficial with unjustifiable and childish actions, especially the main character Galadriel, who since the beginning of the series has shown herself to be almost a tantrum teenager, she doesn't seem to be a elf about a thousand years old.Few characters stand out in the series, as is the case of Durin who gives life to the true essence of a dwarf, which does not occur in the series as a whole, which does not have the essence of Tolkien's universe, congratulations to Amazon for that.

This pains me; I love this world so much.

ipc-title__text: Better than I expected, still not worth its name

Here's a refined version of your review with the additional point:"After two seasons, The Rings of Power heavily leans on the nostalgia of the original Lord of the Rings trilogy but fails to deliver the same depth in storytelling and character development.While the stunning visual effects and grand set pieces are undeniably impressive, they often feel like a distraction from a narrative that struggles to connect on an emotional level.The characters lack the complexity and relatability that made Tolkien's original creations so beloved, leaving viewers without a strong connection to their journeys.Imagine watching for two seasons and not having a single character that stands out or a memorable moment that serves as a lasting reference.Instead of focusing on visual spectacle, the series would have benefited more from tighter storytelling and richer character arcs, creating a world that feels as meaningful as it looks."

ipc-title__text: The increasing mediocrity with each episode.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Seeing people giving it 8, 9, even 10 ratings makes it much clearer where the show's budget is actually going.It was already clear from the trailers, even before the first season came out, that it wouldn't have anything to do with the books and wouldn't properly reflect Middle-earth. But seriously, what is this? I thought, okay, they've interpreted it differently, let's forget the books and just watch it as something loosely related to Middle-earth. The atmosphere alone would be enough. Unfortunately, it's not even consistent within itself. The script is terrible and boring, the dialogues are forced, there's no proper structure, and the acting is beyond mediocre.

I didn't understand many critics.I have watched this serie without any expectations, not because i had no trust in Amazon Production, but because i like to watch things without any prejudice.After season 1 i was excited, good actors, good characters, good photography and cgi, many citation and lore, and an absolutly sense of beauty. Season 2 confirmed this.The beauty is in the costume as well, as in each dialogue, many word are used to speak about the beauty of living things, of light, of corruption, of evil, of every choice that if not made with a pure heart always leads to an unpleasant result.How can you not love all of this? And above all, how can you criticize everything about it?True, much of the story for cinematic reasons is told differently, but how can you say that all this is far from Tolkien's thought? Every stone, every smile, every word is placed to show the beauty of things, wasn't this perhaps the will of a man? I saw great stories, coherent and epic and made from the heart. Those who don't see this in it, well, look elsewhere without speaking badly of it at all costs. Cursing is not a criticism.Considering the money invested, I'm starting to believe that Amazon is not just doing a marketing campaign to make some money, if they only wanted to make money we would have seen many other things, I'm starting to believe that maybe they just want to tell and send a message and that is that "there's some good in this world, Mr. Frodo, and it's worth fighting for" and they believe it so much that they invest more money than others would have done, because beauty "surpasses the gold of the earth as the stars surpass the gems of the mine".

I enjoyed this show. I have read the LOTR and Hobbit books and seen the movies. After seeing the reviews here about how it wasn't as good as those movies, I just re-watched them.It is clearly not as good as the LOTR movies which weren't as good as the books. It has been a long time since I read the Hobbit and perhaps I should read it again. The Hobbit movies were very long and stretched things out longer than I remembered. It was the interactions with Gollum in the Hobbit that left an impression on me. But the movies focused on the fighting. I didn't like the Hobbit movies as much as the LOTR movies for that reason. Still as solid 8.I think this series is in the realm of the Hobbit movies.A couple of points on canon: if you say it isn't per canon then please say what aspect specifically and whether it conflicts with the books, the movies or both. I have yet to read a single review that specifies that. Considering LOTR movies were also not within canon means that a general statement is just not helpful.LOTR movies had the advantage of an actual story to follow and it had a hard time doing so in 3 movies; things were cut. In this case, the writers have to build a story. And being a TV show they have the time to do so. So unlike the LOTR movies, we are given back stories. Lots of back stories. In LOTR you weren't and if you hadn't read the books you wouldn't know the significance of events and characters.Some people are upset Galadriel isn't this ethereal towering creature like the actress in the movies. This TV show takes place thousand(s?) of years before the Hobbit. Why would she be the same? Why can't you imagine that she could be different? And by the way as soon as a reviewer describes and actress as wooden or stony they have lost all of my interest and respect for their opinion. Because some people think every woman and actress should be smiling and flirting to men and male viewers; that it is their job to make men feel good. No, if it doesn't fit the character why would they be cooing and flirty in expression?The Hobbit introduced some love interests that weren't in the books. I don't care for those. I don't think romance is needed or wanted. It also changes who they put in these shows as they tend to pick young pretty men and women. The books are not about young pretty people. And in that way this TV series suffers the same as Hobbit by their inclusion.I don't mind the long back stories. I am enjoying the Gandalf and hobbits one. I like the dwarf one. The people on the island are less interesting but whatever. I mean this whole series had to depend on appendices so it makes sense that it would take the time with the back stories.Some people have commented that the dialogue isn't as good as the books/movies. Well guess what? Tolkien isn't writing for this show. Did you expect that level of literary achievement? Read the books again!On a final note, I distrust a whole whack of reviews that are complaining here. I do so based on one observation: some people want all action all the time. I suspect that is why the Hobbit was lengthened to three movies. (some of those Hobbit scenes were right out of action movies/Indiana Jones and it cheapened it.) The same thing happened with Walking Dead: if it wasn't gore and fighting it was considered boring. Dialogue, plot, character development not welcomed in other word.So I suspect some of the low reviews are people who expected to see armies clashing like in the movies.These are new stories. I love LOTR and am enjoying these early pre-stories. I enjoy the different takes on Star Trek as the series changes over TV, movies, re-boots etc. Some I like better but the idea that this is unwatchable to a LOTR fan does not make sense to me.7-8.

If you're a fan of Peter Jackson's movie adaptation of 'the lord of the rings' and even 'the hobbit'; then save yourself the heart ache and avoid watching this at all costs.This is the equivalent to the final season of the game of thrones, only this further excels in disappointment with over stretched drawn out episodes, lack of any chemistry between forgettable characters, lack of any buildup to setting up of scenes, extremely poor acting by most with the exception of one or two, horrible thoughtless dialogue, and just an overall failure to connect to the viewer.I could go on and on with what so much is wrong with this show, but am so saddened by this production, it's killed any motivation I have to even write a proper review. It's like arriving to a mangled car crash with paramedics and police on scene, you know within the first few seconds that there are no survivors, but you have that glimmer of hope that if you stay, you just might be surprised with some good news; but the longer you stay, the worse and more mangled it gets, and after an hour you start asking yourself why did I even stop to watch this unfold?Ridiculously horrible!

ipc-title__text: Why were they allowed to massacre this story?
ipc-html-content-inner-div: An unspeakable disgrace to the epic story of Tolkien.They have changed and misused the characters in an extremely silly and pointless manner. ipc-title__text: A Visual Spectacle with Room to Grow
ipc-html-content-inner-div: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has laid a strong foundation with its visually stunning depiction of Middle-earth and some standout performances, earning it a solid 7 out of 10 in my book. The show has immense potential but faces significant challenges that hold it back.First, the connections to Tolkien's source material are both a strength and a source of confusion. The showrunners have taken creative liberties, compressing thousands of years of Middle-earth history into a more manageable timeline. While this helps streamline the narrative, it can be confusing for fans familiar with the detailed lore of Tolkien's writings. The focus on younger versions of familiar characters like Galadriel and Elrond provides interesting new perspectives but deviates from their established backstories, which might not sit well with purists.Morfydd Clark's portrayal of Galadriel as a young, fiery warrior is compelling, capturing the character's ethereal yet fierce nature. Robert Aramayo's Elrond offers a more political and diplomatic side, distinct from his future role as a wise elder. The show also introduces new characters like the Harfoots, whose storyline adds charm but sometimes feels underdeveloped.Despite the strong performances, the pacing of the series can be problematic. The first few episodes are heavy on exposition, which slows down the story. This setup is necessary to introduce the complex world and its myriad characters, but it bogs down the narrative flow. Some scenes feel drawn out, making it hard to maintain engagement.Moreover, the two-year wait between seasons is frustrating. This extended hiatus disrupts the momentum and can make it challenging to stay invested in the story and characters over time. Long waits have historically diminished the impact and continuity of many series, and it's a significant drawback here as well.Despite these issues, there is still hope for The Rings of Power. The series has successfully established a richly detailed world with potential for compelling storytelling. The showrunners' willingness to take risks and introduce new elements could pay off in future seasons, provided they streamline the pacing and address some of the narrative confusion.The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is an ambitious and visually spectacular show that, despite its flaws, remains a promising addition to the Middle-earth saga. If the series can tighten its storytelling and maintain its visual grandeur, it has the potential to become a beloved part of Tolkien's legacy.

Disappointing for Tolkien fans. If it were a fantasy series not related to The Lord of the Rings, I would have given it a 6 out of 10, which is what it deserves in my opinion in terms of the quality of the direction and the series itself. Beyond the direction, the characters come across as mediocre, lacking the depth and complexity we've come to expect from a world as rich as Middle-earth. The performances fail to capture the essence of Tolkien's iconic figures, making it hard to forge a connection with them. Moreover, the special effects, a crucial aspect of bringing such a fantastical world to life, fall short when compared to the breathtaking visuals of the Peter Jackson trilogies. The magic and awe that defined the original films seem diluted, with many scenes feeling lackluster and failing to convey the grandeur of the setting. This stark contrast not only disappoints long-time fans but also detracts from the immersive experience that made The Lord of the Rings a landmark in cinematic history.

ipc-title__text: Great scenery..... but what dull series.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: The scenery is excellent. The CGI scenes merge almost seamlessly into each other. Even the costumes are good. It's the plot that let this down. In all honesty, this entire series could have been redone as a sub-2hr film with half an hour to spare. In the end, the pace throughout the series seemed to be so slow that when I got bored of it and missed an episode, it turned out that nothing much had happened and I hadn't missed anything.The acting was 'fair' to 'good'. With the exception of a few of the elven characters. I'm not sure if they'd seen too many Star Trek films but they seemed more Vulcan than Elven. On several occasions I was expecting to hear them telling each other to 'live long and prosper'.

Undoubtedly a high-quality product from many points of view. Captivating music and sets, excellent acting performances (for the most part). The main flaw might be a certain slowness, especially in the first episodes. On the whole, the series is not too catchy, since it does not care to capture the viewer's attention with easy tricks, such as continuous plot twists, unsubstantial mysteries, sex scenes, etc. Although it does not faithfully follow Tolkien's works about the Second Age (which are, moreover, unfinished), it fully reflects their atmosphere. The narration possesses its own classic elegance. I particularly appreciated Morfydd Clark's acting. Having to play an elf she chose to limit her facial expressiveness, but her eyes and gaze are very eloquent and in this sense she reminded me of old Japanese films actresses.

The writing and cast is terrible, I guess the whole budget went into the CGI and costumes.The pacing is so slow, nothing happens for most of the season and even when something does happen I find it hard to care because the terrible writing ruins it. Some of the scenes are just cringeworthy.The cast is awful. The lead female is boring. The harfoots are annoying, I was hoping they would all die. The rest are forgettable apart from a few. The dwarfs are the only redeeming thing about the show.If it is wasn't for the Lord of the Rings lore and story this would be quickly cancelled after 1 season. Won't be watching another second of this trash.

A lot of people are complaining that the show isn't exactly canon and changes history, and honestly that's just a really minor part of the issues with this show. PIf you want to watch a show that should have been a movie, than this is it. There's just about enough content to fill that. Otherwise, the show drags plots out, the pacing is extremely slow and about 50% could have been cut. In addition, the writing is honestly poor, and things that should be big reveals were, at least for me, extremely obvious.A real shame because it could have been so much better. I don't think the format was right.

I didn't understand many critics.I have watched this serie without any expectations, not because i had no trust in Amazon Production, but because i like to watch things without any prejudice.After season 1 i was excited, good actors, good characters, good photography and cgi, many citation and lore, and an absolutly sense of beauty. Season 2 confirmed this.The beauty is in the costume as well, as in each dialogue, many word are used to speak about the beauty of living things, of light, of corruption, of evil, of every choice that if not made with a pure heart always leads to an unpleasant result.How can you not love all of this? And above all, how can you criticize everything about it?True, much of the story for cinematic reasons is told differently, but how can you say that all this is far from Tolkien's thought? Every stone, every smile, every word is placed to show the beauty of things, wasn't this perhaps the will of a man? I saw great stories, coherent and epic and made from the heart. Those who don't see this in it, well, look elsewhere without speaking badly of it at all costs. Cursing is not a criticism.Considering the money invested, I'm starting to believe that Amazon is not just doing a marketing campaign to make some money, if they only wanted to make money we would have seen many other things, I'm starting to believe that maybe they just want to tell and send a message and that is that "there's some good in this world, Mr. Frodo, and it's worth fighting for" and they believe it so much that they invest more money than others would have done, because beauty "surpasses the gold of the earth as the stars surpass the gems of the mine".

I enjoyed this show. I have read the LOTR and Hobbit books and seen the movies. After seeing the reviews here about how it wasn't as good as those movies, I just re-watched them.It is clearly not as good as the LOTR movies which weren't as good as the books. It has been a long time since I read the Hobbit and perhaps I should read it again. The Hobbit movies were very long and stretched things out longer than I remembered. It was the interactions with Gollum in the Hobbit that left an impression on me. But the movies focused on the fighting. I didn't like the Hobbit movies as much as the LOTR movies for that reason. Still as solid 8.I think this series is in the realm of the Hobbit movies.A couple of points on canon: if you say it isn't per canon then please say what aspect specifically and whether it conflicts with the books, the movies or both. I have yet to read a single review that specifies that. Considering LOTR movies were also not within canon means that a general statement is just not helpful.LOTR movies had the advantage of an actual story to follow and it had a hard time doing so in 3 movies; things were cut. In this case, the writers have to build a story. And being a TV show they have the time to do so. So unlike the LOTR movies, we are given back stories. Lots of back stories. In LOTR you weren't and if you hadn't read the books you wouldn't know the significance of events and characters.Some people are upset Galadriel isn't this ethereal towering creature like the actress in the movies. This TV show takes place thousand(s?) of years before the Hobbit. Why would she be the same? Why can't you imagine that she could be different? And by the way as soon as a reviewer describes and actress as wooden or stony they have lost all of my interest and respect for their opinion. Because some people think every woman and actress should be smiling and flirting to men and male viewers; that it is their job to make men feel good. No, if it doesn't fit the character why would they be cooing and flirty in expression?The Hobbit introduced some love interests that weren't in the books. I don't care for those. I don't think romance is needed or wanted. It also changes who they put in these shows as they tend to pick young pretty men and women. The books are not about young pretty people. And in that way this TV series suffers the same as Hobbit by their inclusion.I don't mind the long back stories. I am enjoying the Gandalf and hobbits one. I like the dwarf one. The people on the island are less interesting but whatever. I mean this whole series had to depend on appendices so it makes sense that it would take the time with the back stories.Some people have commented that the dialogue isn't as good as the books/movies. Well guess what? Tolkien isn't writing for this show. Did you expect that level of literary achievement? Read the books again!On a final note, I distrust a whole whack of reviews that are complaining here. I do so based on one observation: some people want all action all the time. I suspect that is why the Hobbit was lengthened to three movies. (some of those Hobbit scenes were right out of action movies/Indiana Jones and it cheapened it.) The same thing happened with Walking Dead: if it wasn't gore and fighting it was considered boring. Dialogue, plot, character development not welcomed in other word.So I suspect some of the low reviews are people who expected to see armies clashing like in the movies.These are new stories. I love LOTR and am enjoying these early pre-stories. I enjoy the different takes on Star Trek as the series changes over TV, movies, re-boots etc. Some I like better but the idea that this is unwatchable to a LOTR fan does not make sense to me.7-8.

If you're a fan of Peter Jackson's movie adaptation of 'the lord of the rings' and even 'the hobbit'; then save yourself the heart ache and avoid watching this at all costs.This is the equivalent to the final season of the game of thrones, only this further excels in disappointment with over stretched drawn out episodes, lack of any chemistry between forgettable characters, lack of any buildup to setting up of scenes, extremely poor acting by most with the exception of one or two, horrible thoughtless dialogue, and just an overall failure to connect to the viewer.I could go on and on with what so much is wrong with this show, but am so saddened by this production, it's killed any motivation I have to even write a proper review. It's like arriving to a mangled car crash with paramedics and police on scene, you know within the first few seconds that there are no survivors, but you have that glimmer of hope that if you stay, you just might be surprised with some good news; but the longer you stay, the worse and more mangled it gets, and after an hour you start asking yourself why did I even stop to watch this unfold?Ridiculously horrible!

Undoubtedly a high-quality product from many points of view. Captivating music and sets, excellent acting performances (for the most part). The main flaw might be a certain slowness, especially in the first episodes. On the whole, the series is not too catchy, since it does not care to capture the viewer's attention with easy tricks, such as continuous plot twists, unsubstantial mysteries, sex scenes, etc. Although it does not faithfully follow Tolkien's works about the Second Age (which are, moreover, unfinished), it fully reflects their atmosphere. The narration possesses its own classic elegance. I particularly appreciated Morfydd Clark's acting. Having to play an elf she chose to limit her facial expressiveness, but her eyes and gaze are very eloquent and in this sense she reminded me of old Japanese films actresses.

ipc-title__text: Boring and shoddy but visually beautiful, a baffling missed opportunity
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I really wanted to like this show. As someone who has studied and written about the interplay between different mediums, and as a lifelong Tolkien fan, I was excited to see what Amazon Studios would offer.That said, I am extremely disappointed. One would not think this is the 'most expensive TV series of all time'. Where did all the money go? It doesn't take half a billion dollars to pump out some impressive CGI. For writing, wardrobe and props, story development, and casting, it looks like they spent the bare minimum.At first viewing, the impressive visuals serve to obscure the bad writing, but after you've had time to let it sink in, you realize how poor it is. You have little parables, like the already infamous 'floating boat' scene, that are stretching for profound meaning but fall far short and end up confusing. It's the equivalent of a poorly written comic book or school play. Then there is writing that is lazy or out of place in an ancient/mythic setting. Think use of the word, 'ok', or Elrond's cutesy, "why didn't you say so." Or, "you smell like an orc" (do ethereal being like elves stink?). I thought some of the best writing came in the Harfoot scenes ('The Sky is Strange!'), but they are all speaking those lines with an odd southern Irish accent.The wardrobe, sets, and props are of inconsistent quality, at best. Some costumes are passable, some look like they were 3D printed and made out of plastic or cheap metal. Again, at first viewing some of the sets look fantastic, but later you realize they felt sort of empty and lifeless, like you could tell they were shot in a warehouse studio. The hair choices for the elves is baffling. Why anyone thought it was appropriate to feature barbershop fades, buzz cuts, and pompadours with copious hair product is beyond me. Bear McCreary's score is passable but does not thus far have the range and grandeur of Howard Shore's LOTR.The acting is also a confusing mixed-bag. Once again, at first viewing it seems passable, but something still feels off. Only upon second viewing or later reflection do you realize that the elves (especially Morfydd Clark's Galadriel) are wooden and expressionless. If you compare with the acting in Jackson's LOTR, it is crystal clear that the acting quality is simply not there in Rings of Power. One might be tempted to think that elves are supposed to be stoic and expressionless, but this could not be further from the truth! The truth is elves are supposed to more human than humans, almost, express more, emote more, simply be more bright and divine than humans ever could be. Peterson's original trilogy did a fantastic job at capturing this, while Amazon studios failed miserably.The casting follows the general theme of: wtf were they thinking? The supreme controversy, both contrived and genuine, about diverse casting is the least of the show's problems. Though there have been perfectly valid arguments that inclusivity could have been artfully done through Rhun (analogous to Asia in Tolkien's universe) and Harad (analogous to North Africa) storylines that intersected with those in Middle Earth and Numenor. As it stands, it is awkward and cheap tokenism, which used to be considered offensive to people of color.Again, elves are supposed to have a timeless quality about them. In this show, Galadriel and Elrond look about forty human years younger than Celebrimbor, while all three are thousands of years old at this point in the story. Elves are supposed to be the fairest and most beautiful beings, some of whom seem to almost emit a holy light. The Rings of Power producers failed miserably at capturing this quality. Furthermore, where are the top class actors? Half a billion dollars couldn't manage to bring in any recognizable actors?The plot is jarring at times because there are simply too many events that flatly defy logic. In the first two episodes, a character jumps off a ship in the middle of a huge ocean with the prospect of swimming at least a thousand miles to land with no plan or guidance. Characters are shown arriving at a destination hundreds of miles away without equipment, guides, or horses, as if they got there while taking a leisurely morning stroll. Supposed elite elven warriors are made into hapless bowling pins for an ice troll. These add up and really hinder the ability to suspend disbelief.All this ultimately amounts to a humongously baffling missed opportunity. Seriously, it makes almost no sense! It seems like this show was rushed to the cutting room floor without any edits, reshoots, or recastings. One can only surmise that the producers thought they could ride the wave of goodwill that the Lord of the Rings name carries without putting the care, time, and hard work necessary to create a good final product.This is the end of the main review. Below I've posted some slightly philosophical thoughts on Galadriel.---Why did the production team want to turn Galadriel into an expressionless, hardened, badass action hero trope? She is the main character of this show. We need to be able to identify strongly with her.The Galadriel I came to know and love from the books and Jackson's trilogy was like a representation of the divine feminine. For myself, I came to regard her as the supreme divine archetypal Anima (from Jung's concepts of the feminine in men and the masculine in women) that is worthy of deep awe and respect.All that is not to say that she could not be a fighter! Even with a sword and full plate armor! Of course she could! But in either case, the actor needs to portray a certain level of emotional depth that is simply not there. I could not believe that Morfydd Clark's Galadriel could ever develop into the powerful, feminine, and divine Queen or Lothlorien that is Cate Blanchett's Galadriel.The misguided effort, presumably, is to make some of these female characters as 'badass' as the stoic male action hero that has been portrayed countless times in movies and TV in the past three or four decades. Not only is this a bad approach because those portrayals of one-dimensional male badasses have mostly been plain bad and/or forgettable, but also because it takes the defining power away from the character of Galadriel. It leaves her with practically nothing but a hollow imitation of badassness. It is a total bastardization of what Tolkien wrote and it shows that modern Hollywood does not know how to write compelling female characters.

ipc-title__text: Oddly Uneven in Quality and Adaptation
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I really wanted to love this, but it's been difficult. If I were able to let it sweep me up into the story, the world, and the characters, I might like it better. Unfortunately, that's become difficult.Design choices seem fine, with the exception of some liberties taken by the filmmakers regarding weapons/armor used; however, some of the sets seem expansive and gorgeous while others come off as being just sets - even to the point where some "outdoor" scenes still feel like a soundstage.Costuming and makeup are all over the place, with cheap wigs in some cases and very realistic wigs in others. Costumes, even for some main characters, seem very low-budget, such as a long-sleeved fabric shirt having "scale mail" armor scales screen-printed on it, or some tunics and cloaks with bad stitching, and most of the costumes seem like they've never even been worn before, much less lived-in. Make-up is just as uneven.The story, though, is the most difficult for me. As a long-time, avid Tolkien fan, I was hoping they would handle the time compression well, and that they would make good choices when moving characters together into scenes where they really should not be (according to Tolkien lore). Unfortunately, they don't seem to be handling either aspect particularly well. It's almost like they didn't want to be constrained by canon in any way, which really hurts my enjoyment of it.I understand the idea that adaptations need to stray from canon for various reasons; however, many of these changes defy reason. Along with certain statements made by the filmmakers, I'm not even sure they understand the source material all that well.This could be a well-done series with more time/effort/budget for the basics, even with the changes from the source material; however, it's not. I can only hope it gets better from this point, but I'm now doubtful of that.

ipc-title__text: They actually made the Stranger be Gandalf
Visually powerful, masterful story telling, Tolkien at his finest
ipc-html-content-inner-div: This video portrayal of the backstory to the "Lord of the Rings" was the most engaging, satisfying fantasy series ever produced. The acting was superb making these heroes come to life. The grandeur of the settings and the incredible action scenes added to the epic quality of the production.There were several engaging story lines. But it helps to know that Tolkien fought in WWI. He is using these myths as an allegory. It was written in the run up to WWII and to the war itself, and clearly the Harfoots, precursors of the Hobbits, represent the common people of Britain who bore the brunt of the battle against the Axis powers, with Sauron representing Hitler. The elves represent the British aristocracy, the Orcs the Axis armies, the people of Numenor were the Americans who were late to help in WWI and took their time in joining the Allied powers in WWII.Every episode is filled with excitement. All the various allies are now set up with their own problems to solve as well as the imminent threat of Sauron bearing down on them. The Elves, Dwarves, men, Harfoots, and wizards are in place for the next part of the saga. Gandalf, Sauron, and Saruman have been introduced along with the forces that drive them, light vs darkness. Galadriel, Elrond, Gilgalad, Arondir remain to lead the Elves. Durin IV will lead the Dwarves. And Elendil and Isildur will lead the men.I hope the next season will live up to this magnificent production which gave Tolkien's genius a fitting tribute.

Definitely an asset to The Lord of Rings movies.Give it a try and enjoy (luckily do not have to be a LoTR guru to enjoy, if anything; this series installs the interest into this whole world/story.Thoroughly impressive.

However, the series is a fascinating interpretation. The music adds to every scene. The characters are growing on me with each passing episode.Folks who bombed the reviews early on due to some of the artistic license the producers took unfortunately skewed the reviews inappropriately.
