ipc-title__text: So bad movies because only movie lotr only P.Jackson
A Fabulous Rich Production with a Unfortunately Unentertaining Storyline
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I am a fervent fan of all the Tolkien stories, but this Amazon production seems far too focussed upon the subtlety of Sauron's machinations and manipulations, and not in telling a good character-based story. Often the story is quite bland and boring. For me, many scenes are desperately underwhelming in their impact upon the audience. It's a real pity because cinematically, overall production values, in terms of recreating Tolkein's early Middle Earth, are simply spectacular. Sauron's portrayal is subtle and powerfully indicative of the character brought to life, but not very entertaining to watch. The breadth and depth of the character portrayals in the second series results in several depictions of numerous strong characters, but without a strong storyline to justify their place or engagement on the screen, in terms of audience interest. This is not always true, specifically, but never the less is a frequently repeated pattern.Unfortunately, the two characters I found most engaging and exciting, the as yet unnamed, Gandalf, and highly endearing, Tom Bombidil, were unfortunately not well represented in the second series. The former, is not actually in this timeline according to Tolkein's origin tales. Dramatically, this is not very engaging as a sequence of events for the audience. The later episodes, seventh and eighth, seem to finally break from this pattern because the rings are basically finished. The battle scene in episode seven is remarkably striking and exciting.The two strongest characters, Elrond and Galadriel, while consistently portrayed on screen, were not particularly compelling agents in this tale. They both seem to be lacking any real strength or vigour compared to their representations in the earlier original Tolkein storylines. Somehow, while these two characters are core to this production, as series two unfolds they both seem to deflate, like a slowly leaking punctured tire. Undoubtedly, this is intentional, as the writers wish to show the desperation of the Elven people at this point in their history. The intent, I imagine, is to portray, through their own weakness, their willingness to unknowingly adopt a corrupted source of power to resolve their problems. Galadriel, for instance just seems more an angry and vengeful character than an inspirational leader of her people. Elrond, while considered and thoughtful, also seems washed out and rather powerless compared to earlier Tolkein portrayals.So, although I understand the importance of the rings of power in the storyline, it seems this production's masters, and in turn, the writers, have sought to emphasise the wrong aspects of this period of Middle Earth mythology. Sure, the rings of power are critical to what happens in both the Hobbit and Lord of the Rings plotlines, but it's the characters which are the most endearing, not the corrupted process of the production of the rings, themselves. That perspective of the story just doesn't translate well into dramatisation.

It's mostly two people talking like in a standard telenovela. There is never a feeling of great urgency, huge consequences or a large scale of events. Characters just talk about it endlessly but hardly anything happens. It's also pitiful how the writers imagine "wise people". The poor writing and direction are evidence that the vision of the source material was not understood and misused to fabricate content to fill up the episodes while they go. There is not an original genuine story that needs to be told. The content for a story is implausible and unconvincing. The world appears tiny and disconnected. The characters act unlikable and illogical. The dialog quality is just generic and shallow. The pacing is incredibly slow and boring. I feel so sorry for all the actual artists wasting their cinematic craft on this, meaning camera, lights, design, costume, music and so on.

For fantasy lovers, the Rings of Power holds big promises, many of which are elegantly fulfilled. The sets and characters are brilliantly developed amid an at times puzzling plot. The biggest problem however is the very poor sound editing. Most of the characters speak in a permanent whisper against a backdrop of loud music and thunderous sound effects. If the hush-hush sotto voce intriguing whispers are supposed to arouse more excitement, they fail, with intermittent advertisements then interrupting with an 80 dB-level alarm.Overall, a wonderful tale that could and should sound better. Those of us who are addicted to the story line will definitely be looking forward to the next season.

Well, I'm hooked. I have read the Silmarillion and the Trilogy, not much else, but I understand enough of Tolkien's monumental work to know that this show is what Middle Earth should feel like. I don't fault the writers for keeping a moderate pace initially, to give the viewers time to digest what's going to be the backbone of the show. Smartly enough, they even keep certain figures nameless for a while, so as not to overload us. But then the momentum increases and things heat up considerably. The opulent sets and the gorgeous CGI certainly help to get oneself immersed, the way Jackson's Trilogy did.The only negative are the dialects: why have them at all? It's not like we would confuse dwarves with harfoots or elves, if they all spoke with a neutral English accent. It just doesn't make much sense to hear obvious Irish or Scottish from any of the characters. In any case, it's a minor gripe: I'm ready for more seasons, please.

ipc-title__text: So bad movies because only movie lotr only P.Jackson
A Fabulous Rich Production with a Unfortunately Unentertaining Storyline
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I am a fervent fan of all the Tolkien stories, but this Amazon production seems far too focussed upon the subtlety of Sauron's machinations and manipulations, and not in telling a good character-based story. Often the story is quite bland and boring. For me, many scenes are desperately underwhelming in their impact upon the audience. It's a real pity because cinematically, overall production values, in terms of recreating Tolkein's early Middle Earth, are simply spectacular. Sauron's portrayal is subtle and powerfully indicative of the character brought to life, but not very entertaining to watch. The breadth and depth of the character portrayals in the second series results in several depictions of numerous strong characters, but without a strong storyline to justify their place or engagement on the screen, in terms of audience interest. This is not always true, specifically, but never the less is a frequently repeated pattern.Unfortunately, the two characters I found most engaging and exciting, the as yet unnamed, Gandalf, and highly endearing, Tom Bombidil, were unfortunately not well represented in the second series. The former, is not actually in this timeline according to Tolkein's origin tales. Dramatically, this is not very engaging as a sequence of events for the audience. The later episodes, seventh and eighth, seem to finally break from this pattern because the rings are basically finished. The battle scene in episode seven is remarkably striking and exciting.The two strongest characters, Elrond and Galadriel, while consistently portrayed on screen, were not particularly compelling agents in this tale. They both seem to be lacking any real strength or vigour compared to their representations in the earlier original Tolkein storylines. Somehow, while these two characters are core to this production, as series two unfolds they both seem to deflate, like a slowly leaking punctured tire. Undoubtedly, this is intentional, as the writers wish to show the desperation of the Elven people at this point in their history. The intent, I imagine, is to portray, through their own weakness, their willingness to unknowingly adopt a corrupted source of power to resolve their problems. Galadriel, for instance just seems more an angry and vengeful character than an inspirational leader of her people. Elrond, while considered and thoughtful, also seems washed out and rather powerless compared to earlier Tolkein portrayals.So, although I understand the importance of the rings of power in the storyline, it seems this production's masters, and in turn, the writers, have sought to emphasise the wrong aspects of this period of Middle Earth mythology. Sure, the rings of power are critical to what happens in both the Hobbit and Lord of the Rings plotlines, but it's the characters which are the most endearing, not the corrupted process of the production of the rings, themselves. That perspective of the story just doesn't translate well into dramatisation.

It's mostly two people talking like in a standard telenovela. There is never a feeling of great urgency, huge consequences or a large scale of events. Characters just talk about it endlessly but hardly anything happens. It's also pitiful how the writers imagine "wise people". The poor writing and direction are evidence that the vision of the source material was not understood and misused to fabricate content to fill up the episodes while they go. There is not an original genuine story that needs to be told. The content for a story is implausible and unconvincing. The world appears tiny and disconnected. The characters act unlikable and illogical. The dialog quality is just generic and shallow. The pacing is incredibly slow and boring. I feel so sorry for all the actual artists wasting their cinematic craft on this, meaning camera, lights, design, costume, music and so on.

For fantasy lovers, the Rings of Power holds big promises, many of which are elegantly fulfilled. The sets and characters are brilliantly developed amid an at times puzzling plot. The biggest problem however is the very poor sound editing. Most of the characters speak in a permanent whisper against a backdrop of loud music and thunderous sound effects. If the hush-hush sotto voce intriguing whispers are supposed to arouse more excitement, they fail, with intermittent advertisements then interrupting with an 80 dB-level alarm.Overall, a wonderful tale that could and should sound better. Those of us who are addicted to the story line will definitely be looking forward to the next season.

Well, I'm hooked. I have read the Silmarillion and the Trilogy, not much else, but I understand enough of Tolkien's monumental work to know that this show is what Middle Earth should feel like. The backdrop is monumental enough; the dialogues are just the right kind of grandiose; and the plot lines are allowed to breathe and develop properly.There's a huge number of characters to introduce, and an entire world with its back story and deities and creatures. I don't fault the writers for keeping a moderate pace initially, to give the viewers time to digest what's going to be the backbone of the show. Smartly enough, they even keep certain figures nameless for a while, so as not to overload us. But then the momentum increases and things heat up considerably. The opulent sets and the gorgeous CGI certainly help to get oneself immersed, the way Jackson's Trilogy did.The only negative are the dialects: why have them at all? It's not like we would confuse dwarves with harfoots or elves, if they all spoke with a neutral English accent. It just doesn't make much sense to hear obvious Irish or Scottish from any of the characters. In any case, it's a minor gripe: I'm ready for more seasons, please.

Galadriel's character should be graceful, powerful and aethereal; Clark's rendering is gritty, sturdy and very human. R. R. Tolkien's works and I think that rings true. ipc-title__text: Does it carry the name with pride?
ipc-html-content-inner-div: In my opinion it does not. So if I ask the biased, preconditioned and very judgy LoTR and Tolkien fan I'd need to give it 1/10... Why did I still rate it 6/10 and why could it be a 1/10? In short if you can step away from the lore it is supposed to come from it is entertaining, visualy amazing, has great costumes, some good characters and it has a pretty decent story so far. So why 1/10? It has a big name to carry and for me it simply doesn't life up to it. 1000s of years of events are compressed into one mashed up timeline, the creative freedom they took on some parts is beyond understanding. Adding hobbits as partially main characters just to please the audience and making galadriel as unlikable as she is are only two sins I struggle to ignore as longtime Tolkien fan. Still I'd like to give it a fair rating as a TV show and as such it is enjoyable.

ipc-title__text: Follow's Tolkien's lore more accurately than LOTR

ipc-title__text: Flawed in concept and falls into the usual traps
ipc-html-content-inner-div: They dont have rights to the Silmarillion, so what story exists there they cant use. They only have rights to LOTR and associated texts, this really puts a limit on how lore accurate it can be. This alone means it will automatically upset Tolkien purists. They could of course still have made a good show if they tried. Unfortunately they didn't.Ignoring the liberties taken with the story its just not a good show, its generic and lazy. It falls into the trap of giving us mystery boxes, which aren't interesting or clever. It also seems insistent on giving us fake 'shipping' story lines. Most of the characters are a bit stupid, and they rely on this fact to drive the story. Relying on characters being dumb and the old trope of having characters not talk to each other about easily resolved things is a sure sign of lazy writing.The pacing is also terrible. Season 1 was basically nothing of importance, the story only seemed to get going in season 2, especially episode 5, but then accelerated away. Everything we've seen so far (to 2x05) could be 5 episodes. Not 13.

Being back in Middle Earth is so comforting. Whilst there are many new locations and characters to meet the entire world is memorizing, it is like being back home for anyone who grew up with the books or the Peter Jackson films.The familiar characters of Galadriel and Elrond anchor the opening episodes but these are younger versions of the Elves we know in Lord of the Rings. Galadriel is more defiant, battle hardened and determined. Elrond is open but his knack for diplomacy and working with other races is there. His friendship with Dwarf Prince Durin is a delight to watch.Other characters fit in easily with the Harfoots standing out, much like Frodo and his friends many years later, Poppy and Nori are being faced with the prospect of an adventure - a dangerous one at that in the form of the mysterious Stranger.This is just the start of hopefully a multi-season story. Evil lurks but as always with Tolkien so does light.

ipc-title__text: Don't let negative reviews stop you
ipc-html-content-inner-div: It is 2025 and I only watched Rings of Power now, because I let the negative reviews deter me from it. Friends of mine who love LOTR as much as I do recently told me to watch it, despite the reviews. Season 1 was OK. Way better than reviews suggested but not exactly great. Season 2 was excellent. It feels like LOTR, the music, the scenery, the visuals are so much like the original trilogy. The character arcs are beautifully written over both seasons. I can't wait for season 3 and it's going to be grand! If you value a good story, great character arcs, good music - you won't regret watching this show. Enjoy!

It's incredible how nostalgia for the real Lord of the Rings can lead you to sit through this series, hoping to relive the magic... only to hit a wall of boredom head-on. The Rings of Power is like ordering a royal feast and being served a salad without dressing: bland, endless, and utterly depressing. Six storylines to follow? No thanks-this isn't a series, it's a marathon of endurance tests.Where are the epic battles, the heroic deaths, and the spine-tingling dialogue, like Gandalf's showdown with the Balrog? Here, after 13 episodes, nothing has happened. They promise grand confrontations, and you end up watching characters chatter endlessly in settings that look like a 2002 RPG. The Grey Havens? More like the Grey Drizzle. Even the orcs seem bored.Elrond, Galadriel, the dwarves, the discount hobbits, Isildur, Sauron... Stop. Too many subplots kill the story. Constantly switching between them leaves you lost and disengaged. Why bother investing if no character has enough depth or development to hold your attention?The cities? Ikea villages. The landscapes? Less memorable than a Windows XP wallpaper. Pelargir looks like a forgotten truck stop town you pass on the highway. Where's the grandeur of Middle-earth? Even the Shire in the original movies had more charm than everything here combined.The only moment I felt a flicker of excitement was Sauron's return with his orcs in episode one. A fleeting reminder of past greatness, quickly smothered by dull writing and flavorless plotlines. Not even the Dark Lord can save this empty shell of a series.The Rings of Power is the anti-Lord of the Rings. No soul, no rhythm, no grandeur. Just an overdose of chatter and uninspired settings. If Tolkien saw this, he'd send a Balrog to burn it all down. In short, a series to avoid-unless you enjoy suffering like Gollum without his precious.

Overall, for sure it is worth a watch. ipc-html-content-inner-div: **This review is for the first two seasons***''The Rings of Power'' is a series based on the lore of Lord of the Rings. A highly anticipated series, with an astronomical budget and hands on a plethora of fantasy material, the series was set out to impress and establish itself as one of the best fantasy shows. However, it failed to do so.Aside from a bad first season, the series finally picks up in the second one, with some enjoyable scenes and plotlines and the actors carrying the so when things got questionable. At this point, I should state that the color of the actors' skin was not at least a factor that brought this series down, as everyone in the cast did an amazing job with their characters and their performances were enjoyable.Unfortunately, the script was not as great. The series has odd dialogues that try to sound like the ones in the book but end up sound cheap, it doesn't handle the story well and ends up being boring, it tries to play with too many plotlines and confuses the audience, as well as leaves most of them half baked.In addition, the series doesn't look equivalent to its budget. Cheap material, bad costumes, and settings that are a knock off of the Peter Jackson's films. I do wish that they gave a new view on the whole LOTR universe and don't try to make it like the films, with the music and everything bringing in mind of Jackson's LOTR.Finally, I liked that they got some creative liberties on the story, but there were times that they changes it too much and often those twists didn't make sense.So, overall, two out of ten. The performances were great, there were some moments of pure enjoyamet, but, the series as a whole is boring and I struggle to understand to whom they were aiming as their target audience: to new fans, but then they should have been clearer about the story and don't anticipate that one should have at least watched the old movies to know what was going on, also make it more interesting, or to LOTR fans, but then they changed the original too much and it is bound to anger them.

This show was never going to start with a clean slate or be received without bias. The expectations were simply too unrealistic, with fans of the Jackson trilogy expecting one thing, fans of the books expecting another, and every wannabe critic looking for reasons to find fault instead of simply sitting back and enjoying what good this show has to offer. The Jackson trilogy is spectacular, but it also arrived without impossible standards. Ignore the haters, even ignore the praise. Just start this series with an open mind and judge for yourself. Appreciate the complexity of the massive world and the fresh cast you're introduced to, without preconceived notions of what they should be. Admire the gorgeous cinematography in every episode. And enjoy the well-designed story that slowly manifests over time.

ipc-title__text: Teetering on the edge of complete and utter failure!
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Whenever the newest episode of "The Rings of Power" comes out, I have to force myself to watch it. Every installment in the series has major flaws that ruin the entire show, whether they mess up Tolkien lore or just include completely unplausible moments that leave the viewer frustrated. The show is just unbearable.Obviously CGI and other special effects have come a long, long way since the Peter Jackson LOTR and Hobbit films released, and the people at Amazon use it to their advantage in the show, but as other aspects of the show like storyline and acting fall short, it feels like cinematography and realistic models/effects are the only things holding the show together.Season One was utterly disappointing for me, as it turned out to be a pretty corny bunch of episodes with poor moments and a protagonist reminiscent of a Karen (Galadriel). She was absolutely LAME (understatement) so thank God this isn't canon. The antagonist pushed by the showrunners (Adar) was also kinda cheesy.Either the ignorance of in-universe lore by the showrunners or a deliberate choice to spoil it left the show in tatters when it came to actually relating itself to Tolkien's work. Both seasons are just stinking piles of crap with no respect for the source material. :(Usually different ethnicities in shows don't bother me, but here it is a problem if there is no source material to justify, let's say, the appearance of an Asian elf. Even if they're onscreen for only a moment, it's still a major disrespect to J. R. R Tolkien, the fans, and the material. Tolkien is probably rolling in his grave right now.A one billion dollar budget and they couldn't hire better actors! The only person I applaud for their effort is Charles Edwards for his role as Celebrimbor, the Lord of Eregion. He does a fantastic job while everybody else looks either WAY too dramatic or way too deadpan, or just unconvincing. For example, the Queen Miriel is a perfect example of overdramaticizing everything. Yes, she was blinded by hot embers, but she gets overemotional in every single scene with her. She's supposed to be this righteous leader, faithful to Numenor, but all I see her do is stand there and tear up, declaring "My place is here" or something about the people. Too corny in my opinion. Sure, you can have a strong leader who happens to be blind, but don't make them cry whenever they speak.In terms of being deadpan, either Gil-galad or Elendil seems to be suitable for criticism. Gil-galad does display emotion at times, but generally he's this corny-ass dude who is supposed to be the composed leader. He's a wise Elf, sure, but in his interactions he's about as diverse in emotion as Todd Howard voice-acting in Oblivion. I'm starting to think he's bipolar. :D Elendil, although he is a morally upright dude who serves as an inspiration to his men/former men, is pretty unemotional unless it comes to having a tearfest with Miriel in her room, or standing before Ar-Pharazon and being restrained by guards in an outrage. Opinions differ, and you might think "Hey, Elendil shows more emotion", and you could be right, but this is what I percieve from watching the show, and I'm especially describing the state of things from the second season as it just concluded, and in the LAMEST closing scene possible.I had high hopes for the show before it first came out, but now I can confidently say that "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power", after two seasons, is the worst live-action TV series I have ever seen. A relaxing Friday (I watch on Fridays) night turns into an hour and a half of torture as I watch this terrible show because I need to. Why? Because I feel obligated to.If you still have sufficient free will, PLEASE DON"T WATCH this, especially if you are a Tolkien fan. You'll be disappointed sorely, I'm sorry to say.

ipc-html-content-inner-div: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power (2022- ) is a series that my wife and I recently watched on Amazon Prime. The storyline follows Middle Earth in a state of peace and a dark menace forming that will impact all races. Trolls have been emerging from under the ground destroying villages and orcs have seen their numbers grow...but why? Can the elves, dwarfs and humans put their petty squabbles behind them and work together to identify their issues and fight the rising dark powers? Meanwhile, beings have fallen from the sky. Whom are they and why have they emerged?This series was cocreated by Patrick McKay and John D. Payne in their debuts and stars Morfydd Clark (Saint Maud), Ismael Cruz Cordova (In the Blood), Markella Kavenagh (My First Summer), Cynthia Addai-Robinson (The Accountant), Dylan Smith (Into the Badlands) and Lloyd Owen (Miss Potter).The production value of this series is over the top good with great narration, settings, costumes, cinematography and props. This series is absolutely gorgeous. The fight choreography is fantastic as is the makeup, masks and the way the characters are presented. Anyway, there is not clear story to bond the series. And most of the episodes do not have center story too. So the script is bad and also very controversial to the lore. If you did not read the books or watch the movies the script does not make any sense. If you read the books it does not make sense too. It kind of works only if you just watched the movies. The cinematography is in general good. The acting - if you ignore the awful personalities, the meaningless and stupid dialogues and the lack of characters development, the acting is good, not great, but not bad. The costumes are all over the place. Some, like the plastic armors of Numenorians are terrible. Some costumes are inspired by Ancient Greece and simply do not fit. Other costumes are good. The action choreography is mediocre. The CGI visual effects are very good.

I didn't read Toulkins' series of books about the story of lord of the rings, but I think that almost everyone who gave poor rating are the fans of Toulkins books, if we ignore that, the show is really good, good actors, story, production, I loved it !The rings of power story is based on the lord of the rings lore and the literature outside of the 4 main books, i.e. Tolkien notes and the silmarillion book (published after his death).To fabricate a TV series based on notes and lore about Tolkien's universe is extremely impressive. The story is a slow burner allowing characters to grow, the characters are likeable or hateable. But it's engaging and entertaining.I'm extremely confused as to why the internet is hating on this, what were people expecting? I really don't know. It seems like it's impossible to please people at the moment.I'm hugely grateful that this story is being told that has the amazing production value that the rings of power has and I really hope they are not discouraged by the few and they carry this on for at least another season.

I have read most of the works that the show is based on and although I do regard the LotR in highly, I won't call myself a super fan of the franchise. Fantasy though is my favourite genre and Tolkien is considered the father of modern fantasy.I also understood that not all the rights for The Silmarillion etc was bought and that some rather large changes will have to be done. Especially with them trying to contract the history to one story line.This show is very aesthetically pleasing and it actually made me switch from streaming this on my laptop to permanently watch the whole show on my television.The cinematography throughout the show was really good. I was happy with the CGI for the most part. I thought the costuming looked really good. Most of the choices for armour etc looked really good, better than I remember them being described, but I was good with that.The show however suffers from a few things.The dialogue does not match with anything Tolkien I have read. For most part, it felt flat and it rarely gave me any insight into the characters.I also feel that they tried to juggle too many story lines in one go, and the one I was excited about was just a few scenes at the end, which I thought would get much more focus.I did not feel invested in the story of many characters, with the most empathy I could feel was with the villain of the season and the Elrond/dwarf story line.My biggest negative is that it broke my suspension of disbelief too many times. Just because it is fantasy, doesn't mean things doesn't have to make sense. You have to make sure you follow the rules of the world you are portraying, which I feel was broken many times during this story.The power scaling seems off, the fighting scenes seem too blatantly to go for the cool look rather than what would make sense. Too many people survive amazing things without explanation or hint of anything helping them.All things put together, I could watch it through, but it is on the bad side of watchable for me.

There doesn't appear to be a big quest as in the LOTR and Hobbit and this lack of a focal point obscures the tale. They rely on Galadriel's almost obsession-like behaviour to find Sauron but this is more of a solo trip. The reason for avenging her brother's death comes out as a weak excuse especially when death for elves in the mortal land is superficial, merely giving up the physical form. Other story-lines span simultaneously following the elf guard Arondir and the discovery of orcs, the pre-Hobbits trying to find a safe haven and ending up with the Stranger (looking like Gandalf the Wizard) and Elrond with Dwarfs. This is a lot to stomach, and it may be the reason why some viewers got alienated. For instance, the whole Arondir storyline was unnecessary since Galadriel found out about orcs at some point anyways.Actors do their best with the somewhat under-performing story. Even Morfydd Clark in Galadriel's role finds some facial expression in the end. It first looks like she has botox treatment when only her lips moved slightly. Harfoots pre-hobbits are nice characters but their overly shabby appearance is quite annoying. This is the thing about this show, everything is a bit too intense. Maybe they were trying too hard.Somehow it was difficult to root for any character, maybe because of the all gimmicks here and there. Last episodes batch some of the weaknesses. Still, one finds hoping that orcs would win and have their land and glory.

ipc-title__text: Not a LOTR fan but I enjoyed this.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: So first let's lay out my prejudice and biases first - I am in no way a LOTR fan. I was bored to tears when I was a kid when my friends kept dragging me to see the Peter Jackson films. I'm not kidding when I say this but I've fallen asleep every single time I tried to watch those movies. I actually remember thinking one Christmas when my mom bought them for me on DVD "My own mother doesn't know me at all".I know that fans of those movies are literally religious zealots when it comes to them but there it is. Can't stand em. No disrespect. In terms of quality and scope as well as just pushing the medium of filmmaking they are an achievement. Even I can admit to that despite not being a fan.Also, the books... Listen LOTR is just not my type of fantasy. When I was a freshman in college my English 1000 professor on the first day of class assigned reading LOTR and I thought I was going to cry. I hated every second of it. Mordor, gondor, dwarves, Galabriel, Galadriel, Orcs, Wizards, Middle Earth blah blah freaking blah. All of that stuff for me takes away from the meat and bones of a great story... the humans and the human conflict. It's distracting not to mention annoying. I'm more of a GOT, Sword of Truth, and Mistborn fantasy fan. Stories that don't get bogged down in the world-building but instead focus on characters that are believable and mirror our own world.Okay, so all of that being said, why did I watch this? Well, to be honest, one thing pulled me in, and one thing only: Morfydd Clark. Lord of the Rings have mercy she's gorgeous. But also the fact that the rabid diehards didn't like it also caught my attention. It sort of confirmed what I think turned out to be true - the producers of this show weren't just trying to appeal to the LOTR base but were trying to achieve what GOT did... they wanted to bring in normie viewers like myself. All the nerd stuff is in there but it's dialed back a bit. Instead, they're focusing on the characters. They've grounded a story I always thought was too ridiculous and childish to be taken seriously and ya know what? I enjoyed it.Alright, so let's get specific - pros and cons:PRO: I think Morfydd Clark is a star. I don't think she will blow up as a direct result of this show but I do think it will be because of the opportunities it leads to. I saw some comments about her character Galadriel on social media and here as well stating that she - CON: Galadriel - is written like a bit of a Karen. Not only is that hilarious but yeah, it is a bit true. Love Morfydd but Galadriel is not exactly written well. It's tough to root for her.PRO: This one was a massive surprise for me but Durin! The second you mention something like Dwarves my eyes immediately glaze over and my attention wanders but the character and his storyline were really a joy to watch. The conflict with his father and his relationship/brotherhood with Elrond was just surprising. Again, it was human.PRO/CON: Sauron - I mean I think it was obvious from the jump. That being said, I enjoyed it all the same. I saw what they were going for and the parallels they were trying to make to let's say other great classic works. And let's be real, coming from a non fan... I want a relationship between Galadriel and Sauron so bad. It would just make for great TV. Galadriel falling in love with the literal thing she's spent a thousand years trying to kill?! And maybe he actually loves her too and starts to question the whole evil thing? C'mon, that would be so much fun!CON: The Stranger - I love Daniel Weyman but the Stranger was just annoying plain and simple.PRO/CON: Cinematography at times felt fantastic and grounded and other times felt very CW network. Specifically, the Numenor stuff... honestly that whole thing felt CW. Too pristine, too pretty, too clean - the actors themselves again looked straight off the crappiest CW hot people with problems show. I'm sure some book nerd is screaming "that's what Numenor is supposed to be!!" I don't care I didn't like it. I just didn't buy it. I didn't believe it. Here's a contrast - GOT - The Red Keep and Lannisters... I believed that was a real sort of middle ages setting.Hollywood is a lazy industry. Always looking for the easiest sell. IP is the name of the game these days. Forget about anything resembling original or at least "fresh" storytelling - the industry will always take what millions and millions of people love and try to repurpose it. There is a lot of great fantasy out there that is less popular but imo far more interesting, complex, yet grounded than LOTR that Amazon could have gone with. Instead, they chose perhaps the most recognizable option and tried to put their own spin on it. I get why diehard fans are miffed. They're right to be. If you want to put your own spin on something... tell your own story. I liked this show and I'll prob check out a few eps whenever S2 happens but I think we can all agree that Rings of Power will never come anywhere near to the GOT effect.By virtue of its straight geek silliness, Rings of Power will never be a cultural phenomenon... all that money spent can't change the fact that LOTR will always be niche.

People tend to forget how everyone "hated" the stars wars prequels in the early 00's and the bad press the hobbit triology recived. This is no different and a great attempt at restarting the story andn ranchise. I just wish people would go into it with a fresh pair of eyes and realise its a new story.Yes the original trilogy is a cinematic marvel and is still my number 1 favourife movies and ive been obssessed with tolkein since i was a small boy, and i can truthfully say i enjoyed this series and feel it would be a shame for it not to continue. People keep comparing galadriel to the movie version but forget she is sooooo much younger in thsi and lets face it we were all different years ago.Please give this a chance its is well worth it.

A good first season, and a good adaptation of parts of Tolkien's history of Middle-earth published in 1977 in "The Silmarillion". This book carries none of the lyrical tone or the songs and does not describe sympathetic characters like in the 1954-1955 book "The Lord of Rings". In this amazonstudios/primevideo adaptation we expect the cataclysmic destuction of glorious kingdoms, the creation of blissful jewels turned as a tool for servitude, the cruel execution of the tallest kings with their people enslaved and turned to evil entirely. Here the Oath of Fëanor, spoken in First Age by the most skilled of Elf lords to his people to relentlessly seek revenge for theft and murder, is perfectly carried down the House of Noldor to Galadriel. This is her story at the end of the Second Age before she becomes the wise queen in the Third Age as described in The Lord of the Rings.

ipc-title__text: Semi-entertaining but suffers the problems of a TV-series.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: So this is a show made by Amazon (who has acquired the rights to the Lord of the Rings franchise), telling the tale of Galadriel and a couple of other major characters, before the timeline of the original films.I could sum it up as "bargain store Lord of the Rings". Don't get me wrong, the actors seem to be trying their best here, and the CGI is quite good. But it just DOESN'T come close to the quality and scope of the original Lord of the Rings films by Peter Jackson.The actors are OK and serviceable, but nowhere near the majestic and iconic actors such as Viggo Mortensen or Cate Blanchett.There are also the limitations of a mini-series, having to pack things in 1 hour episodes.The scenario itself is nothing to write home about.My biggest criticism is the style. It is definitely a more colorful middle earth, less dark fantasy than the original films, but that goes in line with a show made by Amazon for the modern crowd.Finally, they've of course added the diversity element to Middle Earth, with Black elves, dwarves, and hobbits. I ignored this as I don't let it affect my judgment, but it did feel uncalled for and stupid. I might also add that the Elves themselves are stylistically less impressive than the elves of the original films. Galadriel should have had more platinum hair, but this is a pet peeve. And whilst I like the main actress, I feel that Cate Blanchett was so much more impressive.My conclusion? It's a run of the mill Amazon show that will please your "Lord of the Rings" itch. But it's obviously nowhere near the craftmanship and love of the original films, which created such a quality gritty environment that seemed pulled straight out of the books and left such an impact on our memories.I believe that Amazon could have done much better if they had released a trilogy of films rather than make this a TV show. They shot themselves in the foot with the TV show format. Obviously there's a profit element to this, but Lord of the Rings is much more impactful as a movie than making season after season of episodes which will have lots of filler.It's not an absolute monstrosity, but I wish Amazon kept their hands off such an important franchise. Similar to what Disney did with SW.

I didn't know what to expect of the series, having been a huge fan of The Lord of the Rings Theology. But this very good! Great acting and love the special effects. Able to follow and understanding how everything and everyone in the world of Tolkien came to be. So very different worlds of men, elves, dwarfs and orcs and of course wizards. Beautiful contrast and cinematography. Doing my best not to compare to Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings. But all the same The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is excellent! Wish it continued a little longer. Im really happy to see how this all began. Can't wait for season 2.Update: Season 2!!!! Wow!! Each episode gets better and better! Suburb special effects, all actors played their part extremely well! I will be watching Season 2 episodes again, can't wait for Season 3.

ipc-title__text: Fantastic production, but with a few niggles.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: During the Second Age of Middle-earth, thousands of years before The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, after Dark Lord Morgoth the Rings of Power follows rise of the Dark Lord Sauron and the plight of the inhabitants of Middle-earth.Although a little plodding and overwrought at times it's exceptionally well made, particularly when practical and visual effects are seamlessly sucking you in. However, there is the odd occasion when they falter along with the editing and logic taking you out of the action and drama. The costumes, props, locations and production overall are first rate. The performances are on point, notably Morfydd Clark as a young Galadrie and Robert Aramayo as Elrond. However, the monsters, especially the Orcs, Ismael Cruz Córdova as Elf Arondir and Owain Arthur as Durin IV: the Prince of the Dwarven steal the show.When it's fresh Middle-earth story building and in keeping with the feel of the films, you can buy Clark and Aramayo are younger versions of their characters especially as the production is intended to evoke the movies using similar production design; but as good as Maxim Baldry is as Isildur, he doesn't feel like a younger version of Lord of the Rings Isildur. Daniel Weyman has plenty of screen presence as The Stranger who falls from the sky in a flaming meteor; giving a memorable performance; but his story is frustratingly drawn out. Also Charlie Vickers as Halbrand for the most part feels too similar to Aragon.Although a little bumpy -mainly the editing, pacing and some characterisation, the cinematography, visuals and musical score are outstanding. With some fine performances along with a few surprises The Rings of Power is highly recommended.Season 2 has more scope and is a little more dynamic. While it's great as a streaming show, given its cost, it still lacks a consistent cinematic look throughout. The Forest of the Dead and battle scenes are memorable, but at times, it feels a little repetitive, revisiting the same plot points and reiterating goals through the dialogue. That aside, there's some good acting from the supporting cast, including Orc Glûg (Robert Strange) and Sam Hazeldine as Adar, replacing Mawle. Markella Kavenagh's Harfoot character 'Nori,' Aramayo, Cruz Córdova, and Charles Edwards are particularly notable in this second season.

ipc-title__text: Better then Hobbit trilogy almost on par with LOTR trilogy
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I am baffled by so many of the negative reviews of The Rings of Power. It's not a perfect show, there are flaws, however it is almost as good as the original Lord of the Rings trilogy and in my opinion significantly better than the Hobbit trilogy. The Rings of Power has a much more culturally diverse cast then any of the previous films. Adding a more diverse cast that strays from the source material seems to put way to many viewers off of an otherwise entertaining and engaging show. Apparently turning a few hobbits, elves, and royals anything but white makes a show awful in the mind of less open-minded viewers.

ipc-title__text: This is a poorly written fan fiction
ipc-html-content-inner-div: This has to be, hands down, the worst adaptation i have ever seen. It is especially bad for a property like the Lord of the Rings. How this was made i do not know.The story has so many unnecessary changes to the lore and they are not even good changes. Things progress in the story by coincidence or someone doing something unbelievable.(Que Galadriel Jumping into the ocean and planning to swim all the way back to Middle Earth). The writing reads like a fan fiction, a really bad one, that was written in a day. There is no pay off earned, no character works for anything in this show, it is just given to them, i just cannot get over this poor excuse for writing. I feel so bad for these talented actors being given this horrid script to act out.The lore has been torn up and thrown out the window. So if anyone was expecting even a semi faithful adaptation i'm sorry to tell you that you won't even get that. Everyone just teleports around to exactly where they need to be to make the next thing happen and those things are just straight up not what was written. Even if you only read the Lord of the rings books and the appendices (which i believe is what this "showrunners" have the rights to) they have not told it as it was written as part of Tolkiens story. This is Game of Thrones season 8 levels of extremley lazy, poor writing with no regard for the books behind it.I'm sorry but you cannot convince me this was a labour of love based on what was produced. This should never have been made, this should have been rejected and everything stopped. Do not make a second season unless you plan to follow the lore. If you have read the books or watched the movies this is going to leave you bitter and upset that your favourite story has been treated so poorly.

Pretty much the title. Doesn't matter whether you are a LoTR fan or not, you are not going to like this. Reason why is because there is simply nothing in this that is worth watching. Storyline is all over the place, poorly written characters, uninteresting and at time straight up boring storytelling and (to top it all off, in case you are indeed a LoTR fan) they completely misrepresented both the lore and the intent of Tolkien's work. It is really quite a remarkable achievement to spend $1 billion USD on an IP and come up with something this underwhelming. The decision makers behind this mess should really take a good hard look in the mirror and quickly pivot to create something that is worth our time or at the very least vaguely interesting.

Scene transitions are meaningless and sometimes unnecessary, some scenes can even be funny, a production that has nothing to do with the books, the worst ones are those who write the dialogues, those who write the scripts and those who make the final cuts, those who make the visual effects, those who do the visual effects, all races are very close to each other in terms of character development and behavior patterns. What will not happen to this universe, galadriel has become a fascist, I don't understand what kind of ignorance made you put this on the market, I think this story of failure should be the subject of books now Similar things happened for the time wheel series.

ipc-title__text: Makes you immerse into the LotR universe
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I didn't have too high expectations from the series for obvious reasons, but the Rings of Power managed to impress me with the graphics. I was surprised how well the music reflects the spirit is the Lord of the Rings movie, thanks to the Howard Shore involvement. I'd wish they would pay just a little bit more attention to costumes though, I can't help it to not compare the quality and details of they to the ones you can see in the movie. As far as the storyline, it couldn't be a little bit more engaging. Love to see the old good characters again. I would also say they managed to picture orcs best and dwarfs best, while people and elfs are ok-ish. Great impressions overall for any Tolkien fan.

They are milking JRR's name for all it worth. This show is so slow and goes on and on about nothing. Get to the point. It's painfully obvious this is going to go on for years and could have been an awesome 4 hour movie. Instead they drone on and repeat the same action sequences. Random characters getting stabbed to death in fighting sequences but when the main characters get bested in a fight, they just hit them or kick them. Sad film making. Fake. Unbelievable. Suspension of my belief can only go so far. I was really hoping this would be great. Should have let Peter Jackson helm this. Waste of a big budget.

Gave up after the third episode. The story (which is not faithfully told from Tolkein) just doesn't go anywhere...
The main character of the story Galadriel, the poor actress is doomed never to act again due to this terrible writing and how she portrays her.The Harfoots are absolutely awful and very selfish. If Hobbits so called descended from these idiots (again according to the show) it's absolutely insulting due to how different both races actually are. Also they have these weird Irish accents but not all of them do? Why? 2 stars because at time the show does look amazing CGI wise but even some of the outfits just look rushed and really cheap for some reason.

Boring. Soooooooo boring! The pacing is ridiculously slow. The lore is messed up and made up. The sets and scenery look nice, and the acting is average but so far nothing to save the show overall. Too many of the main characters are just not very likeable. You don't hate them, but they are just "meh". What a waste.Peter Jackson should have been brought in to do this. At this point the show resembles a separate fantasy story as opposed to being part of Tolkien's world. It just doesn't have the feel of any of the books or movies. There is the whole "diversity" dilemma as well. It seems good hearted but very, VERY forced which brings the viewer out of the fantasy as well. It seems the producers are long to preach on modern day social issues than attempt to fortify the series with good stories that would do the source material proud.The biggest failing with this show however still remains the story. It just isn't that good. It is just a nice look but very flawed, very poor product. Again, such a waste.

ipc-title__text: Decent show set in Tolkien setting
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I do like many aspects of the show. The looks of course, many of the characters are written well. Not sure I like what they did to the hobbits, they seem too... feral and out of place is the only way I can put it. Arondir is a bit too stoic in the first few episodes, I hope he opens up and has more of a personality. Some of Galadriel's scene are kinda cringe but not horrible. It will be interesting to see some of the established characters develop into what they are in LOTR. I like the Elrond/Durin story the best so far.Overall I can see where the story is headed and I am interested enough to keep watching to find out how it unfolds.

The good part it, most of the expensive money spent on Rings of Power shows well on the production and set design, the costumes, the architecture. One does need to commend the producers for doing their best to create the complex Tolkien-ish world that is Middle Earth.Unfortunately, that doesn't quite save ROP from being bland. For me, one of the things that made Peter Jackson's LOTR trilogy so good was that, they managed to create suspense, thrill and excitement through out. This, despite the fact that most of us knew how the story was going to end. Those of us who've read the story before watching the movies, knew what's going to happen to the characters, yet, we never stopped biting our finger nails as the story unfolds in the movies.ROP fails to create that tension, even though for the most part, it's new material and - I'm guessing - the creative team was allowed a largely free hand to expand the story.I think part of the fault lies in having too many characters to contend with, in the space of only 8 episodes. I find the addition of the Harfoot's story trajectory takes up too much time and totally unnecessary, especially at this juncture in Middle Earth's chronology. It feels like their addition has more to do with having a link with the hobbits of LOTR, although the script does give them meat. Still, it takes away much precious time from the development of other characters, for e.g Elrond - a central character in the history of Middle Earth. Consider this: Elrond appears in Ep 1 and 2, doesn't appear in Ep 3, and shows up again in Ep 4. If only more time had been spent on developing Middle Earth's important characters - from Gilgalad to Celembridor to Elrond to Durin etc, maybe then there would have been better attachment towards the plot.I don't quite buy-in to Morfydd Clark's portrayal of Galadriel as a pompous, hot headed elvish fighter. It's feels so distant from Cate Blanchett's version, who's Galadriel exuded wisdom, patience and benevolence. It does speak of Blanchett's immense talent, that, while her Galadriel didn't occupy a lot of scenes in LOTR, yet she managed to captivate audiences as her ethereal and regal quality.As for action scenes, none so far could match those of LOTR or even the Hobbit trilogy. Even the attack by a sea monster in Ep 2 doesn't quite excite, especially since one hardly gets to see the creature! Even the language suffers from inconsistencies; what's with all this brogue pronouncing of "Morr-dor", "Numenorr", which wasn't there in LOTR or the Hobbit? Did anyone think how that looks for continuity?ROP feels stuck between the place of matching the highs of the book and Jackson's trilogy, and of character and content development. For all the money poured in creating a visually impressive set, one'd wish that the producers had also given thought about proper plot and character development.

ipc-title__text: Visually it is fine, no substance at all.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I'm a LOTR fan and I have a Prime account, so I had to give it a shot despite all the horrible reviews. I made it through episode 1 and I am tapping out. It deserves all the criticism it has recieved and more. The only way I can describe this show is disrespectful, disrespectful to Tolkien, disrespectful to fans, disrespectful to the past films. It is so desperate to show this is a new type of LOTR they forget to add any substance outside of no-so-subtle messages about social issues that are already crammed into everything. I won't be watching episode 2 unless I need a nap. Maybe in the future people who produce entertainment will remember to make it entertaining.

ipc-title__text: Sad some people compare a movie to a TV show
ipc-html-content-inner-div:
Let's be clear, this is a great TV show, on par with the best looking ones like fondation and the likes.But stop comparing Jackson's lotr to this.First of all it's not a rehash of lotr, the story is completely different and it's not from the books either, so comparing Tolkien's book or Jackson's movies is irrelevant, period.So now if you start fresh it's amazing.It looks fantastic, it feels fantastic and the magic is there.Discovering the mines, the beautiful elven cities and more (not naming them for possible spoilers..) is amazing, it's eye candiesSo yeah the story is revealed slowly and so are the characters, but it's a TV SHOW, they don't wanna wrap it up after 6 episodes, and neither do I btw..

I wonder if Amazon will hide this review.It might be a beautiful-looking show but just because something looks good doesn't automatically mean its quality. I would consider myself an average Lord of the Rings. Not a superfan but not new to the world. But this show is just so empty from a writing/story standpoint.

ipc-title__text: A mixed bag of great and garbage.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: The show is a mixed bag.Sometimes the acting is great, sometimes it's horrible.Some of the CGI is good, some of it is immersion breaking bad. Very obviously broken physics, spray on the camera, etc...Some of the costumes are great, some are local theater level.Continuity is almost non existent. Characters teleport around within a scene, crossing a room in a fraction of a second through the magic of a cut.The editing is mostly good other than the continuity errors.The dialogues are a mix of boring and pedantic. A lot of bumper sticker wiseness is dispensed by various characters. The best examples of deepity in modern media...And on the "Lord of the rings" side. Aside from a few names, they kept nothing of the lore.

ipc-title__text: I really like it. Almost certain I will love it.

I think/hope Amazon will see the value in it to keep it going into a second season.Meanwhile HBO has going to caca and will stay there at this rate, just like it's fans/subscribers.This is from a devoted fan of LOTR and GOT until the last season.

This episode does a decent enough job of setting the stage for the rest of the show, but it feels a little lost in what it tries to achieve. It seems to be somewhat vague in mentions of the most important and engaging parts of middle earth's story here, and raises the questions of what exactly we are meant to make of this world without being able to properly engage with it.Not worth one star, however as the actors perform a wonderful job in their roles despite the subpar writing, it just strikes me as strange how so much money could go into a project like this and appear... uninspired. Maybe the rest of the show will make up for it.

ipc-title__text: Poorly Written and Amateurish at best
First episode did not excite me to watch the second
ipc-html-content-inner-div: OK so I'm basing this off the first episode. I'm a big fan of the original trilogy and I really disliked the hobbit trilogy Mostly due to the overuse of CGI and bright colors. It just did not seem to exist in the same universe as the original trilogy. So far this show is after the same start. After the first season of The Rings of Power, I had very low expectations for Season 2-but somehow, they managed to undercut even those. What promised to be a grand spectacle of Tolkien's Second Age has devolved into a frustrating, incoherent mess.The script feels like it was cobbled together by someone who skimmed the appendices of The Lord of the Rings and then immediately forgot what made those stories so compelling. Dialogue oscillates between melodrama and flatness, with most characters delivering lines that are either laughably grandiose or eye-rollingly mundane. The rich lore of Middle-earth is trampled on or ignored, with plotlines that seem invented on the fly and riddled with inconsistencies. The obsession of politically correct scene is ruining the show at every corner, women are always strong and brave, men are always weak and evil, couple are always mixed, orcs are nice people who wants to live in peace....The characters, already thin in the first season, become even more two-dimensional. Galadriel, who had the potential to be an intriguing, complex figure, is reduced to a one-note character with no growth. Elrond, once portrayed as a wise and powerful leader, now feels like a sidekick in his own story. New characters introduced this season lack depth, and their motivations feel arbitrary at best.Long stretches of episodes are devoted to pointless subplots that go nowhere. We slog through endless scenes of exposition with no payoff. Meanwhile, major plot points that should be built up are rushed through with little attention or care. The balance between world-building and narrative momentum is entirely off, resulting in a season that drags even in its supposed "epic" moments. 6 épisodes past and just nothing happened.Visually, The Rings of Power Season 2 is undeniably stunning, but even that cannot mask the glaring issues with the show's storytelling. It's as though the production team believed throwing more money at CGI and breathtaking landscapes could distract us from the hollow core of the series. But no amount of dazzling effects can fix a story so fundamentally broken.What's most painful is how this season feels like a betrayal of Tolkien's vision. Instead of embracing the deep themes of sacrifice, heroism, and corruption, the show opts for shallow thrills and spectacle. The lore is butchered, timelines are compressed in ways that make no sense, and beloved characters are reinterpreted to fit modern trends rather than staying true to the spirit of the source material.The Rings of Power Season 2 feels like a wasted opportunity-a superficial, disjointed attempt to capitalize on the popularity of Tolkien's world without understanding what made it special. Diehard fans and casual viewers alike will find little to enjoy here, except perhaps the stunning landscapes. Beyond that, it's a disappointing slog through a hollow shell of Middle-earth.

ipc-title__text: Flawed but much improved by the end of the season
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Its huge budget and much loved material made for an easy target for naysayers even before it was released. The first few episodes definitely didn't help it.I think the script writers were probably overwhelmed by the daunting task of turning appendices of Tolkien's writing into an actual Tolkien story. In the first few episodes there are too many parallel story lines, and worse some of the dialog is just bad. However, the cinematography is great and it does feel like Tolkien's world. All adaptations of known stories can struggle to create suspense. You watch to see how the narrative plays out, not discover what that narrative is. For Rings, a case in point, it's rather obvious who Sauron is very early on despite some failed attempts to persuade the viewer otherwise.The first season is clearly a set up for the full five. This has meant the writers have tried to subtlety work in the background for a great many future plot lines - many the writers will have invented to supplement the source material from Tolkien. Unfortunately, trying to pack so much setup into the first few episodes usually in chronological order means it's easy to get a bit lost; too much happens, yet also not enough.But it picks up hugely in the last three episodes. There are fewer competing storylines and for the first time there are some quotable lines of dialog that could be worthy of Tolkien. By episode six enough setup is in place they can focus on one main plot per episode, and one subplot. It's more coherent, well paced. The action picks up and the whole episode maintins a tension and excitement previous episodes only managed for fleeting moments. There are then origin stories for many of the key players/places/objects in the Lord of the Rings that play out over this episode and the last two.I feel the producers should have looked at these last three episodes and then revisited and heavily edited the first five to perhaps just three episodes. With these more condensed episodes each only have a maximum of two story lines. Use flashbacks if needed, and the long struggles can be communicated using a montage (and/or bonus material short films).In conclusion, the series is set up very well for an exciting second season. The major players are all introduced, and you want to know what happens next to them. The philosophy that power and power through technology corrupts has had a exciting narrative set ready for it. The writers are more comfortable with the responsibility of adding to Tolkien's legacy and the cast of major characters has been thinned and made more focussed. Most importantly, there's a lot that needs to happen.

ipc-title__text: A slow burn to brilliant brightness
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I'm one of those fans, who read the books in my childhood, the Silmarillion in my teens, adored the movies when they were released and has firmly placed The Fellowship of the Ring as my GOAT. ROP will never beat them (how can a TV series?), but this is a close as it can be.Slightly inferior to those classics of cinema, but massively superior to the Hobbit films. The narrative is vast and wide and yet narrow enough to keep you hooked and sticks to basics. As Tolkien always aimed, this is a tale of good vs evil. Simple and profound. This formula, plus the amazing film sets, costumes, acting makes for a classic show.It's a slow burner, but clearly on purpose. We've been promised 5 seasons and there's a few thousand years and a huge backstory to fill. The main cast are excellent, heroic figures in the same lineage as those we all know and love.I was moved to tears in episode six in the same way I was when the Rohan charged on the Orcs besieging Minas Tirith... I can speak highly enough of this show. I've waited 20yrs for something that comes close to the LOTR saga, and by episode six, all being well from here on in, I believe I've found it.

Some of the characters don't line up too well with how they are portrayed in the original lord of the rings but there is a lot of time between when this and that are set.I am happily continuing with an open mind. ipc-title__text: Flawed but much improved by the end of the season
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Its huge budget and much loved material made for an easy target for naysayers even before it was released. The first few episodes definitely didn't help it.I think the script writers were probably overwhelmed by the daunting task of turning appendices of Tolkien's writing into an actual Tolkien story. In the first few episodes there are too many parallel story lines, and worse some of the dialog is just bad. However, the cinematography is great and it does feel like Tolkien's world. All adaptations of known stories can struggle to create suspense. You watch to see how the narrative plays out, not discover what that narrative is. For Rings, a case in point, it's rather obvious who Sauron is very early on despite some failed attempts to persuade the viewer otherwise.The first season is clearly a set up for the full five. This has meant the writers have tried to subtlety work in the background for a great many future plot lines - many the writers will have invented to supplement the source material from Tolkien. Unfortunately, trying to pack so much setup into the first few episodes usually in chronological order means it's easy to get a bit lost; too much happens, yet also not enough.But it picks up hugely in the last three episodes. There are fewer competing storylines and for the first time there are some quotable lines of dialog that could be worthy of Tolkien. By episode six enough setup is in place they can focus on one main plot per episode, and one subplot. It's more coherent, well paced. The action picks up and the whole episode maintins a tension and excitement previous episodes only managed for fleeting moments. There are then origin stories for many of the key players/places/objects in the Lord of the Rings that play out over this episode and the last two.I feel the producers should have looked at these last three episodes and then revisited and heavily edited the first five to perhaps just three episodes. With these more condensed episodes each only have a maximum of two story lines. Use flashbacks if needed, and the long struggles can be communicated using a montage (and/or bonus material short films).In conclusion, the series is set up very well for an exciting second season. The major players are all introduced, and you want to know what happens next to them. The philosophy that power and power through technology corrupts has had a exciting narrative set ready for it. The writers are more comfortable with the responsibility of adding to Tolkien's legacy and the cast of major characters has been thinned and made more focussed. Most importantly, there's a lot that needs to happen.

ipc-title__text: A slow burn to brilliant brightness
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I'm one of those fans, who read the books in my childhood, the Silmarillion in my teens, adored the movies when they were released and has firmly placed The Fellowship of the Ring as my GOAT. ROP will never beat them (how can a TV series?), but this is a close as it can be.Slightly inferior to those classics of cinema, but massively superior to the Hobbit films. The narrative is vast and wide and yet narrow enough to keep you hooked and sticks to basics. As Tolkien always aimed, this is a tale of good vs evil. Simple and profound. This formula, plus the amazing film sets, costumes, acting makes for a classic show.It's a slow burner, but clearly on purpose. We've been promised 5 seasons and there's a few thousand years and a huge backstory to fill. The main cast are excellent, heroic figures in the same lineage as those we all know and love.I was moved to tears in episode six in the same way I was when the Rohan charged on the Orcs besieging Minas Tirith... I can speak highly enough of this show. I've waited 20yrs for something that comes close to the LOTR saga, and by episode six, all being well from here on in, I believe I've found it.

That being said I do think things could have got going a little sooner and bits of the first few episodes did seem a little weak.Cinematography is great and the special effects are top notch - it looks amazing. Really cool to see some of the different factions in their earlier days. Some of the characters don't line up too well with how they are portrayed in the original lord of the rings but there is a lot of time between when this and that are set.I am happily continuing with an open mind. Really hope they continue with the high their budget. Lots of potential.
